articles.title: The good news out of Cop31? That most of the world’s governments said no to an agreement stripped of meaning | Bill Hare
articles.summary:
Co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia, which is exporting climate pain

The failure of Cop31 in Antalya was a line in the sand moment, a victory for multiculturalism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no. The text they rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels.

The good news is that most of the world’s governments rejected an agreement stripped of meaning. And the power of one particular fossil fuel producer, Saudi Arabia, needs particular scrutiny. What we also know is that co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia. It didn’t work.

articles.title: I covered myself in sleep trackers to find the very best
articles.summary:
Get a better night’s sleep with monitoring and guidance from smartwatches, smart rings, smart bands and sleep earbuds

The best sleep masks and best Bluetooth sleep masks

Getting quality sleep is just as crucial as getting enough sleep. And how you feel in the morning only tells part of the story. Smartwatches, smart bands, smart rings and sleep earbuds can all help fill in the details: how long it took you to doze off, how long you spent in deep sleep, how restless you were, your resting heart rate, even if you have night-time breathing difficulties.

Armed with this information, you can learn how your lifestyle affects your sleep. Maybe your after dinner cappuccino triggers a night of tossing and turning, or you’re more restful after evening workouts. As the wise GI Joe once said, knowing is half the battle. And the more you know about your sleep, the better chance you have of improving it.

articles.title: Cop31 as it happened: EU and others reject deal as longest climate summit comes to fractious end
articles.summary:

Full report: Cop31 climate talks set to end in deep division as key deal rejected

Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, has been looking through the text and says: “This latest text is a total mess and countries should throw it out. It fails to deliver vital climate finance to the vulnerable while promoting far-fetched and eye wateringly expensive carbon removal technologies which is a gift to the fossil fuel industry.

“A sign of how useless the latest cover text is can be seen in the feeble language. It ‘recognises’ the crisis 40 times, ‘recalls’ previous decisions 15 times yet ‘decides’ on action only 5 times. articles.title: Burnham’s public control push is ‘code for renationalisation’, CBI boss warns
articles.summary:
Andy Burnham’s pledge to expand public control “sounds like code for renationalisation”, the boss of Britain’s most influential business group has warned, as she called on the Prime Minister to clarify that private investment would boost growth.

At the body’s flagship conference on Monday, Confederation of British Industry chief Rain Newton-Smith will warn the Prime Minister against sidelining investors in his 10-year plan address in December.

The industry grandee will argue that employers back ambitions to reduce youth unemployment and advancing devolution – but needed “reassurance” that the government would not stamp out the private sector.

“To some, ‘public control’ sounds like code for renationalisation,” Newton-Smith will tell CBI member organisations that include some of the biggest listed companies, banks and manufacturers in the country.

“That is kryptonite to investment. We know that’s not what’s coming – but give us the reassurance we need. Show this is a model built on partnership, not primacy, that the government wants private capital at the table – not heading for the exit.”

‘Burden of doubt’ hangs over public control plans

The CBI’s annual conference is set to feature addresses from top government figures and opposition leaders, plus the likes of Alan Milburn, who led the recent youth unemployment review, and Heathrow chief executive Thomas Woldbye.

In an opening speech, Newton-Smith is expected to say that people across the country had been “too ready to talk ourselves down”, praising Burnham for bringing a “dose of hopes to our politics”.

But she will warn that the UK is stuck in a “financial straitjacket” due to a sky-high tax burden, a range of spending demands and threats to borrowing costs.

She will argue that John Healey’s recent Budget “left too many question marks over our economy” before saying that upcoming decisions at the Spending Review and Burnham’s 10-year plan should provide “action” to lift economic spirits.

“The biggest challenge is not the burden of one tax or regulation – it’s the burden of doubt,” Newton-Smith will say.

“We need more than mañana – because time wasted is investment lost. We have the answers. We know how to electrify. So use the 10-year plan to show how we start delivering, work with us to get British business competing again.”

Burnham’s AI gamble

Burnham’s speech is scheduled to take place before a Christmas break although a date has not yet been agreed.

The government is taking advice from a range of experts both from within the government and at independent groups to lay out plans for “greater public control” and re-wiring the state.

Over the next year, the UK is set to take the G20 presidency. Burnham has said he wanted to write up an “AI code” to be adhered to by the world’s largest economies.

Newton-Smith will say that widespread adoption could turn “British business into global companies” and that the UK could still “catch the economic lightning” from advances in technology.

articles.title: Slumping London flat prices spark landlord return
articles.summary:
Falling flat prices and rapidly rising rental returns are drawing buy-to-let investors back to London’s property market.

Surging rents and cheaper prices for property purchases are leading to landlords buying flats in London at their quickest rate in recent years.

According to estate agent Hamptons, the share of investors based in the capital purchasing flats in London has spiked to an 11-year high to 39 per cent, up from 34 per cent last year, as reported by the Telegraph.

Analysis by the estate agent shows gross rental yields on freshly purchased London flats have risen to 7 per cent, up from 6 per cent last year and the highest recorded level since Hamptons began its dataset in 2015.

Alongside this, the amount of landlords seeing 10 per cent yields on flats has more than doubled, with the share of landlords climbing from 7 per cent in 2025 to 15 per cent this year.

It marks the first time the figure has reached double digits since at least 2025, and stands against the share just being 1 per cent five years ago.

Hamptons’ research director, Aneisha Beveridge, said higher yields “seem to be tempting some investors back into parts of the London market, particularly where prices have adjusted but rents remain strong..”

The data suggests the government’s buy-to-let crackdown, which was launched a decade ago with a three-percentage-point stamp duty surcharge on any additional homes, might be running out of steam in the capital.

Healey’s landlord crackdown on rental income

In his maiden Autumn Budget, chancellor John Healey set out a crackdown on landlords as the UK government looks to increase tax rates on rental income.

Property experts and estate agents told City AM in October that John Healey’s hike to tax on rental income is the latest blow in an assault on landlords, which is already pushing many in the capital to sell up.

articles.title: British Airways owner tells Burnham Heathrow’s third runway ‘doomed to failure’
articles.summary:
The owner of British Airways’ parent company has told Andy Burnham Heathrow airport’s proposed expansion is not affordable in its current form and is “doomed to failure.”

Luis Gallego, chief executive of International Airlines Group (IAG) raised concerns over the £49bn expansion plans for Heathrow’s third runway in a letter to the prime minister, according to The Times.

IAG, which also owns Aer Lingus, Vueling, and Iberia, said in the letter it and Heathrow have been unable to close a £19bn gap between the airport’s predicted costs of the expansion and what IAG believes passengers would be willing to pay through hiked airport charges.

“Unfortunately, in our view and given our knowledge of a market that is so important to us, we are convinced that the preferred scheme for expansion to date is too expensive and, as it stands, is unaffordable and doomed to failure,” Gallego said in the letter.

Private investment ‘will not be enough’

Gallego said the airline group still supports expanding Heathrow, but warned private investment alone would not meet the amount needed to fund the scheme at an acceptable cost.

He told Burnham that “if we want to move forward with the current project, private investment will not be enough.”

IAG has suggested using extra air passenger duty revenues yielded by the expansion to help fund construction costs, or direct government investment to help cover land purchases and finance early engineering work.

Gallego also pushed back on Burnham’s claim the expansion was “a matter for London and Londoners” and said it was a “project of national importance that will benefit every region and nation of the UK.”

A Heathrow spokesperson said: “We welcome IAG’s support for a third runway and are working more closely than ever with airlines to make expansion affordable.”

“We’ve made good progress in narrowing the gap, but there’s more to do. We’re going through the plans together line by line, challenging costs and stripping out anything that doesn’t deliver value.

Expansion must be affordable for airlines and passengers, as well as financeable for investors, and we’re determined to deliver it.”

articles.title: ‘Accept Brexit and move on’, Theresa May warns Burnham
articles.summary:
Former prime minister Theresa May has warned Andy Burnham must “accept Brexit and move on”.

Speaking to the BBC, May said she was “aghast” that the prime minister could be considering rejoining the EU after he said at the Brussels summit this week he wanted to “brainstorm” ideas on the future of Britain’s relationship with the bloc.

May, who was prime minister between 2016 to 2019 before being forced to resign after failing to complete a Brexit deal after spending three years negotiating one, urged Burnham to “just get on” with today’s challenges rather than rehashing Brexit conversations.

“When I was prime minister I was very clear, we should deliver on that vote. So I’m afraid my message to him really is, you know, people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on,” May said.

Speaking to the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, May said Burnham “wants to pat people on the head” by suggesting Brits “got it wrong” with the vote.

May, who was replaced by Boris Johnson after her tenure as prime minister, said:  “What I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that have to be put in – it’s across the whole of government.”

“It’s not just prime ministerial time, cabinet ministers’ time, officials’ time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations. Because you have to negotiate hard in order to make sure that you’re getting out what you want,” she said.

May added: “And that’s one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU. And also we, as a country, we voted for Brexit.”

Burnham agrees youth migration for 100,000 to UK

On Friday at the Brussels summit, Burnham agreed to allow 100,000 young people from EU nations to spend three years travelling, working or studying in Britain in an agreement that could face intense scrutiny.

Burnham argued that a wide-ranging deal with the EU tackled the “biggest challenges of our time” as he hailed alignment on food standards and carbon emissions markets, plus efforts to share data on illegal migration.

articles.title: Sandpapergate: Cricket Australia can’t keep ducking a fresh independent inquiry
articles.summary:
Getting to the bottom of things is part of the job of a litigation lawyer. The same can be said for police officers, investigative journalists and even doctors in search of a diagnosis. A question being posed Down Under is whether it is also part of the job for Cricket Australia.

In 2018, during a Test match between South Africa and Australia in Cape Town, the Australian fielder Cameron Bancroft was caught by TV cameras applying sandpaper to roughen up one side of the ball so it would move more in the air. This was cheating.

Cricket Australia conducted an immediate investigation and relatively quickly singled out three players for punishment. Bancroft, the captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner (all batsmen) were banned for between nine months and a year.

However, questions remained. Why were no bowlers found to have been involved? It was the bowlers who would exploit the altered condition of the ball.

In 2021, following some unwelcome media coverage, the bowling group issued a denial around the use of sandpaper on the field of play.

Now Usman Khawaja says the whole team knew about the scheme. Bancroft says he deliberately withheld evidence of the team’s wider knowledge from the original investigation. Chadd Sayers, a fast bowler, says he took sandpaper off the field during the previous Test at Port Elizabeth and was never interviewed as part of the original investigation.

Pat Cummins, now Australia’s captain, continues to deny knowing about the scheme.

Cricket Australia today is run by different people, who were not involved in the previous investigation. Failing to re-examine what happened runs a serious risk of digging an even deeper hole.

Cricket Australia has proposed a “forum” where players and staff can come forward to give their accounts of what happened. This, however, is a mistake.

While led by an independent lawyer, it is voluntary and confidential. There has even been a suggestion that different versions of the truth may be contemplated.

Why a new Sandpapergate inquiry is unavoidable

What Cricket Australia should do is set up a fresh, truly independent inquiry. Such a process would start by looking at how the original investigation was run and what it was trying to achieve.

Who was interviewed? Who was left out and why? What documents were called for, what was handed over and what has been preserved? The investigators should have access to the original interview records and match footage, and their remit should cover both Tests.

It is surely important to establish why Bancroft chose to hold back information (if indeed he did), whether he was encouraged to do so and, if so, by whom. If the wider group did know about the sandpaper, did the three players who were singled out take a disproportionate share of the blame?

The investigators should test the reliability of the evidence, give those they propose to criticise a fair chance to respond and publish reasoned findings. The findings may be painful for Cricket Australia, but it is essential for the integrity of the organisation going forward that they should be aired.

Indeed, by failing to do this, Cricket Australia risks an external intervention which could be far more uncomfortable.

If this were happening in England and the same scandal was engulfing the England and Wales Cricket Board, I suspect there might be calls for parliamentary intervention. The House of Commons could require the attendance of witnesses and the production of documents – and it may not be long before an Australian senator triggers a move for an inquiry of a similar sort.

One thing is clear: if Cricket Australia does not grip Sandpapergate now, it will forever be a blight on both its game and its administration.

Simon Bushell is senior partner at Seladore Legal and has extensive experience in complex cross-border disputes and investigations.

articles.title: Inflation voters’ top concern as Iran war bites
articles.summary:
A vicious bout of inflation set off by the US’s war in Iran is now British voters’ top concern, according a closely follwed poll that laid bare the scale of economic pessimism that continues to stalk the UK.

Nearly four in 10 (37 per cent) UK adults listed price rises as a big issue facing the country, according to a poll by Ipsos, taking it level with immigration as the issue households are most concerned about.

The score is the highest level recorded since August 2023, when the country was still recovering from a wave of double-digit inflation unleashed by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

“With levels of inflation in Britain reaching a year-long high this month, it is perhaps no surprise that we see a sharp rise in public concern about inflation,” Ipsos research director Mike Clemence said. “It is now as big an issue for the public as immigration, which has been the front-runner issue for much of 2026.”

Inflation adds to economic pessimism

Last month, the Bank of England chose to raise interest rates for the first time in three years in a bid to get ahead of an acceleration price pressure at the start of next year. Inflation is on course to reach nearly four per cent in May, double the Bank’s two per cent target, driven largely by ballooning energy costs from elevated oil prices.

Bills are expected to jump by some 26 per cent in January, when the energy price cap next changes, sparking speculation rate-setters may look to tighten monetary policy again at their next decision in December.

The Ipsos poll, which is the longest running gauge of public concerns in the UK, also found economic pessimism remained rife among voters. Just 13 per cent expect the economy to improve over the next 12 moths, compared with 67 per cent who believe it will get worse.

The finding provides a net economic optimism score of -54, four points lower than October’s figure of -50, researchers said.

“As we approach the end of the year, economic optimism remains weak with two-thirds expecting Britain’s economic performance to worsen,” Clemence added. “This suggests economic and inflationary concerns are likely to remain elevated into the New Year.”

articles.title: Exclusive: Timms welfare review to dismiss change to Pip eligibility
articles.summary:
A government-led review into disability payments will not demand a tightening on eligibility to claims, according to people briefed on the matter, setting Andy Burnham up for a clash between welfare reform for under 25-year-olds and other adults. 

Sir Stephen Timms’ welfare review, which is set to be published on Tuesday, will suggest that claimants of  disability benefits should not be compelled to take up support offered to help people into work, volunteering or other activities, City AM understands.

People claiming personal independence payments (Pips) should also retain access to cash support, the report is expected to conclude. Timms, who is the disability minister, was not mandated to deliver savings ahead of writing the report as he was told to publish findings according to existing projected spending levels. 

The total welfare bill excluding pensioner spending is set to total about £183bn this year, with the Office for Budget Responsibility showing that Pips contribute to about £50bn of the spending figure. Disability benefits are also set to grow as a share of GDP between the years 2026 and 2032. 

Both the Milburn and Timms reviews’ reflections on spending figures have come into focus due to the rise in borrowing costs, a near-record high tax burden and pressures for the Chancellor to fund defence and public infrastructure around the country.

Ahead of the report’s publication, the Institute for Fiscal Studies’ senior research economist Eduin Latimer said that report “should expect claimant numbers to rise and therefore be clear about how eligibility or generosity would be reduced in order to control the costs of the system”.

Burnham’s welfare ‘philosophy’

Timms’ recommendations could put Burnham in a difficult position after the Prime Minister suggested he wanted to apply the “philosophy” behind Alan Milburn’s report on youth unemployment to the wider welfare system. 

Earlier this week, Milburn recommended that benefits for young people should be cut by about £3.6bn a year by tightening eligibility criteria, which could involve some people with anxiety, depression or ADHD to “get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system”. 

Cuts to benefits on the health element of Universal Credit will be superseded by a near-£6bn injection of investment in employment support under Milburn’s plans. 

The Tony Blair-era health secretary has now been appointed to a government role to lead reforms of the welfare and employment system for those aged between 16 and 24. 

On Friday morning, it was reported in the Financial Times that there could be reforms introduced to distinguish different health conditions. 

The Timms review has focused on increasing capacity for face-to-face assessments, ensuring that people can access the welfare system by easier means, and curb the number of reviews for people with lifelong or degenerative conditions. 

Tricky territory for Labour

The disability minister was commissioned to write the year-long review after Labour backbenchers rebelled against Sir Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves’ plans to slash the benefits bill by about £5bn in mid-2025. 

The cuts divided the party and severely weakened support for the former Prime Minister. 

Cabinet ministers Louise Haigh and Anneliese Midgley were in the 127-strong rebel group that  signed an amendment opposing the cuts. 

Burnham has insisted he wanted to “get the welfare bill down” but would not impose “crude cuts”. 

Opposition figures have meanwhile pledged drastic welfare reforms in order to fund proposed tax cuts. 

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whateley has pledged to cut the bill by £36bn if the Tories are elected, mainly by tightening eligibility for claimants, slashing access to some foreign nationals and re-introducing a two-child benefit cap. 

Reform UK has meanwhile promised to cut the bill by £50bn through more radical reforms. 

A DWP spokesperson said: “Supporting disabled people to participate fully in life will always be our top priority.

“The Timms Review interim report made clear, PIP is no longer fit for purpose.

“When the final report is published, we will consider the recommendations alongside the Milburn review.”

articles.title: Image rights: HMRC’s new tax rules for footballers take the biscuit
articles.summary:
As well-known sports personalities, footballers can make a lot of money from exploiting their image, especially in the age of social media. As a bonus, they can put structures in place to minimise the tax take on these earnings.

Not for much longer, though. HMRC has been scrutinising these arrangements, and from April 2028, new rules mean revenue from image rights “related to an employment” (ie: deriving from their club activities) will be treated as employment income. As a result, payments will be subject to PAYE and National Insurance Contributions (NICs) for both player and club.

While sensible on paper, this raises questions over implementation: what do the new rules catch, and who polices them?

Why image rights can be lucrative – for the taxman

Consider the tax at stake when a footballer receives £100,000 from their club for image rights exploitation. Currently, the club can claim it as an allowable expense, saving Corporation Tax, and the payment goes into the player’s image rights company, attracting Corporation Tax at 25 per cent.

Treated as employment income, the payment would cost the club NICs at 15 per cent, and cost the player tax and NICs at 47 per cent.

No wonder HMRC wants to change the rules: it expects additional tax receipts of £40m-£45m annually from 2028, plus an extra £10m in the preceding two tax years, presumably due to agreements being amended ahead of time.

The rules go beyond payments from clubs to players, and cover third-party payments arranged or facilitated by the club or received “by reason of… employment”. But the scope of the legislation’s wording here is uncertain and open to interpretation that ultimately will be settled by the courts.

However, HMRC’s guidance sets out its view: a player obtaining the club’s permission to enter a third-party agreement would not be caught by the rules, nor would an employer simply providing a player with contact details to a brand.

Yet if a club recommends or selects a player for an opportunity, negotiates on a player’s behalf, or receives remuneration as part of any agreement, this would fall within the new rules. Clubs must be careful in their dealings with brands to ensure they do not inadvertently breach these conditions.

Fair play?

HMRC provided an example that considerably widens the potential scope of the rules. In its hypothetical scenario, a club wins the league for the first time, prompting a local biscuit brand to sponsor the captain.

The biscuit brand is named after the same location as the club, uses similar colours in its branding as the club, and uses the term “for winners” in its advertising. HMRC says this is sufficient for sponsorship payments to be treated as employment income, even though the club was not involved in the agreement in any way.

But how is the club to know of its obligations in this situation? Should it check all output involving players for potential links that could create a tax charge? What if the biscuit brand’s colour scheme was already similar to the club’s? Is it possible that different tax outcomes could arise for a team captain who has won numerous trophies to another that won just one, and is this fair?

Some would argue that, rather than the sponsorship being based on team achievements, success on the pitch enhanced the individual players’ image: therefore, exploitation is not team (or employment)-specific.

HMRC guidance is not law, merely its interpretation of the legislation. The courts will decide how these rules are applied.

The taxman’s strict approach may be designed to encourage an overly cautious approach from clubs: after all, they expect to raise £10m before the rules are even introduced.

What happens next will be closely watched by everyone with skin in the game.

Adam Jefferies is a Private Client Director at PKF Littlejohn.

articles.title: JP Morgan boss Jamie Dimon to set ‘example’ after Healey’s bank tax hike
articles.summary:
The boss of JP Morgan has warned he will seek to claw back the costs of John Healey’s bank tax hike after branding the move “unfair”.

Jamie Dimon, regarded as one of the most influential figures in finance, said at an event in London on Thursday he would look to find ways to offset the Chancellor’s tax rise on the banking sector.

Healey doubled the UK banking surcharge, which sits on top of corporation tax, to six per cent in his Budget for a 15 month period to strum up cash for an energy support package.

Dimon said he plans to set “an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”.

He added that any move to offset the bank tax would be “more in sorrow” than anger, in comments first reported by the Financial Times. He did not specify what areas he would target to claw back costs.

JP Morgan quickly became one of the most vocal critics in the aftermath of Healey’s Budget. The lender said at the time that the tax increase “lacks principle” and hit out at Labour for singling out the banking sector.

Budget watchdog warned bank profits could be driven overseas

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) has forecast the hike will raise around £1.5bn, with surcharge receipts pulling in £2.4bn in 2027. But the watchdog warned around £190m in receipts would be wiped out as some banks move profits out of the UK in response to the higher rate. It added that the total size of profits lost was “uncertain”.

JP Morgan has laid out plans for a new mega-tower in Canary Wharf, which is expected to inject £10bn into the local economy and create 7,800 industry jobs.

Dimon warned ahead of the Budget that any tax increases on the industry would have “adverse consequences”.

The Wall Street giant also has a major campus in Bournemouth, where it employs some 5,300 staff processing more than $1tn of global transactions each day.

There was speculation ahead of the Budget that the banking surcharge could be returned to its eight per cent rate. Share prices rallied following Healey’s announcement as the tax hike came in lower than expected.

David Postings, the boss of trade body UK Finance, told a City audience this week: “It may be a smaller increase than some called for but a tax rise is still a tax rise, making an already uncompetitive regime even less competitive.”

JP Morgan declined to comment.

articles.title: City of London Christmas lights: Lord Mayor switches on Cheapside as King Kenny lights up Fleet Street
articles.summary:
The Lord Mayor of the City of London Bronek Masojada this week switched on the Cheapside Christmas lights at the Royal Exchange before a crowd of City workers, with St Paul’s Cathedral’s children’s choir singing.

The lights went on at the grand Royal Exchange pillars and six festive trees around Bank Junction, as well as installations along Cheapside and Threadneedle Street.

The event was run by Cheapside Business Alliance, the City’s first Business Improvement District (BID) in collaboration with the Royal Exchange, Fortnum & Mason, St Paul’s Cathedral, Mansion House and the Bank of England.

St Paul’s Cathedral’s children’s choir on the steps of the Royal Exchange (Cheapside Business Alliance)

Cheapside Christmas lights: A first for the Royal Exchange

Charlotte Fletcher, chair of Cheapside Business Alliance, said: “It’s wonderful to see so many of you here for the first Cheapside lights switch-on at the Royal Exchange, and the start of the festive season in the heart of the City, [where] Cheapside has brought together history, business and community for centuries.”

The lights on the Royal Exchange’s columns were funded by owner The Ardent Companies and the building’s retailers, and designed by Fier & Folk. Fortnum & Mason decorated the Christmas tree, which was funded by Cheapside Business Alliance.

The Royal Exchange Christmas tree, decorated by Fortnum & Mason (Cheapside Business Alliance)

Choirs, carols and mince pies

St Paul’s Cathedral’s children’s choir performed before and after the countdown. Gospel group Keynotes Choir, who have performed with Emeli Sandé and Sam Smith, then did an hour-long set, and singer Emmanuel Kelly closed the night with his new single, Christmas Love (Marry Me). Fortnum & Mason handed out hot chocolate, mulled wine and mince pies.

Gospel group Keynotes Choir performed an hour-long set (Cheapside Business Alliance)

Fleet Street Quarter Christmas lights

The next evening King Kenny – best known from The Traitors – switched on Fleet Street Quarter’s lights at Ludgate Circus alongside Lady Lucy French OBE, chief executive of Fleet Street Quarter.

The event also launched the Dennis & Gnasher Mega Mischief Trail, 12 sculptures made with Beano and Wild in Art to mark 75 years of Dennis the Menace, which runs until 15 January 2027.

French said: “Fleet Street has been home to Beano since 1938.”

King Kenny said: “As a Londoner, it’s an honour to switch on my first Christmas lights in the city.”

King Kenny and Lady Lucy French OBE at the Fleet Street Quarter switch-on (David Parry/Assignments/PA)

The City of London Christmas lights switch-ons follow Davina McCall lighting up London’s tallest Christmas tree last week.

articles.title: Brexit: Rejoin and leave campaigns can’t win with yesterday’s arguments
articles.summary:
Brexit is back on the agenda, but research shows leave and rejoin campaigners will need new arguments to win over today’s voters, says Morgan Jones

Today, as you will likely be aware, the EU-UK summit will be taking place in. It’s the most tangible step so far in Andy Burnham’s re-opening of the conversation about rejoining the bloc. The Prime Minister’s clear language about the failures of Brexit indicates that this is likely to be a key theme over the coming years and indeed at the next general election. In response to this new push to rejoin, we have also seen the launch of new campaigns, “Stay Out” – more Tory aligned – and “Enough Official” – more Reform aligned – which will look to strengthen and re-affirm the leave case. Despite its triumph at the ballot box a decade ago, most polling now suggests that a plurality of Brits favour rejoining and a majority consider Brexit a mistake.

At Persuasion UK, we aim to get behind headline figures like this and test, as much as is possible, how they translate when mapped onto the messy processes of the real world. Testing opinion on Brexit is exactly the kind of thing that requires this approach, because so much of what people feel about being in or out of Europe was created through the process of the referendum and subsequent debates. As political scientists Sarah Hobolt and James Tilley have compellingly argued, Brexit created, rather than brought to the fore, the tribes of “leaver” and “remainer”. How will the toplines we’re currently seeing – where the success of Brexit is rated catastrophically low even by leave voters, and where demographics alone swing the population into a pro-EU position – be acted on by a live campaign? What issues can we expect to be most salient?

Voter exhaustion

The main beat “Stay Out” hit in their first press release was about the increased cost of membership of the EU. The figures at the heart of this – not unlike certain other numbers associated with the leave cause – are disputed, but our research clearly showed that budget contributions are an area of significant concern for the public, with hostile media on this sinking rejoin numbers by nine points amongst the sample shown them. Any suggestion that Britain might have to join the Euro is also a point of real difficulty. However, despite the centrality of immigration in “Enough Official”’s launch video, our research suggests free movement clearly no longer provides the attack line it did a decade ago. While immigration might have been at the core of the case Farage and others made about the EU in the 2010s, our testing suggests it would not be particularly potent at destabilising rejoin sympathies today, particularly given people’s deep frustrations with increased barriers to travel since Brexit.

One area of concern for rejoiners, which might be described as process rather than policy, is voter exhaustion. In our research, the longer you tell people a process of negotiating and rejoining will be, the less appealing it is. This chimed with things I found while writing a book on the People’s Vote campaign: the committed activists campaigning for a new referendum often struggled to internalise the fact that even if many people basically agreed with them, their primary preference was to simply have the whole thing over and done with.

A lot has changed in ten years. Both sides of the issue will have to learn to play new games and make new arguments. Arguably this is even more true for the leave side, simply because arguments which were successful beforehand are naturally more tempting than those which failed you. But any campaign re-heating past points will quickly find that yesterday’s arguments don’t necessarily map onto today’s political terrain.

Morgan Jones is the deputy director of Persuasion UK and the author of “No Second Chances: The inside story of the campaign for a second EU referendum

articles.title: Anthropic shares plunge as AI fears erase debut gains
articles.summary:
Anthropic’s shares plunged at market open on Friday, as investors’ fears over the AI boom wiped away most of the gains from its record-breaking debut.

The Claude maker’s shares fell as much as 10 per cent per cent to $87.8 (£66.9) after Wall Street’s opening bell, a sharp reversal from its 17 per cent surge on Thursday.

Anthropic’s shares opened 33.4 per cent higher than its IPO price yesterday at $111, before easing somewhat to close at $97.1.

But the decline extended in early trading on Friday, as the AI lab was swept up in a tech-wide rout that has dominated global equity markets for the past week.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 was down 1.5 per cent in early trades, while the S&P 500 tumbled 0.4.

Dashing hopes

Anthropic’s listing was initially billed as a defining moment for the AI boom and wider global markets, giving investors the chance to gain exposure to a company at technology’s frontier.

But analysts said its debut would likely not be enough to dissipate growing fears on the sustainability of the debt-fuelled boom.

Neil WIlson, UK investor strategist at Saxo, said: “It was a pretty brutal selloff across tech… the strength of the Anthropic IPO couldn’t mask the wider trouble facing the tech and AI ecosystem in terms of raw sentiment. “

Chipmaker Nvidia, which has been embroiled in reports that former chief executive Jensen Huang committed multiple extramarital relationships including one with a Chinese spy, fell 3.8 per cent to $140.3. It is down

Meanwhile Broadcom and Micron slid 2.6 per cent and 6.9 per cent.

Anthropic pressed ahead with its debut despite the Democrats’ resounding US midterm victory. The result triggered a wave of investor concerns that the rapid expansion of data centres would slow, atter their build-out became a flashpoint in several key Senate campaigns.

Shaking Asia

Investors’ worries over the longevity of the boom seeped into Asia, triggering losses in tech-heavy indexes.

“It’s probably too much to call this a melt-down, but to say that investor sentiment has started to sour is an understatement,” said David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation.

“Anthropic may have debuted with an impressive premium… but it didn’t take long for most of it to dissipate. Asian-Pacific markets followed through, taking their lead from Wall Street’s hefty selloff yesterday, and posted some thumping losses.”

Earlier, South Korea’s Kospi plunged 5.2 per cent, bringing its monthly losses to 15 per cent.

Index heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix led the decline, shedding 7.1 per cent and 5.8 per cent respectively.

In Japan, the Nikkei 225 slid 5.1 per cent, as Soft Bank plunged 14.8 per cent to 3,025 yen (£1.7).

Jitters also spread over to Taiwan, home of star chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC).

The Taiex plunged 6.2 per cent, as it heads towards its biggest weekly decline since 1991. TSMC suffered a 4.7 per cent decline.

articles.title: Range Rover Electric costs £19,000 less in tax than the V8
articles.summary:
The first electric Range Rover costs more to buy than the V8, but a company car driver paying 40% would hand HMRC around £19,000 a year less. Wednesday’s Budget has now set company car tax rates up to 2030/31, and the gap only grows.

The Range Rover Electric went on sale in September from £154,070, about £8,900 more than the £145,145 V8 Autobiography. Run one as a company car and a 40% taxpayer pays around £2,465 a year in company car tax, against almost £21,500 for the V8.

Add charging, road tax and the Congestion Charge for a weekday commute into central London, and our sums put the electric car’s yearly bill at about £6,500, against nearly £29,500 for the V8. Your employer will pick up some of those bills, but the company car tax comes straight out of your pay.

Even the plug-in hybrid, the obvious alternative, costs more in tax this year and far more from 2028. Our figures assume 10,000 miles a year, charging at home and 230 working days driving into the zone, and they use this tax year’s rates.

What the Budget means for Range Rover drivers

Wednesday’s Budget left company car tax alone for the next four years and added rates for 2030/31, when electric cars move to 10%, plug-in hybrids to 20% and the V8’s band to 40%, according to the Treasury’s published rates.

Road tax rises with inflation from April 2027, taking the standard rate from £200 to £210 and the V8’s first-year bill from £5,690 to £5,950. The 3p-a-mile pay-per-mile charge for electric cars still starts in April 2028, and the Budget documents contain nothing on the heavy car tax that had been rumoured beforehand.

Two smaller changes affect running costs. The 0% VAT on home electricity now runs to the end of June 2027, which keeps home charging cheap, and the 5p cut in fuel duty lasts until the same date, so petrol prices shouldn’t jump before then either.

Range Rover Electric price and specs

Orders are open now. The Autobiography opens the range at £154,070 and the First Edition costs £157,610. Prices then climb through the SV (£176,230) and SV Black (£190,320) to £225,240 for the long-wheelbase SV Black, with SV Ultra prices still to come.

Range Rover quotes 542bhp from two electric motors, a 118.5kWh battery and an official range of up to 372 miles, which it reckons means around 333 miles in everyday driving.

City AM’s Richard Aucock drove it briefly at JLR’s Gaydon proving ground. He found it quieter and smoother than most electric cars, and came away convinced it felt more luxurious than any Range Rover before it.

Range Rover Electric company car tax

Company car tax is charged on a percentage of the list price. For 2026/27 that’s 4% for an electric car and 37% for anything emitting 160g/km of CO2 or more, and the V8 is rated at 261g/km.

So a 40% taxpayer pays about £2,465 a year in the electric car and £21,481 in the V8, and a 45% taxpayer £2,773 and £24,167. Your employer saves too, because its 15% National Insurance on the benefit falls from about £8,100 to about £920 a year, which tends to catch a finance director’s eye.

Company car tax for a 40% taxpayer

Tax Year ElectricPlug-in-hybirdV8

2026/27£2,465 (4%)£3,878 (7%)£21,481 (37%)

2027/28£3,081 (5%)£4,432 (8%)£21,481 (37%)

2028/29£4,314 (7%)£9,972 (18%)£22,062 (38%)

2029/30£5,547 (9%)£10,526 (19%)£22,643 (39%)

2030/31£6,163 (10%)£11,080 (20%)
£23,223 (40%)

Even in 2030/31, when the electric rate reaches 10%, the electric car still saves about £17,000 a year over the V8.

Range Rover Electric vs the plug-in hybrid

Most company car drivers will weigh the electric car against the P550e plug-in hybrid, which costs around £138,500 in Autobiography trim. Its electric range of around 70 miles puts it in the 7% band this year, so a 40% taxpayer pays about £3,880, roughly £1,400 more than in the electric car, and it pays the full £18 Congestion Charge too.

The gap opens up in April 2028, when every plug-in hybrid moves to 18% however far it goes on electricity, and the Budget has now confirmed 20% for 2030/31. Over the four tax years to 2029/30, the hybrid would cost a 40% taxpayer about £28,800 in company car tax against £15,400 for the electric car, so anyone signing a four-year lease now should base the decision on the 2028 rates.

Range Rover Electric charging costs

Range Rover quotes official efficiency of up to 2.8 miles per kWh, so 10,000 miles uses about 3,570kWh. On an off-peak home tariff of around 9p per kWh that costs about £320, and on a standard tariff at the 26p price cap it’s about £940.

Public rapid chargers cost far more. They averaged 79p per kWh in September, according to Zapmap, which would push the bill to about £2,800 and wipe out most of the fuel saving.

The V8 manages up to 24.6mpg officially, so with petrol at around 174p a litre the same 10,000 miles costs about £3,200. Neither car will match its official figures in real driving, so expect your own bills to come in a little higher.

Range Rover Electric road tax

The electric car pays £10 in its first year, then £640 a year from years two to six. That’s the £200 standard rate plus the £440 Expensive Car Supplement, which applies to electric cars costing more than £50,000.

The V8 pays the same £640 from year two, but its first-year bill is £5,690 because it emits more than 255g/km, rising to £5,950 for cars registered from April 2027. On a company car that first-year bill usually lands with the employer.

Does the Range Rover Electric pay the Congestion Charge?

It does. Electric cars lost their exemption at the end of 2025, and since 2 January they’ve paid £13.50 a day when registered for Auto Pay, which is 25% off the £18 charge TfL has the details.

Over 230 working days that’s £3,105, against £4,140 for the V8 or the hybrid, a saving of about £1,035 a year. The discount drops to 12.5% from 4 March 2030.

Range Rover Electric running costs compared

Yearly cost from year two, company car, 40% taxpayer

Range Rover ElectricRange Rover V8 Autobiography

Company car tax£2,465£21,481

Charging or fuel, 10,000 miles£320 (home, off-peak)£3,216

Road tax, years two to six£640£640

Congestion Charge, 230 days£3,105£4,140

Total£6,530£29,477

Private buyers pay no company car tax, so from year two the yearly gap shrinks to about £3,900 for a London commuter and £2,900 outside the zone. In the first year, though, the V8’s £5,690 road tax bill pushes the saving to about £9,600 in London and £8,600 elsewhere.

That pays back the £8,900 premium within the year in London, and within a couple of months more everywhere else.

If you’d rather spend a lot less on a big luxury SUV with a plug, the Zeekr 9X Super Hybrid is worth a look, and we’ve lined it up against the Range Rover.

What changes from 2028

From April 2028, electric cars pay 3p a mile on top of road tax, which adds about £300 a year at 10,000 miles, and plug-in hybrids pay half that. The Budget confirmed both rates, which rise with inflation from 2029/30.

It trims the electric car’s advantage over the V8 without coming close to closing it, and it’s small next to the hybrid’s jump to 18% company car tax in the same month. Regit has worked out what pay-per-mile tax will cost you at different mileages.

The electric Range Rover still pays the £440 Expensive Car Supplement every year until it’s six years old, just like the V8, and you can see what your current car costs to tax with Regit’s free car tax checker.

What we like

•        It saves about £1,035 a year on the Congestion Charge against the V8 or the hybrid.

•        Home charging works out at about 3p a mile on an off-peak tariff, about a tenth of the V8’s fuel bill.

•        It looks almost exactly like the regular Range Rover, so nobody will know you’ve saved a fortune.

What worries us

•        It tows 2,500kg, a tonne less than the petrol and diesel Range Rovers.

•        Without a home charger, public rapid charging at 79p per kWh wipes out most of the fuel saving.

•        Pay-per-mile tax adds about £300 a year from April 2028, twice what the hybrid pays and a cost the V8 won’t face.

Verdict

If you’re a company car driver choosing a Range Rover, choose the electric one. You’d keep around £19,000 a year that would otherwise go to HMRC on the V8, and from 2028 it saves you about £5,000 a year over the plug-in hybrid as well, with the Budget’s new 2030/31 rates keeping that gap in place.

Private buyers who can charge at home should go electric too, because the V8’s first-year road tax and fuel bill cover almost all of the £8,900 premium in the first year. The only people who should stick with petrol are those who tow heavy loads or have nowhere to plug in.

articles.title: A Ferrari, Rolls-Royce or Bentley for under £70,000
articles.summary:
The badges on these cars still say six figures, but the prices in the dealers’ windows say something much closer to a well-specced family SUV, because the first owners have already swallowed the biggest losses for you. The bills, sadly, haven’t got any smaller.

A Ferrari or a Rolls-Royce costs a lot less than most people think, as long as you don’t mind that someone else has owned it first. When we checked used listings on 11 November, the lowest-priced Ferrari California was up for £59,480 and the lowest-priced Rolls-Royce Ghost for £64,948, while a Bentley Continental GT in its current shape started at about £67,000 and Regit’s listings had a McLaren 540C for £71,950. Every one of them cost well over £100,000 new, and the Ghost was £170,000 when it went on sale in 2010.

There is a catch, which is that what these cars cost to keep on the road doesn’t fall with their value, so for each one we’ve worked out roughly what it costs to run for a year if you drive a modest 5,000 miles, and what to check before you hand over the money. Here are the five brands we’d look at.

Used Ferrari California price

So what does a California cost to run?

The California was Ferrari’s go at a car you could use every day, a front-engined V8 convertible with a folding metal roof and two small rear seats, and it cost £143,000 when UK prices were announced in October 2008. AutoUncle had 107 for sale when we checked, from £59,480 up to £152,850 for the later California T, so the lowest-priced cars have lost well over half their price.

Those bargain cars will be early ones, which is where you need to be careful. PistonHeads’ buying guide says most gearbox trouble was on 2009 cars, and fewer than 200 early engines had faulty crankshafts that Ferrari replaced free under a 2012 recall, so ask to see the paperwork. There’s no cambelt to change, and Regit’s figures put a Ferrari service at about £800 to £1,200 today, but an engine failure can mean a Ferrari quote of around £45,000.

Plenty of owners cover that risk with Ferrari’s Power15 extended warranty, which Regit’s figures put at £3,500 to £4,500 a year, but it only runs to 15 years from first registration, so the oldest cars are already too old for it. That makes a later car, from 2012 on, the smarter buy even if it costs a few thousand more.

Regit’s own listings show what that later car costs, with Californias from £74,999 and a California T, the turbocharged update from 2014, at £76,990. If you need four proper seats, the same listings had a four-wheel-drive Ferrari FF for £89,900, a car that cost about £227,000 when it went on sale in 2011, so its first owner has lost well over £130,000.

So what does a California cost to run? Driven 5,000 miles a year at a real-world 16mpg (PistonHeads reckons owners see the mid-teens), it’ll use about £2,450 of petrol at the AA’s November average of 172p a litre, and these cars are happiest on pricier super unleaded. Add £790 road tax for a car registered before April 2017 (£760 for most California Ts) and a service, and you’re at roughly £4,000 to £4,500 a year before insurance, or £7,500 to £9,000 with a Power15 warranty.

Used Rolls-Royce Ghost price

The Ghost was the “small” Rolls-Royce when it arrived in 2010

The Ghost was the “small” Rolls-Royce when it arrived in 2010 at £170,000 (the current one starts at about £287,400), and it’s the car on this list that has lost the most in pounds. AutoUncle had 20 for sale, from £64,948 to £299,950, and Regit’s own used listings had four first-generation cars between £68,250 and £114,995. The cheapest tend to have big mileages, which is no bad thing on a car built to waft up and down motorways.

It’s the one that will cost you most to keep, though. PistonHeads’ buying guide lists air suspension faults, failing door motors and the odd injector repair that can run to five figures, and puts brake discs and pads at about £1,000 a corner, although an independent service was a reasonable £600 to £700 every other year when it checked in 2022. A first-generation Ghost was registered before April 2017 and puts out more than 255g/km of CO2, so it pays the top £790 rate of road tax, and you’ll see the mid to high teens to the gallon from its twin-turbo V12.

At 5,000 miles a year and a real-world 18mpg, a Ghost will get through about £2,170 of petrol, so with £790 road tax and a specialist service averaged out at around £350 a year, you’re looking at roughly £3,300 a year before insurance, and more if you stick with a Rolls-Royce dealer or the air suspension plays up.

Used Bentley Continental GT price

Bentley’s official 23.2mpg works out at about £1,690 of petrol for 5,000 miles

This is the third-generation Continental GT, the shape Bentley still sells, which went on sale in 2018 at £165,400 with a W12 engine. AutoUncle had eight 2018 cars for sale, from £66,995 to £109,995, with an average of about £92,500, so even the dearest has lost a third of its price and the cheapest has lost well over half.

If you don’t mind the previous shape, which Bentley sold from 2011 to 2017, the price drops a long way further. Regit’s own listings had nine of them between £32,250 and £40,550 when we checked, and you can browse them on Regit. Those older cars were registered before April 2017, so they pay £760 or £790 a year in road tax depending on the engine, and they’ll need more looking after than a newer one.

It’s the newest car here at this money, and it has one tax quirk worth knowing. Petrol cars over £40,000 pay a £440 supplement on top of road tax for five years, but a car first registered in 2018 has finished those years, so it now pays the £200 standard rate. PistonHeads’ guide says the electronics and air suspension are the things to watch, along with brake hoses Bentley wants replaced every five years, and specialists were offering fixed-price servicing from £599 in 2022.

Running one is a lot less frightening than the badge suggests. Bentley’s official 23.2mpg works out at about £1,690 of petrol for 5,000 miles, and with £200 road tax and a specialist service from about £600, a 2018 car costs roughly £2,500 a year before insurance, the least of any car here.

Used Aston Martin DB11 price

The V8 coupe from 2018 on is the one we’d go for

We’ve looked at the DB11 in detail on regit.cars, but it earns its place here because Regit’s valuation figures put an early V12 at £55,000 to £65,000, against £165,000 to £175,000 new with options. Regit’s own listings had DB11 coupes from £59,990, with two more at £62,999 and £63,999.

The V8 coupe from 2018 on is the one we’d go for, at £65,000 to £75,000, because it has held its value better than the V12 and costs less to look after. Aston Martin’s Timeless approved used scheme covers cars up to 10 years old, which takes in almost every DB11.

Auto Express’s used buying guide puts DB11 V8 servicing at £650 and £760 in alternate years, and reckons on about 23mpg in real driving, which is around £1,700 of petrol for 5,000 miles. A V8 registered between 2018 and 2020 has finished paying the £440 supplement, so it’s £200 a year in road tax, and the total comes to roughly £2,600 a year before insurance (a 2021 car still pays the supplement, so add £440).

Used McLaren 540C and 570S price

The 540C was its entry-level car when UK prices were announced in 2015

If you want a proper mid-engined supercar, McLaren is the surprise here. The 540C was its entry-level car when UK prices were announced in 2015, at £126,000, with the 570S at £143,250, and Regit’s own listings had a 540C coupe for £71,950 and a 570S Spider for £79,995. That’s a carbon-fibre-tubbed, twin-turbo V8 McLaren for not much more than our £70,000 line, and the softer McLaren GT, which arrived in 2019, was on the same listings at £92,988.

These are cars that punish a skipped service. PistonHeads’ buying guide says missing an annual or 10,000-mile service voids the warranty, and lists coolant hose leaks, leaking dampers, broken coil springs, cracked glass and a fiddly infotainment system among the things to check. McLaren’s extended warranty can run up to 12 years from new, so a 2016 car still has a few years of cover available if it passes inspection, and that’s the first thing we’d ask the seller about. Carbon ceramic brakes were standard, which is good news for how long the discs last and bad news if they ever need replacing.

McLaren’s official 25.5mpg for the 540C means about £1,530 of petrol for 5,000 miles, though you’ll struggle to match it if you use the performance. A 2016 car registered before April 2017 puts out 258g/km, so it pays £790 a year in road tax, and Carbuyer says a dealer service can cost well over £1,000, so budget at least £3,300 a year before insurance.

How much does a used luxury car cost to run?

All five of these meet the ULEZ standards, so there’s no daily charge in London, but none are electric, so the Congestion Charge is the full £18 a day. If you’d rather go electric, City AM’s used luxury EVs guide covers the BMW i7 and Mercedes EQS.

Insurance is the cost that varies most, because it depends on your age, postcode and record. Confused.com’s average quotes for other Ferraris in 2025 ran from about £2,600 for a 488 Spider to £4,600 for a Roma, so as a starting point we’d allow £2,500 to £4,500 a year for any of these, and get a real quote before you fall for one, because a cheap Ferrari is still a Ferrari to an insurer. Pay for an independent inspection too, which PistonHeads reckoned costs under £500 for a California. A full service history matters more on these cars than on almost anything else, because skipped services on a V8 or V12 turn into big bills later.

Before you ring about that £65,000 Ghost, run a free MOT check with Regit on its number plate, because the mileage from every past test will show you whether it’s been driven properly or left sitting in a garage.

What we like

A Ferrari California from £59,480 costs less than half its £143,000 price new.

A 2018 Continental GT costs roughly £2,500 a year to run for 5,000 miles before insurance, because it has finished paying the £440 supplement.

A McLaren 540C for £71,950 is a mid-engined supercar for about the price of a well-specced SUV.

What worries us

The oldest Californias are too old for Ferrari’s Power15 warranty, and an engine failure can cost around £45,000.

A first-generation Ghost pays £790 a year in road tax and about £1,000 a corner for brakes.

These are dealer asking prices on the day we checked, and they change daily.

Our verdict

If we had £70,000 to spend, we’d buy the Bentley, because it’s the newest car here, it’s past its expensive tax years and it’s the one you could use every day without wincing. The Ferrari is the one we’d want, and a 2012-on California with a Power15 warranty is a fair way to have a Ferrari on your drive, but the low-priced Rolls-Royce is the one we’d be most wary of, because it costs Rolls-Royce money to keep however little you paid for it.

articles.title: Is BYD’s Yangwang Altior Rolls-Royce rival coming to the UK?
articles.summary:
BYD built its name in Britain selling sensible electric family cars, and now it wants a share of Rolls-Royce money. The Yangwang Altior is aimed squarely at the Ghost, and the question for anyone in Mayfair is whether it will ever be sold here.

BYD revealed its Rolls-Royce rival, the Yangwang Altior, in Abu Dhabi on 7 November, and the first version, a limited edition reported to be capped at 399 cars, is listed at 2.08 million yuan (about £230,000) in China. BYD hasn’t said whether it’s coming to Britain, and so far only Yangwang’s U8 SUV and U9 supercar have been earmarked for Europe, with the brand due here in 2027. We think the Altior will follow them, and our estimate is that it would cost between £200,000 and £240,000 if it does.

Is the Yangwang Altior coming to the UK?

BYD’s Europe boss, Stella Li, said in September 2025 that Yangwang would arrive in the UK in 2027, after BYD’s other premium brand, Denza, and Denza has now kept its side of that, launching here this summer with the Z9 GT from £95,000. The U8 and U9 are the models named for European sale so far, and Li hinted at more to come, including the U7 saloon.

Abu Dhabi, a city with no shortage of Rolls-Royces, was a fitting place for the debut, and Yangwang chose the UAE for the global launch, though orders have so far opened only in China. Yangwang has done this before, as the UAE was its first overseas market, with the U8 on sale there from about AED 650,000 (about £130,000) well before any UK date. Gulf cars are left-hand drive, though, so the real sign to watch for here is a right-hand-drive Altior, and BYD has already been testing right-hand-drive U8s. It would be odd for BYD to bring its U9 supercar here and leave out the car built to take on the Ghost.

Yangwang Altior price and specs

BYD’s Europe boss, Stella Li, said in September 2025 that Yangwang would arrive in the UK in 2027, after BYD’s other premium brand, Denza, and Denza has now kept its side of that, launching here this summer with the Z9 GT from £95,000. The U8 and U9 are the models named for European sale so far, and Li hinted at more to come, including the U7 saloon.

Yangwang would arrive in the UK in 2027

Abu Dhabi, a city with no shortage of Rolls-Royces, was a fitting place for the debut, and Yangwang chose the UAE for the global launch, though orders have so far opened only in China. Yangwang has done this before, as the UAE was its first overseas market, with the U8 on sale there from about AED 650,000 (about £130,000) well before any UK date. Gulf cars are left-hand drive, though, so the real sign to watch for here is a right-hand-drive Altior, and BYD has already been testing right-hand-drive U8s. It would be odd for BYD to bring its U9 supercar here and leave out the car built to take on the Ghost.

How much would the Yangwang Altior cost in the UK?

BYD won’t give a UK price until it confirms the car for Britain, so this is our estimate, and here’s how we got there. The limited edition is reported at 2.08 million yuan in China, about £230,000, but BYD doesn’t simply convert its Chinese prices. Its Denza Z9 GT costs the equivalent of about £35,000 in China and arrived here at £95,000, a price set against the Porsche Panamera it’s aimed at.

So we’d expect BYD to price the Altior off its rivals, and the Chinese price nudges our best guess up to £200,000 to £240,000. That’s still around £50,000 under a £287,400 Ghost, enough to get a company director’s attention, and comfortably above the £178,180 Mercedes-Maybach S580, because a luxury car that looks cheap is a harder sell. It would put the Altior on the same shopping list as the Bentley Flying Spur, which is where we think its real rivals are.

Yangwang Altior vs Rolls-Royce Ghost

The Ghost Series II starts at £287,400 in the UK, and the Extended version, with more room in the back, costs £317,400. Rolls-Royce’s electric car, the Spectre, is a two-door coupé, so there’s no electric Ghost for the Altior to fight directly. If you want an electric limousine you can buy today, the BMW i7 is the closest thing. Against the Ghost, the Altior gives its back-seat passengers more room, with a longer wheelbase than either Ghost and 1,209mm of rear legroom.

The Altior is fully electric

For City AM readers the bigger gap may be in company car tax. The Altior is fully electric, so it sits in the 4% band this tax year, rising to 5% next April. At £220,000, the middle of our estimate, a 45% taxpayer would pay about £3,960 a year now and £4,950 from April, against about £47,850 for a Ghost in the 37% band. We did the same sum for the Range Rover Electric, and the gap there was big too. A saving that size could make an unfamiliar badge much easier to live with.

Would a Mayfair buyer take a BYD seriously?

BYD has come a long way in Britain in a short time. Earlier this year it overtook Tesla, Kia and BMW to become the UK’s best-selling electric car brand, with more than 7% of electric car sales from January to April, according to SMMT figures released by BYD. But it built that lead on affordable family cars, and its Seal saloon starts at £45,730, so asking buyers to spend Rolls-Royce money on one of its cars is a very big leap.

That’s why the Yangwang name matters. BYD is keeping its own badge off its most expensive cars, much as Toyota did with Lexus, and the U8 has already shown the brand can do luxury. CAR magazine tried one on the Goodwood circuit in 2024, called the ride “magic carpet-esque” and found the cabin properly upmarket, though it was a track drive and the writer wondered how something that size would cope with narrow, battered British roads.

BYD is keeping its own badge off its most expensive cars

A Ghost buyer is paying for more than leather and silence, of course. Rolls-Royce has been building cars at the top of the market for well over a century, and that kind of history can’t be bought with a lidar sensor and a lower price. So the Altior’s best chance is with buyers who care more about technology and value than heritage, and in the City, with that tax gap, there may be more of them than Rolls-Royce would like.

​WHAT WE LIKE

·        On our estimate it would cost around £50,000 less than a Rolls-Royce Ghost.

·        It’s electric, so company car tax at 4% is a fraction of the Ghost’s 37%.

·        It’s longer than a standard Ghost, with a longer wheelbase than even the Ghost Extended and the same rear-hinged back doors.

WHAT WORRIES US

·        BYD hasn’t confirmed it for the UK.

·        Nobody yet knows how a Chinese luxury badge will hold its value in Britain.

·        At 5.6 metres long, it’s a big car for London streets and multi-storey car parks.

If you’re running a big luxury saloon now and wondering whether a Chinese newcomer could replace it, get a free car valuation with Regit first, so you know what yours is worth before you start weighing up the alternatives.

Verdict

On paper, the Altior gives you Ghost-sized luxury for what we expect to be around £50,000 less, and because it’s electric, the tax savings would make it a serious option for company directors. We think it will come, probably once the U8 and U9 have opened Yangwang’s doors here, but until BYD commits it’s a car for Abu Dhabi and Shanghai, and anyone in London who wants a limousine this size will still be heading to a Rolls-Royce showroom.

articles.title: BMW i3 2026: 566-mile range makes it a serious executive EV
articles.summary:
BMW’s new electric 3 Series promises long-distance range and proper driver appeal. Motoring journalist Tim Barnes-Clay drove the i3 50 xDrive M Sport to see whether it delivers.

The new BMW i3 has the range to make electric motoring less of a compromise for company car drivers, but it’s the way it drives that makes the strongest impression. This is an electric 3 Series with the comfort, composure and handling expected of BMW’s compact executive saloon.

I drove the i3 50 xDrive M Sport from the leafy outskirts of Arundel to the busier cathedral city of Chichester. It was a cold day, and the roughly 20-mile route took in rural lanes, dual carriageways, suburban roads and city streets.

The car felt settled and refined throughout. It’s quiet and easy to drive at lower speeds, yet has the grip and agility to make a more demanding stretch of road enjoyable.

For London business drivers, the appeal is obvious. A long-range electric saloon that can cover substantial distances between charges, while offering the refinement expected of a premium executive car, makes a compelling proposition for journeys between the capital, regional offices and business meetings around the country.

How far can the BMW i3 travel on a charge?

Two important range figures matter before you look at the BMW i3.

The i3 50 xDrive in standard Base trim has an official maximum range of up to 566 miles. However, that’s not the figure for the M Sport I tested.

My car had 20-inch wheels and optional equipment, and BMW quotes a maximum range of up to 519 miles for this specification. That’s still an impressive figure for an electric executive saloon, although you should check the range attached to your chosen trim and wheel combination.

Nicola Verrall, BMW UK’s product operations manager, told me: “The range of the i3 50 xDrive at 566 miles is phenomenal. We know a lot of our customers like M Sport, so they would still get really good range.”

The car has a 108.7kWh battery and two electric motors producing 469hp and 645Nm of torque. It accelerates from 0-62mph in 4.7 seconds, with a top speed of 124mph.

BMW claims DC charging up to 400kW, enough to add a claimed 263 miles of range in 10 minutes under suitable conditions. An optional 22kW AC charging system is also available.

On my short drive, the car returned 3.0 miles per kWh. That was below BMW’s official 3.9-4.6 miles per kWh figure, although the cold weather and mixed route need to be taken into account. 

If you’re regularly travelling between London and other UK business centres, the headline range could make a difference. Fewer charging stops mean less disruption to working days, although actual journey planning will still depend on weather, speed and access to suitable charging points.

What is the BMW i3 like to drive?

The ride is comfortable, if a little firm, but that’s always been the case with the 3 Series, as, let’s face it, they’re built to be driven enthusiastically. I can’t help but smile every time I’m behind the wheel of a BMW, and this i3 is no different. You don’t want to thrash it, but you want to have fun, and I did.

The firmer setup means the i3 resists body lean well. There’s little to no wobble over potholes and bumpier surfaces, and the BMW feels well planted, taking no time to settle back down.

It’s a hoot to thread around corners, too, with loads of grip and keen handling dynamics. The i3’s responsive, feedback-rich steering weights up gradually as you quicken the pace.

At low speeds, though, it’s still very capable, hushed and easy to drive around busier streets. In my opinion, the i3’s refinement makes it one of the best EVs produced to date.

BMW has also introduced its Heart of Joy computing system, which the company says coordinates key vehicle functions and driving dynamics. Verrall explained that BMW developed it in-house to deliver the familiar 3 Series driving character.

“We have the Heart of Joy, created internally by BMW. That really delivers all of the driving dynamics and delivers on that 3 Series feeling that customers get when they drive the 3 Series,” she said.

If you’re using a car as a mobile office between meetings, refinement matters as much as outright performance. The i3’s quiet cabin and composed motorway manners will, I reckon, make longer business journeys less tiring, while its handling gives it the driver appeal expected of a BMW.

How much does the BMW i3 cost?

The i3 50 xDrive M Sport starts at £54,925, although my particular test car cost £63,162. That figure includes its optional equipment and isn’t the standard M Sport price.

Those extras included a heated steering wheel, electric bootlid, BMW Iconic Glow, M Sport brakes with dark blue callipers, panoramic glass sunroof, sun protection glass, 22kW AC charging, automatic air conditioning, Motorway Assistant, Parking Assistant Professional, a 3D head-up display, Harman Kardon surround-sound audio and BMW Digital Premium.

That’s a substantial list, and it helps explain the difference between the starting price and the cost of the car I drove. You should check the specification carefully before comparing prices.

How much does the BMW i3 cost?

For London-based company car drivers and employers, the financial case is worth examining alongside the purchase price.

The benefit-in-kind rate for fully electric company cars is 4% in 2026/27, so using £63,162 as an illustrative P11D value, a 40% taxpayer would stump up around £1,011 a year in company-car tax. Of course, the actual calculation will depend on the vehicle’s final P11D value.

You also need to consider the Expensive Car Supplement. Because the i3’s list price is above £50,000, the additional £440 annual charge applies to vehicle excise duty for years two to six.

London drivers should also remember that electric cars are no longer completely exempt from the Congestion Charge. From January 2026, eligible electric cars registered for TfL Auto Pay receive a 25% discount, reducing the daily charge from £18 to £13.50.

What do you get as standard?

The i3 is offered in three specification levels: Base, M Sport and M Sport Pro.

Base specification includes 19-inch alloy wheels, heated front seats, a 17.9-inch angled infotainment touchscreen and BMW Panoramic Vision, which projects information across the lower part of the windscreen.

M Sport brings sportier styling, while M Sport Pro adds further visual and equipment upgrades. The result is a cabin and exterior that feel suitably premium, although the options list can quickly push the price upwards.

Verrall described the car as a compact saloon with familiar BMW character.

“We’ve made it look sportier, and you’ve got some of these classic design cues. It feels like a sports saloon.”

She also said charging has become part of her everyday life.

“I charge at work, or I charge in public, and it’s just become part of my everyday now.”

That reflects an important consideration for London businesses. Workplace charging can make an electric company car easier to live with, particularly for employees who regularly travel into the capital or use their vehicles for regional business trips. If you don’t have home charging, you’ll need to consider your access to workplace and public infrastructure.

What we like

Excellent refinement and a comfortable, composed ride.

Engaging handling, strong grip and responsive steering.

Impressive claimed range.

Rapid DC charging capability.

What worries us

The £63,162 price of my test car shows how quickly options add up.

The ride is on the firm side, so it may not be ideal if you have a bad back.

Real-world efficiency will depend heavily on weather, route and driving conditions.

As mentioned, the BMW i3 50 xDrive M Sport qualifies for the luxury car supplement, so check your car tax with Regit and see what your current vehicle costs before you change cars.

Verdict

The BMW i3 50 xDrive M Sport is a convincing electric executive saloon. It combines the refinement and driving enjoyment expected of a 3 Series with a headline range that should make longer journeys far less daunting.

The Base model’s possible 566-mile range is the big talking point, although the M Sport I drove is rated at up to 519 miles. That distinction matters when comparing specifications and deciding which version offers the best balance of equipment, price and range.

For London business users, the combination of long-distance ability, premium refinement and favourable electric company car taxation makes the i3 particularly interesting. It can serve as both a comfortable executive commuter and a capable car for longer journeys beyond the capital.

My test BMW’s £63,162 price, including options, is a sizeable outlay, but the underlying car is impressive. If you’re a company car driver looking for a premium electric saloon with genuine long-distance ability and a rewarding drive, the new i3 deserves serious consideration.

articles.title: Tech firm forced to pay SFO £2.5m after breaching bribery deal
articles.summary:
A technology company was ordered by a criminal court to pay £2.5m to the Serious Fraud Office (SFO) after breaching a bribery deal.

In October 2018, hardware and engineering technology firm Güralp Systems finalised a Deferred Prosecution Agreement (DPA) with the anti-fraud office.

The Reading-based group accepted charges of conspiracy to make corrupt payments and failure to prevent bribery, and agreed to pay £2,069,861.

Despite that deal, the SFO told the court the company breached the DPA in November 2024 after the business “failed to pay under the terms of the 2019 agreement”.

Earlier this year, the High Court ruled the DPA was enforceable by the SFO and denied the company permission to appeal to the Supreme Court.

First payment due soon

On Friday, the Southwark Crown Court approved a variation to the DPA, requiring the company to pay the outstanding balance in full, plus interest and costs, on an agreed schedule. The court also drew up a new, stricter plan that forces them to pay the original debt plus up to £400,000 extra to cover interest and the SFO’s legal costs.

The SFO said the first payment of £400,000 will be made on 1 December, and a schedule for the outstanding balance has been set.

Jason Williams, head of division at the SFO, said: “The SFO pursued the company to honour their agreement and today marks a successful outcome with Güralp Systems committing to pay in full with interest and costs.

“Companies that enter into a deferred prosecution agreement must comply with its terms, or we will terminate the agreement and seek a prosecution,” they added.

Dr Cansun Güralp, Andrew Bell, and Natalie Pearce were charged with conspiracy to make corrupt payments in 2018, but after a trial at Southwark Crown Court, all three individuals were acquitted and found not guilty by the jury.

articles.title: Burnham agrees youth migration for 100,000 EU citizens to Britain
articles.summary:
Andy Burnham has agreed to allow 100,000 young people from EU nations to spend three years travelling, working or studying in Britain in an agreement that could face intense scrutiny. 

In a summit in Brussels, Burnham argued that a wide-ranging deal with the EU tackled the “biggest challenges of our time” as he hailed alignment on food standards and carbon emissions markets, plus efforts to share data on illegal migration. 

Burnham and EU leaders Ursula von der Leyen and Antonia Costa revealed that the UK had clinched a deal to be subject to the EU’s food standards rules, which ministers said would reduce paperwork and regulatory burdens for producers on both sides of the Channel. The new arrangement, which was central to the summit, will apply from March 2028.

Internal Treasury analysis suggests that the food standards arrangement could add about 0.5 per cent to GDP in the UK. 

Separately, an agreement to join the UK’s carbon emission markets in electricity to the EU will add modest growth benefits although critics have slammed the net zero effort over immediate costs to some businesses.

The Prime Minister also said a new ‘Youth Experience Scheme’ for people under the age of 30 would “lift life chances” for young people in Britain and Europe. He added that further discussions would take place on cutting tuition fees for European students. Around 100,000 EU and 100,000 British citizens between the ages of 18 and 31 will be allowed to take part each year.

“Brexit did take away opportunity from young people,” Burnham said. 

“I can say to the young people of Britain that you will have, as a result of this deal, a new freedom.”

Burnham also emphasised there was “hope on the horizon” as a result of the latest round of negotiations.

Burnham to initiate ‘brainstorming’ session on EU relations

The handout also outlined a commitment to build closer cooperation on defence. A bill to implement the deal will be introduced into the parliament next week. 

The Prime Minister was joined by several Cabinet colleagues in Brussels, including the Chancellor, business secretary and the chief whip. 

On Thursday, Burnham’s spokesman said negotiations had gone “down to the wire”, suggesting that some of the finer details were not agreed until just before the summit. 

The second iteration of the UK-EU summit mainly confirmed initial proposals laid out by the former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer last year. 

But Burnham has signalled that bolder proposals on alignment with the EU could follow the summit.
