At the press conference, Burnham said he start a “brainstorming” process to consider how the UK could become more closely aligned to the EU after the next election.

Following his Labour Party conference address, Burnham suggested he was open to go “all the way” and propose returning the UK to the EU. 

Several senior figures of Starmer’s government have made the case for the UK to rejoin the bloc. While Rachel Reeves said she envisaged a return in her lifetime, ex-business secretary Peter Kyle and and former foreign secretary David Lammy urged the Prime Minister to kick start negotiations for rejoining the EU.

Other Labour backbenchers have expressed their concern over closer relations, with Red Wall MPs pushing back against closer ties. 

‘Played like a fiddle by Brussels’

Researchers across Westminster are feeding in contributions on the economic impacts of closer trade. A report by the Productivity Institute estimated that joining the single market would add about 1.8 per cent to growth. 

On the other side of the Commons, Brexiteers have re-launched a ‘Stay Out’ campaign pumping out warnings over rejoining the EU. 

Oliver Lewis, chairman of Stay Out, said: “This whole thing has been a humiliating spectacle for the Prime Minister.

“Burnham has been played like a fiddle by Brussels, which took one look at how badly he wants a deal and decided British taxpayers should foot the bill for cheaper fees for EU students before it will sign anything.”

articles.title: Inheritance tax receipts hit fresh high as HMRC predicts another rise
articles.summary:
Inheritance tax receipts rocketed to yet another record high in the seven months to October 2026, as frozen thresholds continued to plague ordinary households.

Receipts hit £5.5bn over the period, according to the latest figures from HMRC, a 6.5 per cent increase from the prior year, where receipts reached £5.2bn.

In September alone, inheritance tax (IHT) receipts reached the highest on record at £936m, up from £671m in 2025.

The tax authority admitted it anticipates higher receipts in the coming years, amid the government’s decision to extend frozen tax thresholds until April 2031.

Industry figures have also pointed out the incoming changes to the IHT system from April 2027, where unused pension funds are set to be included in the value of a person’s estate.

Samantha Warner, legal director at Winckworth Sherwood, said: “IHT revenues have continued to steadily rise due to the prolonged freeze on thresholds.

“It remains a persistent and unavoidable inheritance tax planning issue, and one that should not be ignored.”

The Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts that receipts will hit £9.5bn by the end of the 2026/27 tax year, up from £8.5bn the previous year.

Rising values

HMRC said rising asset values, such as properties and investments, have also contributed to the sharp uptick in receipts, pulling more middle-class families into the tax net.

The nil-rate band has remained at £325,000 since 2009, while house prices have steadily climbed, particularly in the South East. Average house prices in the region hit £400,000 last month, while London prices reached £546,000.

But Sarah Coles, head of personal finance at AJ Bell, said that while frozen bands are “bad enough” the introduction of pensions being subject to IHT will further buckle households.

This is expected to drag another 10,500 estates into the inheritance tax net that year, hike the amount of tax paid by 38,500 estates and increase the tax due by £34,000 each on average.

Total receipts

Total HMRC tax receipts and national insurance receipts also hit a fresh record high of £546.6bn between April and October.

This was an increase of £33.4bn from 2025, reflecting broad growth across numerous revenue streams for the government authority.

Income tax, capital gains tax and national insurance remained the largest drivers, increasing by £20.5bn.

Elsewhere, VAT rose by £3.7bn, while business taxes increased by £7.9bn.

But other tax duties declined, reflecting wider socioeconomic and policy changes. Tobacco receipts and environmental taxes both slipped five per cent.

articles.title: London private credit firm Northwall Capital sued by e-commerce group
articles.summary:
Private credit firm Northwall Capital is being sued by an e-commerce group in the High Court following a dispute over an $80.7m (£61.6m) loan and the lender’s takeover of the company.  

E-commerce brand aggregator Accel Club has alleged in court documents, filed on 9 November, that the Mayfair-based lender unlawfully asked for an immediate payment of the loan before taking control of the firm’s holding companies. 

Under the terms of the loan agreement, Northwall Capital was only permitted to take control of the business’ holding companies if Accel Club was actively ‘in default’ – meaning a formal breach of the debt terms.

Accel Club, which generated around $225m (£172m) in annual revenue in the last year, argued in its filing that Northwall Capital triggered the takeover because of allegedly invalid default notices, including $4.1m (£3.1m) of interest the e-commerce firm claims had already been settled. 

Accel Club, which buys and grows third-party brands on Amazon, further argued that the interest had originally been deferred under revised payment terms, claiming it settled the $4.1m (£3.1m) interest payment in July. 

The e-commerce group further argues that Northwall Capital acknowledged the receipt of the interest payment in August through its Ireland-based lending vehicle, Denali European Opportunities. 

In its argument, it alleges the takeover, which took place in September, amounted to “unlawful enforcement.” It additionally claims it offered to re-pay the loan in full through refinancing prior to the takeover. 

Max Firsau, co-founder of Accel Club, said in a statement: “In August we secured a term sheet that would have repaid NorthWall in full. Days later, Northwall took control of the business before any court had examined its purported claims of default, and we are now asking the Commercial Court to do exactly that.”

Northwall to ‘vigorously’ defend proceedings 

City AM understands that Northwall Capital contends Accel Club was in default for a period of months, according to sources familiar with the matter. 

A spokesperson for Northwall Capital said in a statement: “Northwall is aware of the proceedings. They are contrived, meritless and will be defended vigorously.” 

The private credit firm is yet to file its defence in the High Court.

articles.title: Wealth fintech FNZ to axe 1,500 roles and slash office footprint
articles.summary:
Wealth fintech FNZ is to slash its headcount by a quarter and cut its global office footprint as the firm hopes to return to profit after years of steep losses, City AM can reveal.

The London-headquartered group confirmed at the beginning of November it would reduce its headcount in a bid to simplify operations and reduce duplications.

City AM understands around 1,500 roles from its near 7,000-strong global workforce will face the chop as a result of the plans. The firm is also weighing up plans to shrink its office footprint to around 15 global hubs from its current 44, sources close to the matter said.

A source close to FNZ said that of the 29 offices at risk of closure, the majority were inherited from legacy acquisitions and were not major client hubs. 

The group has completed a string of takeovers over the last few years, including snapping up Icelandic tech firm Authenteq and Zurich-based software company Appway in 2022 and US fintech YieldX in 2023. 

FNZ is set to maintain a focus on four core growth markets of the UK, North America, Australia and New Zealand as part of its transformation strategy, the person said.

The platform counts major financial institutions, including banking giants Barclays, Santander and Lloyds, as well as asset managers Aberdeen and Quilter, among its client base. The business helps institutions run and scale investment and wealth services, with more than $2.5trn in assets held on its platform.

FNZ looks to turn tide on losses

The job cuts form part of a broader overhaul to rein in FNZ’s steep cash burn – the net amount of cash the business is spending each month beyond what it brings in from clients – from roughly $80m a month down to around $30m, sources said.

FNZ’s chief executive Blythe Masters stepped down as chief executive in September after two years in the post. Group chair Stephen Welch is serving as interim chief while the company hunts for a replacement. 

The group’s pre-tax loss nearly doubled to $1.4bn (£1.1bn) in 2025. This came despite nine per cent year-on-year growth in revenue to $1.1bn.

The firm faced a whopping $471.5m impairment charge against intangible assets following its flurry of takeovers, as well as a $10m write-down on its 25 per cent stake in retail investing platform Hatch.

In the group’s UK accounts, client revenue was flat at £262.1m over the last year, while operating expenses surged 18.4 per cent to £387.9m. Its pre-tax loss widened 129.7 per cent to £57.2m. Former Natwest boss Dame Alison Rose has served as chair of FNZ UK since November 2025.

FNZ declined to comment.

articles.title: Poundland dealmakers brace for crunch weekend to avert collapse
articles.summary:
The advisers running the sale of Poundland are preparing for a hectic weekend as they review last-ditch offers to pluck the beleaguered retailer from the jaws of collapse. 

Staff at Alvarez & Marsal, the City advisory firm running Poundland’s sale, expect to work through the weekend to determine whether the small number of bidders proposing to buy the retailer can stump up the cash they need before it goes bust. 

The discount retailer, which has been a mainstay on British high streets since 1990, has until Thursday to find a new home, before creditors rush in to demand their debts are repaid. 

Advisors are understood to be considering three bids to take on the company as a whole, including from Irish firm Martin Property Group and little-known investor Xyra Group Holdings. 

Bidders have been told they have until the end of Friday to demonstrate to Gordon Brothers, which owns Poundland, how they would fund their proposals to buy the retailer, sources close to the process told City AM. 

These suitors will need to explain whether they will ask Gordon Brothers to continue funding an £85m asset-based loan it has used to prop up Poundland, or propose to refinance it themselves. 

Advisers will spend the weekend and the early part of next week reviewing these proposals, before deciding by Wednesday which is their preferred bid. “People will be working through the weekend,” a person close to the process said.

Late bidders could emerge

It is not too late for new bidders to emerge, City AM understands. Late entrants to buy Poundland could come to the table over the weekend or as late as early next week, it is understood, though they would have little time to complete due diligence and provide proof of funds.

“There’s still the possibility for new parties to enter into the mix. There are new parties that are still getting in touch at the moment,” a second person close to the process said.

These bids to keep Poundland trading as a whole company could yet fail, meaning the retailer’s 600 stores, 12,000 staff and its stock would be auctioned off to the host of retail rivals waiting in the wings.

The companies which are understood to be eyeing Poundland stores include Tesco, B&M, Lidl, Iceland, The Range and Poundstretcher. 

On Thursday, a moratorium blocking Poundland’s creditors from calling in their debts is set to lapse. This was triggered when the retailer’s management filed a notice to appoint administrators last month. 

They extended this deadline last week, giving the retailer 10 extra days to find a new home. The moratorium could be pushed back again, but there would be a “very high bar” for a second delay, sources close to the matter said.

Poundland has been stuck in limbo since Gordon Brothers’s attempts to sell it have gained pace. The retailer’s management and its founder, Steve Smith, had claimed the investment firm was starving it of access to its own funds, preventing staff from restocking its shelves.

Gordon Brothers made about £20m available to Poundland last week and it set to release a bigger payment next week to allow it pay its staff. 

But ITV News reported on Friday that the retailer remains unable to access £60m in cash receipts which it has generated from sales, meaning its shelves are at risk of becoming empty during the crucial Christmas trading period.

And last week, business select committee chair Liam Byrne accused Gordon Brothers of “jeopardising” thousands of jobs and “strangling” the retailer’s access to its own funds.

Poundland jobs in spotlight

A collapse of Poundland would be the most significant failure in Britain’s retail sector in years and would strike a blow to Andy Burnham’s pledge to revive the high street.

“The truth is that too many high streets have been left to hollow out, leaving town centres a shell of what they once were,” Burnham said in September. “That must change.”

He has previously called on Gordon Brothers to protect as many jobs as possible. He said last month: “If there was a potential owner to avoid [collapse] that hasn’t been accepted, then the business secretary and I want to know why that is the case.”

Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds is set to meet again with Gordon Brothers next week, after a previous meeting in which the investment firm assured him it would prioritise jobs when finding a deal for Poundland.

The retailer’s owner appeared to have distanced itself from this pledge in the following weeks, as Byrne claimed its boss “refused to say it will prioritise saving jobs” during a two-hour grilling at the select committee. 

A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said: “Funds necessary to support Poundland’s ongoing trading continue to be released.  We are assessing multiple bids for the sale of the whole company and we are taking due care to ensure that any successful offer can provide the funds required to acquire the business and see it through to sustainable cash generation.”

articles.title: Abramovich urged to release Chelsea funds as £103m interest accrues
articles.summary:
Former Chelsea owner Roman Abramovich has been urged to release billions of pounds promised for victims of the Ukraine conflict after the club’s sale proceeds accrued another £103m in interest.

The Russian oligarch, a former regional governor under Vladimir Putin’s leadership, is being pressed to transfer £2.5bn from his sale of Chelsea to a charity that would provide aid to victims of the war in Ukraine.

After Abramovich’s sale of Chelsea in 2022 due to sanctions imposed on him at the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it was agreed that money made from the sale would be put in a foundation “for the benefit of all victims of the war in Ukraine”.

A Treasury minister in the House of Lords reiterated government warnings that the Russian oligarch could be taken to court after confirming that the funds had “not yet been released”.

Lord Pitt-Watson, who was offered a job by Chancellor John Healey, said he was “limited” in what he could say publicly during a parliamentary debate although officials had written to the foundation’s chief to set out how money from the sale “must go to humanitarian purposes in Ukraine”.

“The government [has] laid out a clear legal route for the transfer of the money and are fully prepared to go to court if necessary to enforce the commitment that was made when Chelsea was sold,” Pitt-Watson said.

Chelsea sale funds grow by £103m

The funds remain stuck in Fordstam Limited, the investment company that owned Chelsea during Abramovich’s tenure. New files released this week show that interest accrued on the cash holdings totalled £102.8m in the year to June 2025.

KPMG, the Big Four auditor tasked with independently looking over the holdings, was paid £180,000 for its work.

Lawyers for Abramovich have previously written to the government to stress that the oligarch “remains fully committed to ensuring that the funds are used for charitable purposes”.

A letter earlier this year said he would be prepared to fight the government if it followed through with legal action.

The letter reportedly said: “Strangely, the UK government appears to be treating this proposed donation as a form of punitive measure against Mr Abramovich. This is fundamentally incorrect.

“It is important to emphasise that the funds — although currently frozen — remain the property of Fordstam Limited, which is wholly owned by Mr Abramovich.

“Should the UK government believe it has the legal basis to confiscate these funds instead, it is of course open to initiate formal confiscation proceedings, which will be contested in court.”

articles.title: Wasps submit training centre plans as rugby club targets return to Prem
articles.summary:
Wasps have announced “a meaningful step forward” in their plans to resurrect the iconic rugby club after applying for permission to build a training centre in Swanley, Kent.

The planning application, submitted earlier this month and published this week, is for a community and academy training facility featuring two pitches – one for under-13s and one for under-8s – and a pavilion.

It comes as Prem Rugby pushes ahead with plans to expand the top division from 10 teams to 12 in 2029. Wasps, London Irish and Worcester Warriors, who all went bust after the pandemic, are expected to apply to rejoin the English elite game.

“Submitting this planning application is an important moment in our journey to return Wasps to the professional game,” said Wasps owner and chairman Christopher Holland.

“We recognise what this club means to its supporters, its former players and the communities with which it has been connected for generations.

“Our ambition is to build a sustainable and resilient future that honours that history while creating a strong foundation for the years ahead. We know there is still work to do, but this is a meaningful step forward.

“A club like Wasps is more than just a ground. It is more than just a league position. It is a memory of those who wore the shirt. That memory never left, and nor did Wasps. We owe our legends and the faithful a future worthy of their past.”

Wasps training centre to serve Kent catchment area

Wasps remain one of the most recognisable brands in rugby, having won six domestic titles and two European crowns during their heyday in the 1990s and early 21st century.

Formed in north London, they have called Middlesex, West London, High Wycombe and, most recently, Coventry home but have targeted Kent as an opportune site for their relaunch.

“Kent has around 56 rugby clubs, with as many as 180 clubs potentially falling within Wasps’ wider sphere of influence when the club is established once again within the RFU ecosystem,” the club said in a statement.

“There are also an estimated 120 schools that play rugby within that catchment. Our stated ambition is to create a playing facility that supports the development of the game at every level, providing opportunities for young players, schools, community clubs, and the next generation of professional rugby players.”

The club’s hopes suffered a setback in June when proposals to build a 28,000-capacity stadium near Swanley were dropped from Sevenoaks District Council’s local plan in June.

Wasps outlined ambitions in 2023 to construct the facility, which was to include four training pitches, a hotel and restaurants, but faced opposition from some local residents.

It comes after London Irish announced their plans to return to professional rugby as soon as next season under new ownership.

articles.title: Net zero is an egregiously bad deal for the UK
articles.summary:
As diplomats gather for Cop31, Bjorn Lomborg runs the numbers on how much net zero would cost and how much it would deliver – and finds it to be an egregiously bad buy

Right now, thousands of diplomats, bureaucrats and campaigners are meeting in Turkey yet again for the 31st United Nations climate summit. The demand will be the one made repeatedly at previous conferences: net zero by 2050. What nobody will say is what that costs, or what it buys. That is odd, because the UN already owns the tools to find out. Yet, in 30 summits, nobody has used them to ask whether the policy pays. So I have.

Running the numbers on net zero

I built NetZeroCostBenefit.com that lets anyone see what the United Kingdom, or any other country or group of countries, would achieve by reaching net zero in 2050, what it would cost and what the climate benefit would be worth. None of the inputs are mine: the climate model, MAGICC, is used throughout the UN’s own climate reports and can translate any country’s promised emissions cuts into lower temperatures by 2100. The costs come from the UN’s own surveys of economic models, and the damage estimates from the two most recent syntheses of the economics of warming. Anyone can check the arithmetic, though few delegates in Antalya will want to.

For its latest report and updates, the climate panel gathered nearly a thousand model estimates of what climate policy costs. Almost none of them get anywhere near net zero by 2050, because it is so hard and costly. Only three models reach net zero starting from today’s actual emissions, rather than assuming cuts that began years ago. They find that global net zero would cost between three per cent and 19 per cent of global GDP in 2050, because expensive energy throttles growth. My website uses the middle one, estimating a loss of 7.2 per cent of GDP in 2050, measured from current policies.

The benefits come from the two most recent syntheses of the damage from warming, by one of the most quoted climate economists, Richard Tol, and the other by William Nordhaus, the only climate economist to win the Nobel prize in economics. Given the warming the UN model projects under current policies, they find that climate change will cost the world 1.8 per cent to 2.8 per cent of GDP by 2100. That is a real loss, but nowhere near the catastrophes bandied about. It is also a lot less than a 7.2 per cent loss of GDP, and a lot further away. Moreover, net zero only avoids part of the damage.

The cost to Brits

Nor does one country’s effort buy much. If the United Kingdom reaches net zero in 2050 and stays there, the UN model says global temperature in 2100 would be 0.0038°C lower. Nobody would notice. Yet, Britons would certainly notice the cost: by 2045 the annual cost would be £70.3bn a year. Over the century the cost adds up to £695bn in today’s money. The global climate benefit adds up to just £74bn. The British sacrifice delivers eleven pence of benefits for every pound spent.

Some will object that no country should look at its own numbers this way, because if everyone notices large costs but tiny benefits, nothing will get done.

But a global deal that only works if nobody checks the numbers is not much of a deal. And the math doesn’t improve by pooling: the website shows that each end up doing much less good for the world than what they put in.

Indeed, when you look at the whole world, global net zero by 2050 would avoid $24 trillion in climate damage this century but cost $255 trillion, both in today’s money. Nine cents on the dollar. The policy itself costs more than it delivers.

Fossil fuels remain cheap and plentiful, despite price fluctuations. It is little wonder that fossil fuels still supply more than four-fifths of global energy, and emissions rose again last year. At the pace of the past half century, they won’t be gone by 2050. They’ll be gone a millennium later, in 2997.

What would actually help

There are much better buys, although most won’t be on the climate agenda at COP31. The summit president has already made the August glacier flood in Nepal, which killed more than 1,400 people, his exhibit A: “If we want to understand the consequences of climate change, we need only look at Nepal.” Yet nothing agreed in Antalya will make the next flood measurably smaller. Early-warning systems and sturdier bridges would save far more Nepalese lives, far sooner, for far less money. Lifting people out of poverty, in Nepal and around the world, will make everyone less climate vulnerable and do far more good. None of these solutions costs anywhere near $255 trillion.

It doesn’t mean that climate change is harmless. But it means that net zero by 2050 is an egregiously bad buy. Across 30 climate summits, delegates have ignored that reality. Now anyone can run the numbers.

Bjorn Lomborg is president of the Copenhagen Consensus, a visiting fellow at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution and author of False Alarm and Best Things First

articles.title: UK banks struggle to find top boss to spearhead Visa and Mastercard alternative
articles.summary:
Britain’s banking giants have struggled to recruit a chief executive for their new domestic payments network that will rival Mastercard and Visa, City AM can reveal. 

Around 19 of the country’s biggest financial services groups have united to support the early setup of a UK payments network, including the big four banks Barclays, Lloyds, Natwest and HSBC.

The collective is currently operating under the moniker of the ‘Payments Delivery Company’ and has sought to raise £50m to fund the project through until 2028.

But the group has faced issues scouting for a permanent chief executive to lead the initiative. The recruitment process had narrowed candidates down to the final two, City AM understands, before the search was re-opened after investors were dissatisfied. 

“It’s back to the drawing board,” one source familiar with the matter said.

Vim Maru, the chief executive of Barclays UK, is leading the group as chair designate until a permanent recruit has been found.

Payments blueprint to come in early 2027

Candidates are still being reviewed for the chief executive position. The group continues to carry out interviews for board positions with more to take place over the coming weeks, City AM understands. 

The industry-owned organisation is partnered with the Treasury and Bank of England to usher in the next generation UK retail payments infrastructure. Mastercard and Visa are also understood to have participated in the foundation work of the project.

To join the group, firms must be authorised, regulated or overseen by the Financial Conduct Authority, Prudential Regulation Authority or central bank for banking or payment activities. They also must hold a strategic connection to the UK retail payments system and consider an equity investment in the Delivery Company. 

The Bank of England’s Retail Payments Infrastructure Board (RPIB) is expected to deliver its first formal blueprint for the programme in the first quarter of 2027.

A spokesperson for the Payments Delivery Company declined to comment.

articles.title: Manchester United drone YouTuber apologises and denies Liverpool put him up to it
articles.summary:
The YouTuber who used a drone to film and publish footage of Manchester United training has insisted he was not put up to it by rival clubs.

The content creator behind the account CC Overview, who has until now specialised in aerial footage of stadium constructions, apologised for filming Mauricio Pochettino’s first session as United manager yesterday.

He added that he had not broken any laws but had removed the 12-minute video, which had already been widely shared, and denied acting on behalf of other clubs including Liverpool, United’s opponents on Sunday.

“I would like to speak about yesterday’s incident,” he wrote in a community post on his YouTube channel’s page.

“A total error of judgement on my part led to me filming some of the Manchester United training session at Carrington, whilst the flight was legal in terms of drone laws I fully accept it was unethical on my part.

“My aim was to picture Mauricio Pochettino in his United training kit for the supporters to see for the first time. I had wrongly presumed that with it being close to the start of the session that no meaningful training sessions would have started so would have been some harmless warming up shown. I also wrongly assumed that the training session would have been open to various media outlets.

Apology to United and Pochettino

“I would like to apologise to Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino and the players for my actions and sincerely hope those actions do not affect the outcome of any match.

“I would also like to state that Liverpool Football club or any other football club were not involved in my decision to film at Carrington yesterday.”

Pochettino was taking his first training session after being appointed as United’s new head coach last week, succeeding Michael Carrick who was sacked with the club in the relegation zone heading into the international window.

articles.title: Mothercare future hangs in balance after Boots and Middle East blow
articles.summary:
High street darling Mothercare may be sold or broken up as soon as Christmas after its chair called for a swift end to a strategic review launched to avoid it running out of cash in months.

The AIM-listed retailer posted a £2.2m loss before tax in the six months to 27 September, while sales fell 14 per cent after a succession of blows to its earnings.

Mothercare lost a key distribution deal with high street giant Boots, and in September warned its future was “highly uncertain” after a Middle East franchise partner shuttered the majority of its stores in the region.

Net debt at the embattled retailer, which sells baby products online and through partners in the UK, ballooned to £9.3m in September, up from £5.8m over the same period the previous year.

Mothercare chair Clive Whiley said the barrage of headwinds had “seriously undermined” the firm’s ability to continue operations.

“Accordingly, although Mothercare has sufficient resources to trade for a number of months, the imperative now is to prioritise discussions to conclude our strategic review of all business and pensions scheme options before the end of the year,” he said.

The group is part-way through a strategic review kicked off after the sudden loss of its Middle Eastern store, which Whiley branded a “heavy blow” when revealing it to shareholders in September.

Mothercare in pension deficit

Alongside the review, the company is locked in a thorny pension deficit negotiations. As part of efforts to turn the under-fire business around, it has not been paying pension contributions, and its pension deficit now stands at £6m.

The business was dealt a further blow by the ongoing Iran war, which has hampered trading in its remaining stores in the Middle East.

Whiley said: “The scheduled closure of the substantial majority of our leading Middle Eastern franchise partners’ franchised stores in the territory in 2027 has seriously undermined our core objectives.”

The company said it was pressing ahead with the appointment of a new franchise partner in the Middle East as one of several last-ditch measures to turn the firm around. It is also engaged in talks with new partners in the UK and has received “expressions of interest” in its intellectual property from overseas.

articles.title: Tech stocks fall as Anthropic fails to revive AI trade
articles.summary:
Technology stocks in Asia fell on Friday as Anthropic’s blockbuster debut failed to reignite the faltering AI trade.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s Kospi led the decline in the region, sinking 5.1 per cent over the course of trading.

Soft Bank suffered the largest loss in Japan, falling 14.4 per cent to 3,025 won (£1.7).

AI jitters also spread over to Taiwan, home to chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) , where the Taiex tumbled 6.2 per cent as it heads towards its biggest weekly decline since 1991, down 17.1 per cent. TSMC suffered a 4.7 per cent decline.

The sell-off in Asia was triggered by declines across Wall Street, with the Nasdaq Composite Index closing 2.3 per cent lower, marking its lowest closing value since April 14, despite rising 2.2 per cent mid-morning.

US chipmakers also suffered sharp falls, with Nvidia slipping 3.3 per cent, despite receiving a boost in early trading, closing at $145.9 (£111.2).

Micron and Broadcom both fell 2.1 per cent respectively. Intel managed to avoid wider losses, gaining 2.1 per cent, after it announced the signing of a new customer for its chips.

The S&P 500 fell two per cent, while the Dow Jones slid 2.1 per cent.

“Enthusiasm did not last long,” said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote.

“The wake of Anthropic’s IPO is quite rough. The blockbuster debut couldn’t sweep those worries under the rug.”

Anthropic shares popped

Anthropic shares popped 17 per cent to close above its listing price on its market debut, as investors raced to get their hands on the equity at the centre of the AI boom.

Shares opened at $111.5 on Thursday, nearly 35 per cent above its initial price of $83.

The Claude maker’s stock continued to soar over the course of trading to nearly as much as 39 per cent over the listing price, before ultimately closing at $97.1.

The AI lab also secured a market valuation of £1.3 trillion at Thursday’s closing price, or $1.7 trillion fully diluted. 

The share price had fallen below the price of SpaceX at the end of its first day.

The jump in share price granted the company’ seven co-founders, who quit OpenAI to start a rival firm,a fortune of around $23bn each. The IPO also turned the majority of the lab’s staff into paper millionaires.

Widespread interest

The Silicon Valley lab upsized its global share offering from 825m shares to 980m shares.

The offering attracted orders almost seven times the shares available, selling around 3.6m shares in the UK alone, amounting to around $300m, according to regulatory filings.

Nearly 9.7m shares were sold to investors in the European Union, Norway and Switzerland, raising $801m.

Institutional investors also scrambled to try to secure equity, but around half of this group received no shares while retail  investors were also allocated a lower than expected 15 per cent.

Thursday’s valuation makes Anthropic the sixth most valuable public company in the world, behind Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet and Amazon.

articles.title: Government stockpiling push helps boost retail sales
articles.summary:
Retail sales grew unexpectedly last month as shoppers snapped up stockpiling essentials on advice from the government.

The volume of retail sales in the UK grew by 0.7 per cent in October, despite expectations of flat growth, up from a drop of 0.6 per cent in September, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Rising spending comes amid a slight improvement in consumer confidence. The closely-watched GfK index bounced two points to -22 in November, after falling to its lowest level since Brexit in October.

Last month’s unexpected jump in retail sales was driven by rising demand in supermarkets for “emergency items such as UHT milk and tinned goods,” analysts at the ONS said.

This comes after the government launched its ‘Be Ready’ campaign last month, which urged Brits to build up a three-day supply of tinned food and bottled water in the event of a cyber attack or extreme weather event. 

Supermarkets have reported higher spending on long-life products following the stockpiling orders, and tinned tuna maker Princes said earlier this month it has seen “an increase in demand” for its goods.

Non-food sales rose faster than the overall rate, by 1.1 per cent, driven by rising spending on art galleries, sports equipment and toy stores. 

The ONS said in-store clothing sales increased in October, as shoppers bought more items per visit after their spending was constrained in September due to “inventory issues” at some big retailers. 

Stockpiling boost ‘one-off’

Sandra Prince, head of corporate consumer at Lloyds, said: “While this might be a short-term spike, it shows how quickly shoppers react to changing circumstances. Interestingly, some retailers are now rethinking traditional seasonal stock and moving towards more frequent monthly adjustments to reflect the changing weather conditions.”

But Rajeev Shaunak, head of consumer at consultancy MHA, said October’s stockpiling boost is “probably a one-off which hides the challenges facing retailers as they head into the crucial festive trading season”.

He added: “Squeezed budgets and fragile consumer confidence leave little room for spending beyond the essentials. Black Friday may tempt shoppers to open their wallets, but a rush for discounts is not the same as a recovery in demand.”

October’s pick-up in spending came ahead of a slight recovery in consumer confidence this month, as reported by GfK. Following October’s “dramatic” deterioration, November brought “some welcome relief,” said consumer insights director Neil Bellamy. 

He added: “That should reassure manufacturers and retailers ahead of the crucial Black Friday and Christmas trading period that there are still people out there willing to spend. Perceptions of the wider economy have also improved.”

But both GfK’s consumer confidence and purchasing indices remain in deeply negative territory, suggesting that “confidence remains fragile and vulnerable to further economic pressures in the months ahead,” Bellamy said.

articles.title: British fintech Oaknorth lands US banking licence
articles.summary:
British fintech Oaknorth has secured a US banking permit after its expansion across the Atlantic helped lift revenue over the last year.

The small business lender has landed a full-fat US National Banking Charter from the Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC).

It will allow the firm to become a US bank holding company following its acquisition of Michigan’s Community Unity Bank. 

Earlier this year, the Federal Reserve ordered Oaknorth to switch its domicile from Jersey in order to get the regulatory green light for the takeover.

Rishi Khosla, founder of Oaknorth, said the permit would allow the firm to support more of the nation’s “banking needs” and serve entrepreneurs in the lower mid-market.

The licence will pave the way for Oaknorth to expand beyond lending and offer a broader range of banking products and services, including checking and savings accounts.

Oaknorth turns to US for growth

The US has become a fruitful area of expansion for Oaknorth over the last year. The total volume of new loans across the group reached $1.4bn in 2025, more than trebling from $400m in 2024. Originations in the US made up around 40 per cent of new lending for the group.

In March, Oaknorth’s annual report said the US provided “growth opportunity” while the UK was a “subdued environment” with a more “challenging lending backdrop than expected”.

The new regulatory win makes Oaknorth the first foreign digital bank to secure a US National Banking Charter.

Several European giants have sought approval this year, including payments firm Wise and neobank Bunq, which both had initial efforts blocked by the regulator.

Revolut cleared the first hurdle to a full US permit earlier this year after receiving conditional approval from the OCC. The process marks the firm’s second bid for a US permit after it made a play at the state-level in March 2021 through Californian regulators.

articles.title: Government borrowing rose higher than expected before Budget
articles.summary:
Government borrowing rose higher than expected in the lead-up to the Budget in October, official data has shown, as a heap of spending pressures put the Chancellor in a precarious position. 

Government borrowing in October, the difference between spending and tax receipts, came in above forecasts set by the Office for Budget Responsibility earlier this year, as about £11.2bn in spending on debt interest and £29.3bn on benefits piled pressure on the Chancellor. 

Borrowing reached £17bn, which was more than five per cent higher than last year and £800m above the OBR’s previous projections. It was the third-highest October borrowing figure since monthly records began.

The rise in borrowing levels largely came in the lead-up to the fiscal statement delivered on 28 October, where Healey set out nearly 100 policies largely designed to ease the cost of living on business.

Figures suggest that public borrowing could top four per cent of GDP for the seventh year in a row, according to Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics.

Debt interest problems

The Office for National Statistics measured public debt as a share of GDP at 95.8 per cent, higher than at the same time last year.

“Income-related taxes’ receipts grew particularly strongly,” said Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS.

“However, monthly borrowing was up on last October, partly due to higher debt interest.”

The latest set of borrowing figures reflect the intense difficulty the Chancellor faces in restraining spending after about £70bn of cumulative tax hikes made in the first two years of Labour in government. 

Healey’s borrowing problem

The state of public finances will come into focus ahead of next year’s crunch Spending Review, where Healey is expected to pull cash from some areas of the state to fund Andy Burnham’s priorities.

Healey has said that Cabinet ministers are tasked with finding cuts and savings across government departments in order to fund support for defence, supporting young people into work and long-term policies in the Prime Minister’s upcoming 10-year plan. 

In the near term, departments could face a squeeze in spending due to higher inflation, which is expected to peak as high as five per cent in the middle of next year. 

The Chancellor has argued that “innovative” financing will help the UK raise defence spending to three per cent of GDP by 2030. 

Separately, the government is under pressure to accept Alan Milburn’s proposals for up-front investment in employment support and tax cuts for businesses. 

According to reports in the Financial Times, there is “resistance” to the idea that employers’ National Insurance contributions should be cut for under-25-year-old workers. 

Milburn said cuts in taxes should occur over a five-year period and first be targeted at the hospitality and retail sectors.  

The spread of decisions facing Healey in the run-up to next year’s Spending Review will be closely watched by City figures.  

Speaking to MPs on the Treasury Committee, Healey refused to rule out imposing further tax rises before the next round of budget settlements.

Chief secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds said: “Fiscal discipline underpins the decisions this government makes everyday. Britain is showing stand-out resilience despite the global impact of the conflict in Iran. We’re building on that.

“This year we’ve cut borrowing faster than any other G20 country. Now we’re going to cut waste and bureaucracy by reprioritising spending and making public services more efficient with AI.”

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: “These latest borrowing figures show the government has lost control of the public finances.”

articles.title: As it happened: FTSE 100 falls as Anthropic rattles global markets
articles.summary:
Welcome back to City AM‘s FTSE 100 liveblog.

It’s Friday and the FTSE 100 is falling as the AI trade comes into focus following the blockbuster IPO of Anthropic.

The Claude maker surged over 17 per cent in its first trading session after raising $81bn in its New York float.

But global markets are feeling the impact with shares in Japan’s Softbank plunging some 16 per cent overnight, leading a broader sell-off in Asian technology stocks. Softbank is one of the biggest backers of OpenAI, a major rival to Anthropic, with it having invested a total of $64.6bn in the ChatGPT maker.

Stick with us for all the latest business and economic news from global markets.

Here’s a few of our top headlines this morning:

articles.title: Prem Rugby expansion should start with a proper London club
articles.summary:
On Wednesday Prem Rugby launched the first step in expanding the English top flight from 10 to 12 teams by formally inviting expressions of interest.

It is a big moment for the competition, having been cut to 10 teams after three – London Irish, Worcester Warriors and Wasps – all fell into financial difficulties. While the remaining teams have managed to stabilise a listing ship, successfully expanding will mark the league passing a key milestone on the way to profitability.

We can expect the three aforementioned clubs, in their new forms, to express interest, while a number of Champ Rugby teams and ambitious start-ups could also get involved at this early stage. This step of the process is open until February before a full tender later next year.

We could see an audacious entry from a Welsh team with one eye on being cut from the regional game across the River Severn, or a new stadium and fan base in a previously untouched part of the UK. Where would I start, though? A proper London club.

Prem Rugby expansion

Despite their established homes – in Twickenham and Barnet – I just don’t really associate either Harlequins or Saracens with being a proper London club, no matter how much the latter tries to push its narrative.

For me, Wasps in White City or London Irish’s spell in Brentford felt like more authentic London teams, and the return of a central side within zones one or two would be great fun.

It could be someone like Ealing Trailfinders, who yet again find themselves at the top of the second tier, the Champ, but they’ve long had issues with their ground in west London. Elsewhere, a reincarnated London Irish would be a shoo-in for me as an expansion franchise.

Beyond the capital you’re likely to see regions without top-flight clubs given priority, I should think. Whether that be a new Yorkshire team based out of Leeds or the mooted Sevenoaks development by Wasps, it will be interesting to see where Prem Rugby sees growth.

If Christopher Holland’s bid to rebuild Wasps is successful, he will not be able to own both the former European champions and Champ Rugby side Worcester Warriors. The latter, then, could be sold into the ownership of another organisation.

Further afield

One option could be the reported franchise bidders Knighthead Capital – owners of Birmingham City – who could base the team out of the M5 corridor while playing key matches in the second city, adding to a growing portfolio which includes the Birmingham Phoenix Hundred team.

Stadiums are less important, so long as fans are turning up, but new clubs can easily be held to higher entry standards than existing ones – as is the case with expansion teams in the US. I would ensure they have links to universities and schools, in place of academies, before they join, and mandate a financial security mechanism so that they can’t fold after a few seasons.

Growth is exciting but Prem Rugby must ensure this is done correctly, and strategically, because to get this wrong is to return the top flight to its status a few years back: staring into an abyss, being chased by an impending doom it has somehow managed to avoid.

Former England Sevens captain Ollie Phillips is the founder of Optimist Performance. Follow Ollie @OlliePhillips11

articles.title: Cleverly vows to fight Burnham on tax and red tape in London
articles.summary:
Sir James Cleverly has vowed to battle Andy Burnham on business taxes and red tape in London as he pledged to be the capital’s “primary salesman”. 

At the end of a three-hour boat trip down the River Thames, Cleverly told City AM that he envisaged “rowing with central government to ease the cost and the burden of regulation that’s holding London back” if he becomes mayor. 

In an interview onboard the small boat, the newly-announced Conservative candidate for mayor of London also said he would regard being mayor as the “most important job”. 

His top priority will be to make the capital safe, adding that “hiding” from evidence that crime was worsening “doesn’t benefit Londoners or the people that visit London or work in London”. 

“I will always push back against misinformation and disinformation and people trying to talk London down,” Cleverly said. 

“But ultimately, the mayor of London has got to deal with the reality, and the reality is crime has gone up, and police numbers have gone down, and that is Khan’s fault, and I intend to do something about it.”

Cleverly argued that the mayor had to be the “primary salesperson for London”, citing his experience as foreign secretary as part of his plan to support workers and businesses driving the country’s richest region. 

But in a sign of his potential battles as a Tory mayor under a Labour government, Cleverly said much of his time could be spent arguing for lower taxes and less red tape to be introduced by ministers. 

“I want to make it cheaper and easier to start a business, grow a business, and employ people. 

“Some of that is in the mayor’s direct control, and a lot of that, frankly, will be me rowing with central government to ease the cost and the burden of regulation that’s holding London back.”

Cleverly hits out at devolution

He also questioned whether Burnham was presiding over devolution, saying he saw devolution as the “opportunity for people to put up taxes”. 

“I want to make sure that when I attract business and investment to London, that London benefits from that and doesn’t have that money taken off it by central government and wasted on vanity projects in other parts of the country.”

Potential Labour opponents are yet unknown. Sir Sadiq Khan has not yet commented on whether he will stand again in 2028.

Cleverly refused to be drawn on which Labour candidate he would like to face in 2028.

The former home secretary said he would not get “distracted” by competitors’ messages on returning to the European Union, claiming he would “focus on the things that Londoners want fixed, the powers the Mayor actually has, and the influence that the Mayor actually can bring to bear”. 

‘Mamdani takes his job seriously – Khan doesn’t’

Digital campaigning has also radically changed since leftist Democrat Zohran Mamdani became New York City’s mayor at the beginning of the year. Cleverly hinted at leading Whatsapp groups and posting more short-form videos to boost his campaign. 

Speaking about Mamdani, Cleverly said: “I disagree with much of his politics, but he takes the job seriously. He is passionate about being Mayor. He’s had more cut-through and influence in a week than Khan has had in a decade. 

“The point is, the person putting themselves forward to be mayor of London should regard that as the most important job they can possibly do.”
