articles.title: English village votes to "leave UK"
articles.summary: Residents of the small English village of Barnham voted on Saturday in a symbolic referendum to leave the UK, in protest against government plans to house 931 asylum seekers at a nearby former air force base – more than the village’s own population of 584. The vote follows a similar protest in another village in September, highlighting growing tensions over immigration across the country. Earlier this week, the leader of a far-right anti-immigration group was jailed, but supporters have vowed to keep the movement alive. Jack Pownall reports.

articles.title: 'GTA VI': When the biggest-ever entertainment release becomes the biggest headline
articles.summary: This week FRANCE 24's media show "Scoop" looks at how the press covered the release of "Grand Theft Auto VI". Pre-orders and first-day sales totalled more than $2.3 billion. What does the game and the franchise's success mean for the future of entertainment? Our guest is Margaret Wallace, a video game developer and an associate professor of the practice of media innovation at Boston University.

articles.title: Anthropic shares slide on second day of trading as AI jitters fuel tech sell-off
articles.summary: Anthropic's much-hyped arrival on Wall Street fizzled out on Friday as ​nosediving tech stocks showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector. Shares in the AI firm dipped below $90, one day after soaring to over $110 during a record-breaking Nasdaq debut.

articles.title: Anthropic goes public after blockbuster IPO but fails to revive AI trade
articles.summary: Anthropic has become the first pure-play AI developer to be publicly traded on the stock market, following a record-setting IPO. The stock opened 34 percent higher, briefly valuing the company at more than $2 trillion, before ending its first day of trading up 17 percent. However, Wall Street indexes closed sharply lower as investors took profits, reflecting underlying market jitters about the AI trade.

articles.title: How much do businesses want to pay for AI?
articles.summary: Four years after ChatGPT went mainstream, generative AI is transforming how we live and work. It's also been a major driver of economic growth, with massive amounts of money poured into expanding global computing capacity. But now, there are signs of a slowdown in AI spending as companies take a reality check: are they getting sufficient returns on their investments and how much artificial intelligence do they actually need?

articles.title: Anthropic blows past $2 trillion in Nasdaq debut, beating SpaceX's June listing
articles.summary: Anthropic hit $2 trillion in market value as its shares soared in their Nasdaq debut on Thursday, with investors rushing to own a stake in the maker of the Claude chatbot, the world's first publicly traded frontier AI company. Shares began trading at $111.5, 34% higher than the IPO price of $83.

articles.title: AI lab Anthropic sets stock market record with $81 billion IPO
articles.summary: Anthropic becomes the first "pure play" AI lab to go public, with an eye-watering $1.5 trillion valuation, a bellwether moment amid growing concerns of a financial bubble in the sector. Meanwhile, a scientific study shows US data centres are emitting as much greenhouse gas as entire nations.

articles.title: Inside Limoges city hall, devastated by arson attack during French riots
articles.summary: Work is underway to restore the city hall of Limoges, in central France, which was devastated by an arson attack during riots on October 17. More than €1.7 million has been raised through an online fundraising campaign in the wake of the disaster. Also on the show, the highly anticipated video game "Grand Theft Auto VI" has finally been released, with gamers in Oceania among the first to get a taste of the latest instalment in the franchise.

articles.title: 'Extreme wealth can become a type of brain damage': Journalist Alexander Hurst
articles.summary: An international journalist who poured his meagre savings into highly risky options trading at the start of the Covid-19 pandemic and quickly made $1.2 million, before losing it all again, has spoken to FRANCE 24 about his experience. Alexander Hurst works for a number of media outlets, including the Guardian as a correspondent based in Paris.

articles.title: 'Failures, incompetence, broken promises': Deutsche Bank exposed in major leak
articles.summary: PRESS REVIEW – Wednesday, November 18: A joint investigation following the leak of 15 million documents shows that Deutsche Bank turned a blind eye to the criminal activities of some of its clients. Next, for its 175th birthday, The New York Times has chosen the top 10 stories that made history. Wired is focusing on the moments that defined 2026. Finally, we bring you a story about American parents whose children dream of becoming Formula 1 drivers. But how much does that dream cost?

articles.title: Nvidia posts blockbuster quarterly results amid leadership crisis
articles.summary: AI chipmaker Nvidia posted Q3 revenues double those of last year and 20 percent higher than last quarter, while the company board says it has no intention of reinstating disgraced former CEO Jensen Huang. Also in this edition: gaming tourists flock to Miami amid a marketing blitz for the upcoming release of the latest edition in the "Grand Theft Auto" franchise.

articles.title: AI giant Anthropic to start trading after record-breaking market debut
articles.summary: Anthropic on Wednesday is expected to finalise the pricing for its initial public offering amid a volatile stock market rattled by the Nvidia spy scandal, setting the stage for what is expected to be America's second-biggest IPO after the record set by SpaceX in June. The AI lab is considering pricing its shares in a range of around $80 to $85 each, according to Bloomberg News.

articles.title: COP31 climate talks end without consensus on how to fund vulnerable countries or move the world away from coal, oil and gas use
articles.summary: After two weeks of tough talks, the COP31 climate summit has closed without a consensus on how to quit fossil fuels or fund countries struggling to adapt to a hotter world.

articles.title: China, ASEAN countries struggle over South China Sea code of conduct
articles.summary: The Philippines wanted a South China Sea code of conduct in place by 2026. But persistent disagreements between China and ASEAN countries are slowing progress toward a deal.

articles.title: Dozens missing as deadly fire hits Indonesian candy factory
articles.summary: At least three people were killed in a devastating fire at a confectionery factory on Java. Officials said many more people remain unaccounted for, prompting fears of a much larger tragedy.

articles.title: Mexican special forces arrest drug kingpin 'Chapo Isidro'
articles.summary: The alleged leader of the Beltran Leyva gang and one of the FBI's most wanted fugitives, known as "Chapo Isidro," was captured by the Mexican military following a raid and a shootout in the coastal state of Sinaloa.

articles.title: Russian helicopter suspected of violating Finnish airspace
articles.summary: Finland's Defense Ministry thinks the incursion is linked to a drone strike earlier Saturday on a Russian cargo ship, which is on a US sanctions list.

articles.title: EU and Indonesia sign trade deal
articles.summary: A deal covering 730 million people promises lower tariffs and new investment opportunities as the European Union seeks to diversify trade ties amid growing global economic tensions.

articles.title: New EU budget proposal aims at tax gobal tech giants
articles.summary: European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a smaller EU budget for 2028-2034, including a 3% tax on major digital firms to ease member states' contributions. France has already rejected the plan as inadequate.

articles.title: Russia strikes Zelenskyy's hometown, killing 2
articles.summary: The attacks follow Russian President Vladimir Putin's vow of a "painful" response to Ukraine's attacks this week on the Kerch Bridge, linking Russian-occupied Crimea.

articles.title: Anthropic researcher uses AI to solve math's greatest riddle
articles.summary: The proposed breakthrough could reshape mathematical research, but still needs independent verification. It's the latest in a string of cases where AI has outpaced humans in solving famous maths problems.

articles.title: Man convicted of arson over deadly 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles
articles.summary: A 30-year-old man has been convicted of causing one of the most destructive wildfires in the history of Los Angeles. The verdict came after the case was retried.

articles.title: Brazil ex-President Jair Bolsonaro taken to hospital over abdominal pain
articles.summary: Jair Bolsonaro has been hospitalized in Brasilia with intestinal obstruction. The former far-right Brazilian leader is receiving pain medications, his son Carlos said.

articles.title: COP31: No agreement on climate science, disinformation spreading
articles.summary: Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

articles.title: Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?
articles.summary: German automakers are pulling back on investments at home, sparking fresh anxiety about the auto sector's future. Some industry watchers think there is still a narrow window to stem the decline. But how?

articles.title: Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports
articles.summary: According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned.

articles.title: Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?
articles.summary: From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?

articles.title: Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
articles.summary: Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.

articles.title: No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal
articles.summary: One of the most fraught debates at the UN climate talks in Turkey has revolved around the future of coal, oil and gas. Now, all mention of fossil fuels has been removed from the summit's new draft agreement.

articles.title: Anthropic trading tests investors' appetite for AI
articles.summary: Anthropic was valued at $2 trillion after shares started trading on the Nasdaq following a record $81 billion IPO. Its performance will put investor confidence in AI to the test.

articles.title: Iran balances ties with China and Russia as Trump ramps up pressure
articles.summary: As Donald Trump seeks to tighten economic pressure on Iran, China remains its biggest oil customer and Russia a key partner. But both powers are balancing support for Tehran against broader interests with Washington.

articles.title: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
articles.summary: The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms and the Nvidia scandal has cast doubt on Anthropic's IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.

articles.title: How a green economy could help reverse climate change
articles.summary: Green growth promises a future in which economies thrive without destroying the environment. But is this vision realistic?

articles.title: Nvidia forms national security committee after Huang affair
articles.summary: Nvidia has created a board-level committee for national security and export control. This follows the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over extramarital affairs, allegedly including one with a Chinese intelligence asset.

articles.title: Could the Airbus €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?
articles.summary: The US says a record €3 billion financing package for Airbus may conflict with a transatlantic aircraft-subsidy truce. EU officials insist the funding complies with market-based rules.

articles.title: COP31 draft deal calls for 'immediate' shift away from fossil fuels
articles.summary: The preliminary agreement at UN climate talks in Turkey calls for a rapid reduction of planet-warming emissions and at least $120 billion to help countries adapt to climate change.

articles.title: Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?
articles.summary: In April, about 60 countries held an unprecedented meeting in Colombia to work out a plan to slowly quit oil, coal and gas. How influential is this coalition at the COP31 climate summit?

articles.title: Lucy Powell promotes UK education in China despite risks
articles.summary:
LONDON — Education Secretary Lucy Powell will travel to Beijing this week to promote closer ties between schools and universities in the two countries, as the U.K. government makes a fresh push for high-level engagement with China.

She will take part in a U.K.-China summit — the first for nine years — aimed at helping British educational institutions and businesses build new links with Beijing.

The trip is expected to expand opportunities for British providers of vocational training, overseas campuses, online learning and the export of educational materials such as textbooks, learning platforms and classroom supplies.

Powell’s visit comes days after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting hosted his Chinese counterpart, Dong Jun, in London. Streeting praised Andy Burnham’s government for having “stepped up our interaction with China.”

Powell said ahead of the summit that education was one of Britain’s “greatest strengths” and “expanding that internationally is a massive opportunity for our economy and wider society.”

She vowed to use it to “support growth, strengthen our global standing and stand up for what matters to Britain.”

Closer cooperation on education will form part of “clear-eyed engagement with China” by the government, she said, as she promised to champion freedom of speech and academic freedom during her trip.

Her efforts to promote British education abroad come despite the security services warning about the scale of Chinese attempts to spy on the U.K.

More than 100 academics linked to British institutions have unwittingly assisted China’s espionage operations by taking funding from a Chinese spy agency, MI5, the U.K.’s domestic intelligence agency, revealed in September.

Powell specified that she would seek to “protect U.K. institutions from any collaborations that could undermine national security, or attempts to benefit covertly from research done in partnership with U.K. universities.”

U.K. officials said the trip would recognize the contribution of the 150,000 Chinese students currently studying at U.K. universities rather than actively seeking to invite more.

articles.title: Global climate talks have collapsed. Here’s what just happened.
articles.summary:
ANTALYA, Turkey — There’s an old adage in politics: never let a crisis go to waste. Yet governments at crucial U.N. climate talks just did exactly that.

The Antalya summit lurched to a chaotic conclusion Sunday when a draft deal on tackling global warming collapsed, despite a desperate scramble for an agreement which had already taken negotiations 48 hours over the scheduled finish.

Countries failed to strike a final agreement despite fresh scientific warnings and an energy price shock which many governments said offered more momentum than ever for ditching planet-heating fossil fuels.

That means countries are leaving Antalya after two weeks of intense negotiations with only a handful of technical agreements to their name. There is no political deal to show how they intend to pull the planet back from the verge of dangerous climate change.

U.N. climate chief Simon Stiell stressed that the summit made “real progress,” despite the lack of agreement on the main text (called the “cover decision”).

Others weren’t as generous.

“This ridiculous system of having absolute consensus, where 192 countries and 100,000 people who are here in Antalya agree on absolutely everything, it’s a recipe for disaster,” Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s climate minister, told POLITICO earlier in the week. “COPs have turned into a laughing stock.”

‘Complicated and fraught’

Governments arrived in Turkey knowing the world stands on a precipice. This summit marked the first climate conference since the U.N. announced the world was sure to overshoot the target to limit long-term global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.

“The situation coming into this talk was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory, and also, in ways I very much sympathize with, the impacts of climate change [are] getting worse,” Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who co-hosted the talks, told reporters Sunday.

Missing the 1.5C target, the Paris Agreement’s most ambitious aim, loomed large in Turkey. Many nations cited the impending overshoot as justification for agreements to make deeper cuts to pollution, take stronger action to prepare for disasters and increase financial support for poorer countries.

But countries rich in oil and gas resources fought to keep any mention of fossil fuels — the main cause of global warming — out of the final text, while wealthy nations were reluctant to commit to specific funding goals. 

U.N. Climate Change executive secretary Simon Stiell speaks to media after the COP31 U.N. climate summit in Antalya on Nov. 22, 2026. | Yasin Akgul/AFP via Getty Images

The final impasse that brought down the talks revolved around the future of energy. A coalition of 130 countries, led by the European Union and small island states, demanded the COP31 text include a reference to a three-year-old commitment to phase out fossil fuels. But that was too much for some petrostates. Even recommitting to this earlier agreement was a red line for countries such as Saudi Arabia.

Another point of conflict was a paragraph in earlier drafts of the deal that appeared to put contentious carbon capture technologies on equal footing with clean power sources such as renewables. The anti-fossils coalition wanted those references deleted, arguing they catered to Riyadh’s interests to prolong the use of oil and gas.

On Sunday, Saudi Arabia pushed back. “We cannot reconcile a position that stated so publicly that we need to keep 1.5 degrees within reach, and yet called carbon capture, utilization, and storage technologies greenwashing,” said country negotiator Mohammad Ayoub.

In a fractious final plenary session, the EU and small islands, alongside the United Kingdom, Norway, Switzerland, several Latin American nations and a group of the world’s poorest countries, rejected the deal drawn up by Turkey and Australia, the conference co-hosts. 

“We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5 degrees back to within reach,” said Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU. 

“We will not endorse a cover decision,” he added, “that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time.”

All Turkish minister Murat Kurum, presiding over the talks, could do was admit defeat. He walked off the plenary floor not long after, before the conference — which had by then turned into the longest climate summit in its 30-year history — had ended. 

Some pointed to deals made on the margins of the talks, in the so-called action agenda, as well as the conclusion of technical agreements, as evidence the U.N. climate process was still working.

“I share the disappointment of many,” Stiell told reporters Sunday evening. “We must also recognize that this COP process has two tracks, and across the action agenda COP31 has delivered real progress and concrete results.”

Let down

The conference was not always destined to end in disarray. The geopolitical momentum was on the Turkish-Australian presidency’s side. 

Beside U.N. warnings about overshooting the 1.5°C barrier, the talks coincided with growing public anger over high fossil fuel prices caused by the Iran war. Many governments around the world, alarmed at rising costs of oil and gas imports over which they had little control, were already speeding up their switch to clean energy, citing affordability and sovereignty as well as climate action.

Co-hosts Australia and Turkey sought to harness that crisis through proposals to accelerate efforts to replace fuel-burning gasoline-powered cars with electric alternatives such as EVs.

But their proposed flagship target to increase electricity’s share in the world’s energy consumption from 23% today to 35% in 2035, included in the final draft text, was rejected along with everything else.

It was discussions around the electricity target that started the debate that, ultimately, led to the conference’s breakdown. 

The International Energy Agency says that to reach net-zero emissions by the middle of this century — a key effort to meet the Paris Agreement goals — the global electrification rate must increase in line with that proposed target, but also that clean power like wind and solar must supply 90% of electricity by then — up from 42% today.

That pushed several countries to lobby for an agreement on “clean” electrification — to ensure that the electrification push does not open the door to more high-polluting coal, oil or gas. 

“EU citizens will not accept a fossil fuel COP,” a senior European official said Friday afternoon, warning of a “no-deal scenario” over “insufficient language on clean electrification” in a draft version of the accord.  

The EU then teamed up with small island states and dozens of other nations that had backed a push for exiting fossil fuels at last year’s conference in Brazil. Together, the gang of more than 100 nations marched into the presidency offices on Saturday night to state their demands: a reference to the previous energy transition agreement and the deletion of the Saudi-linked carbon capture text.

When tweaks to the text during the final plenary did not deliver what they wanted, many of these countries rejected the text outright. 

“We came here expecting the world to deliver a comprehensive and urgent response on reducing emissions, on protecting our people, and on providing the finance to do this,” said Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, a negotiator for the Marshall Islands. “We have been let down on all sides.”

Not all countries rejected the text. China, India and a group of African nations said they would not stand in the way of its adoption. U.N. climate summit decisions, however, require consensus from all the nearly 200 nations in attendance. 

Tired and tetchy

Discontent with the Australian-Turkish co-hosts started brewing early this week. 

A first draft of the deal — a laundry list of all possible demands from countries — baffled many national delegations when it was published on Monday. A second draft only came on Thursday, setting off days of shuttle diplomacy behind closed doors.

After many delays, a third and supposedly final draft decision appeared just after midnight Sunday, long after the conference was meant to wrap. Exhausted and disgruntled diplomats were by then in no mood to make further concessions.

“The process is basically mismanaged,” Xolisa Joseph Ngwadla, an adviser to the chair of the African negotiating group, told reporters Saturday. “We haven’t seen text in more than 48 hours. We haven’t met as all parties in more than three days. We’ve all seen just snippets of text. That’s not conducive to a transparent and inclusive process to work towards an outcome. You don’t get an outcome like that.”

But the conference backdrop also spelled trouble. The stakes were low — while Australia and Turkey insisted on pushing for a political agreement, no blockbuster deal needed to be done. 

It was all happening while geopolitical tensions soared amid wars in Iran and Ukraine. A rising far right and tight budgets at home put many rich countries on the defensive — while many developing countries, reeling from worsening climate disasters and mounting debt, demanded more financial support. 

The EU, smarting from last year’s conference where it was left isolated pushing for more climate action, was gearing up for a fight. 

And the absence of the United States from the process, after President Donald Trump withdrew his country for the second time, shifted the power dynamics toward emerging economies. Privately, several European diplomats said that with the “old U.S.” in the room, Saudi Arabia could have been contained. 

The draft deal would also have done little to address the overshoot of 1.5°C, which scientists say can be brought back under control only through dramatic emissions cuts and large-scale deployment of technologies for sucking carbon from the atmosphere. Most such tech is unproven to work at the scale required.

European diplomats said Saudi Arabia even questioned the science behind the overshoot, suggesting that research is not settled unless it appeared in reports of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change — while simultaneously allegedly trying to delay future reports from the IPCC. The Saudi energy ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

An attempt to resolve the standoff over science, injected into the presidency’s draft decision, failed alongside the rest of the text. 

The talks also collided with skyrocketing global electricity demand, driven by the sudden expansion of data centers, modernizing economies and an explosive uptake in electric cars worldwide. 

Artificial intelligence alone poses new risks to international climate efforts, as tech companies increasingly use natural gas to run new power plants dedicated to data centers’ massive compute capacity. Yet the summit barely addressed those growing climate threats. 

Some negotiators tried to put a quick brave face on the collapse.

The EU and Britain both insisted they would continue pushing for global climate agreements. “Our position is not a rejection of multilateralism, but a defence of multilateralism that delivers,” Ireland’s O’Brien and the bloc’s climate chief Wopke Hoekstra said in a joint statement. 

“History will not judge COP31 by whether a decision was adopted, but by whether the international community rose to the challenge of our time,” they added.

This time, at least, it didn’t.

articles.title: Global left rallies in Paris to make ‘not so radical’ case for taxing billionaires
articles.summary:
PARIS — The left wants voters to know there is nothing radical about taxing billionaires.

“Radical would be cutting their heads off. But we are not proposing that,” former Chilean President Gabriel Boric told a summit against “international oligarchy” in Paris on Saturday. A minimum tax on the world’s largest fortunes, he said, is “arithmetic.”

Boric was among the left-wing politicians, union leaders and economists brought together by French economist Gabriel Zucman at the Théâtre de la Concorde, a city-owned venue within sight of the U.S. embassy and a short walk from the Elysée. 

The gathering drew lawmakers from the U.S. Congress and opposition leaders from Italy, Germany, Britain and the Netherlands, united in the belief that taxing the super-rich could help the left regain the political initiative.

Their pitch was that Zucman’s proposed annual minimum tax of 2% on billionaires’ wealth is a modest measure that most voters already support — and a potent answer to the far right.

“It’s the status quo which is radical,” said Zucman, who cites polls that put support for his tax in France at 86%.

“Remigration will not make your life better, but redistribution will,” said Elly Schlein, leader of Italy’s Democratic Party.

The summit ran for almost 12 hours in a hall the size of a small community theater that was packed for much of the day. Proceedings spilled into corridors and side rooms, where politicians and union leaders from the U.S., Europe and Latin America met between panels.

The event also marked the launch of the Paris Manifesto, a declaration against “international oligarchy” that pairs a minimum tax on the ultra-rich with protections for journalists and a new ownership model for AI companies. More than 100 researchers have signed it, including Nobel Prize-winning economists Joseph Stiglitz, Esther Duflo, Paul Krugman and Daron Acemoglu.

Most of those making the case were out of power, with Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani appearing by video message. Mamdani’s chief of staff, Elle Bisgaard-Church, attended and met European politicians and labor leaders.

The European Commission was not represented, while France’s presidential hopefuls stayed away ahead of next spring’s election. Their parties were represented by figures including Socialist leader Olivier Faure and Éric Coquerel, a lawmaker from the left-wing France Unbowed party who chairs the National Assembly’s finance committee.

Nobel Prize-winning economist Joseph Stiglitz, economists Gabriel Zucman and Jayati Ghosh, Californian trade unionist Dave Regan, economist Thomas Piketty and journalist Juliette Garside at the Paris summit against the oligarchy. | Daniel Perron/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

Musk, Bezos, Arnault

The billionaires were present in name throughout the day.

Jesse Klaver, parliamentary leader of Dutch progressive party Pro, opened his speech by saying he had spotted Bernard Arnault — head of French conglomerate LVMH and a frequent target of Zucman’s — on an evening walk in Paris’ tony 8th arrondissement on his way in.

“I [first] thought that you invited him too,” Klaver said. “That would have been a great idea actually, because he could see what energy is here in the room — and that he should be worried.”

Arnault, France’s richest man, has called Zucman a “far-left activist.” The economist said the fight over his tax in France last year showed him the reach of billionaire media owners, who he said control at least 85% of the country’s private press. An LVMH spokesperson declined to comment on Arnault.

Elon Musk drew the most fire. Zack Polanski, leader of the Green Party of England and Wales, said the Tesla chief had called him “a scumbag and a traitor,” and proposed a “Musk tax” on social media companies to fund local news. 

Nobel laureate Stiglitz cited Jeff Bezos’ ownership of the Washington Post as an example of the super-rich buying influence over the media. He dismissed warnings that billionaires would stop working if they were taxed: “They want to be top dog, alpha male,” he said.

Americans in Paris

The U.S. contingent arrived weeks after Democrats won control of Congress in midterm elections and after California voters rejected a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of billionaires.

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) told POLITICO he will introduce a billionaire tax bill with Bernie Sanders, the independent senator from Vermont, in the first week of the new Congress. “We need to have a fight in the Democratic primary about whether we’ll have a wealth tax,” he said, referring to the 2028 presidential race.

The internal Democratic Party argument on tax is largely settled, said Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) in an interview. “I think we’ve won that debate,” she told POLITICO.

Dave Regan, the union leader behind the California measure, said it lost only narrowly after its opponents spent close to $500 million. He said Gov. Gavin Newsom “should be ashamed of himself” for campaigning against it, and described “a bipartisan consensus at the very top of both political parties to defend the ultra rich.” Regan plans to put a permanent tax to voters in 2028, and is planning referendums in Nevada and Michigan.

Newsom’s office has argued that a state-only wealth tax would drive money and jobs out of California.

Both lawmakers had a message for Brussels, where European Council President António Costa is weighing a tax on U.S. tech giants. 

“I think you should be active with your tools,” Jayapal said of the EU’s rules for Big Tech. Khanna called for a transatlantic approach to tax and antitrust, and said “it should not be the United States bullying or dictating to Europe.”

Waiting for power

Europe’s left had a fresh win to show off: Dutch lawmakers last week narrowly passed a tax plan that raises wealth taxes to pay for cuts to payroll taxes after two centrist governing parties sided with Pro.

“For the first time, we are going to tax millionaires in the Netherlands,” Klaver said. “A divided left loses. A united left wins.”

Elsewhere, however, the idea is stuck, with the French Senate rejecting Zucman’s tax last year. EU tax laws, meanwhile, need the backing of all 27 governments.

Manon Aubry, co-chair of The Left group in the European Parliament, told POLITICO that a wealth tax should be part of talks on the EU’s next 7-year budget. “The left remains the only, or at least the main, political force that is pushing,” she said.

Dutch Greens MEP Ufuk Kâhya told POLITICO that Europe wants greater security and a stronger economy without settling the question who will pay for it all. Of the European Commission, he said: “They want to eat the cake. But no, you have to also bake it.”

In France, economist Thomas Piketty said a billionaire tax could pass by referendum, on one condition: “We need to win the presidential election. This is the only detail.” The French left has “lots of left-wing candidates. Maybe too many,” he added. France votes next spring.

Critics dispute that diagnosis. François Geerolf, an economist at Sciences Po’s OFCE economic think tank, has argued that Zucman overstates how lightly billionaires are taxed.

But for some in the room, a wealth tax doesn’t go far enough.

“We need to eliminate billionaires, not just tax them,” said author Naomi Klein, who called for a cap on wealth. University of Massachusetts Amherst economist Isabella Weber told POLITICO that “even if we had the most perfect wealth tax, I don’t think it would be enough” without measures to bring down the cost of living.

Regan had a suggestion for billionaires who threaten to leave if they are taxed.

“We should all put our money together and give them the means to get to Mars,” he said.

articles.title: Cyprus expels Russian diplomats on suspicion of espionage
articles.summary:
NICOSIA — Two Russian diplomats have been expelled from Cyprus on suspicion of espionage, two Cypriot officials confirmed over the weekend following a report by broadcaster ANT1 Live.

According to two senior government officials who were granted anonymity to discuss the matter freely, the country’s intelligence services have uncovered a network which was seeking to obtain classified information on the security of Cyprus and the European Union.

The network was also seeking access to information on technology prohibited for transfer to Russia under EU sanctions, the officials told POLITICO.

They added that the two diplomats were forced to leave Cyprus last week and were suspected of working for Russian intelligence under diplomatic cover. The men were in contact with Cypriot citizens who had access to confidential information, the officials said.

POLITICO contacted the Russian Embassy in Cyprus for comment on the matter but did not receive a response at the time of publication.

Moscow was once considered a primary source of foreign direct investment for Nicosia and the Mediterranean island previously served as a banking hub for Russian investors, from arms dealers to gambling firms.

But in recent years, EU sanctions, regulatory pressure and shifting geopolitical alignment have forced Nicosia to move away from these kinds of investments. Cyprus, an EU member, has backed the bloc’s escalating sanctions against Russia in the wake of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

European countries have expelled more than 700 Russian officials from diplomatic establishments since Russia began its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service.

articles.title: COP31 : l’accord capote sur fond de désaccord sur les énergies fossiles
articles.summary:
ANTALYA, Turquie — Les pays participant aux négociations de la COP31 ne sont pas parvenus à conclure un accord définitif après deux semaines de pourparlers très controversés. Les dirigeants ont rejeté un projet de décision qui effaçait toute référence aux combustibles fossiles et n’apportait qu’une réponse insuffisante à la hausse des températures.

L’Union européenne, le Panama et plusieurs autres pays, dont des petits Etats insulaires, ont déclaré rejeter l’accord proposé par la présidence de la COP31. D’autres intervenants ont pris la parole pour exprimer leurs inquiétudes concernant l’aide aux pays les plus exposés à la crise climatique, ainsi que sur certains passages du texte qui mettaient l’accent sur la nécessité de la capture et du stockage du carbone.

“Il semble que certaines parties s’opposent à ce texte, a déclaré Murat Kurum, président turc de la COP31. Je comprends qu’il n’y ait pas d’accord sur ce texte. C’est pour cette raison que ces décisions n’ont pas été adoptées.”

Près de 200 pays ont débattu sur différents aspects de la transition énergétique, et notamment l’impossibilité de limiter le réchauffement climatique à long terme à 1,5 ° au-dessus des niveaux préindustriels.

Alors que les négociations touchaient à leur fin, les parties n’ont pas réussi à surmonter leurs divergences. C’est la première fois en 17 ans, à Copenhague, que les négociations de la COP n’aboutissent pas à un accord.

“Il est inacceptable que nous ayons une décision-cadre qui ne fasse aucune référence aux combustibles fossiles […] C’est pour cette raison que l’Union européenne s’oppose fermement à ce texte”, a déclaré le ministre irlandais du Climat, Darragh O’Brien, s’exprimant au nom de l’UE.

Le Panama a qualifié cet accord de “revers”. Les Iles Marshall ont déclaré qu’accepter cet accord reviendrait à une trahison. “Nous n’accepterons pas un résultat qui compromettrait notre sécurité et menacerait notre avenir”, a déclaré la négociatrice Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner.

La ministre britannique de l’Energie, Miatta Fahnbulleh, qui dirigeait la délégation de son pays à la COP, a déclaré : “La situation exigeait une ambition audacieuse, et nous avons travaillé sans relâche pour tenter de parvenir à un consensus. Il est extrêmement décevant que nous n’ayons pas réussi à y parvenir.”

“Ce texte nous ramène en arrière. Il efface toute mention de la sortie des énergies fossiles, relègue la science au second plan et laisse croire que des technologies dont le déploiement à grande échelle reste incertain suffiront à régler le problème”, regrettait Monique Barbut, ministre de la Transition écologique un peu plus tôt dans la journée.

Silence sur les combustibles fossiles

L’incapacité à parvenir à un accord sur un texte polarisant montre à quel point les négociations sont devenues tendues, à un moment où les objectifs climatiques mondiaux s’éloignent de plus en plus et où les chocs liés aux prix de l’énergie, la guerre et l’inflation mettent à l’épreuve la volonté des gouvernements de prendre de nouveaux engagements.

Ce chaos constitue également un échec pour les co-organisateurs, la Turquie et l’Australie, qui avaient plaidé dès le début en faveur d’un accord soulignant l’importance d’une augmentation de la production d’électricité.

La COP31 était le premier sommet sur le climat depuis que l’ONU a averti que le réchauffement planétaire dépasserait 1,5° — l’objectif le plus urgent de l’Accord de Paris — et qu’il faudrait redoubler d’efforts pour limiter la poursuite de ce réchauffement.

Une version préliminaire du texte final prévoyait que 35% de la consommation énergétique mondiale soit électrifiée d’ici 2035, contre 23% aujourd’hui — un objectif défendu notamment par la Turquie.

Le texte rejeté ne précisait pas que l’électrification devait être “propre”, comme l’exigeaient de nombreux pays, mais il indiquait que le développement de nouvelles sources d’énergie devait s’accompagner d’efforts visant à “accroître la part des énergies propres, améliorer l’efficacité énergétique et renforcer le déploiement d’autres technologies à faibles émissions”.

Selon les prévisions actuelles, l’économie mondiale devrait atteindre un taux d’électrification de 30% en 2035, a déclaré cette semaine l’Agence internationale de l’énergie.

Mais le texte ne faisait aucune mention des combustibles fossiles — principal facteur de la hausse des températures —, trois ans après que les pays ont conclu leur premier et unique accord visant à réduire progressivement leur dépendance au charbon, au pétrole et au gaz naturel. De nombreux petits Etats insulaires, ainsi que l’Union européenne, avaient exigé que le texte fasse référence à une réduction progressive de l’utilisation des combustibles fossiles.

Points de friction

Lors de la séance plénière de clôture, la Russie a déclaré qu’elle ne pouvait accepter aucune mesure visant à éliminer progressivement les combustibles fossiles, bien qu’elle se soit engagée à le faire en 2023. L’Arabie saoudite a reproché aux pays développés leurs émissions historiques et leur manque de volonté de faire des concessions en matière de financement.

Alors que les négociateurs se disputaient pour savoir s’il fallait mentionner les énergies fossiles dans le texte final, trois des plus grands producteurs d’énergie au monde — la Chine, les États-Unis et la Russie — ont conclu, à des milliers de miles de là, à Shenzen en Chine, un accord visant à augmenter la production de pétrole.

D’autres points d’achoppement — notamment l’aide financière des pays les plus pauvres pour faire face au réchauffement climatique et les technologies permettant de capter le carbone présent dans l’air — ont également prolongé les négociations bien au-delà du temps imparti.

Les négociations ont permis de finaliser plusieurs décisions prévues au départ. D’autres ont été reportées à l’année prochaine, lorsque les négociations se tiendront en Ethiopie. Aucune décision de principe n’était requise lors du sommet de cette année, mais la présidence de la COP31 avait insisté pour qu’un accord soit trouvé.

“C’est la première fois, en 31 Conférences des Parties, que je déclare qu’il vaut mieux ne pas adopter une décision qui nous ferait reculer et qui irait à l’encontre de ce que disent les petites îles et les populations vulnérables”, a déclaré aux journalistes l’ancienne envoyée allemande pour le climat, Jennifer Morgan.

Cet article a été initialement publié par POLITICO en anglais et adapté en français par Alexandre Léchenet.

articles.title: Climate deal crumbles amid fossil fuel rows
articles.summary:
ANTALYA, Turkey — Countries at the U.N. climate talks have failed to reach a final deal after a fortnight of highly divisive negotiations ended with leaders rejecting a draft decision that omitted any mention of fossil fuels and delivered a weak response to rising temperatures.

The European Union, Panama and several other countries, including small island states, said they rejected the deal being pushed by the COP31 presidency. Others took to the floor to voice concerns over finance for countries on the frontline of the climate crisis and areas of the text that emphasized the need for carbon capture and storage.

“It seems that there are parties that object to this text,” Turkish COP31 President Murat Kurum said. “I understand there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted.”

Nearly 200 nations were locked in intense debate over issues involving energy transitions and how to respond to the reality that the world will miss its most urgent climate target — to limit long-term global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.

As talks sped toward a conclusion, they were unable to bridge the divides. It is the first time in 17 years that COP talks have failed to reach agreement.

“It is unconscionable that we will have a cover decision that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transition away from fossil fuel, and it is for that reason that the European Union strongly objects to this text,” said Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU.

Panama called the deal a “setback.” The Marshall Islands said accepting the deal would be a betrayal. “We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security and threatens our future,” said negotiator Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner.

The U.K.’s Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, who led her country’s COP delegation, said: “The moment required bold ambition, and we have been working tirelessly to try to build consensus. It is immensely disappointing we have been unable to do so.”

Fossil fuel silence

The inability to land a deal on a deeply divisive text illustrates how fraught the talks have become, at a time when the world’s climate targets are drifting further out of reach and energy price shocks, war and inflation are testing governments’ willingness to embrace new pledges.  

The chaos also represents a failure for the joint hosts from Turkey and Australia, which pushed for a deal early on that would emphasize the importance of scaling up electricity.

COP31 was the first climate summit since the U.N. warned the world would exceed 1.5°C of warming — the most urgent target in the Paris Agreement — and would need to redouble its efforts to limit further heating.

A draft of the final text had called for 35% of global energy use to be electrified by 2035, up from 23% today — a target championed in particular by Turkey.  

The rejected text failed to specify that electrification should be “clean,” as many countries demanded, but it said scaling up new sources of power should occur alongside efforts to “increase clean energy, improve energy efficiency, and enhance deployment of other low emission technologies.”

The global economy is currently projected to hit 30% electrification in 2035, the International Energy Agency said this week. 

But the text failed to mention fossil fuels — the main driver of rising temperatures — three years after countries had reached their first and only agreement to wind down their dependence on coal, oil and natural gas. Many small island nations, as well as the EU, had demanded a reference to a fossil fuel phasedown in the text. 

Sticking points

At the final plenary, Russia said it could not agree to any phasing out of fossil fuels, despite agreeing to do so in 2023. Saudi Arabia pointed the finger at developed nations for their historical emissions and lack of willingness to give on finance.

As negotiators tangled over whether to mention fossil fuels in the final document, three of the world’s biggest energy producers — China, the U.S. and Russia — reached an agreement thousands of miles away to scale up oil production.

There were other sticking points — around funding to help poorer nations respond to global warming and technologies that suck carbon from the air — that also pushed the talks well into overtime. 

The talks did manage to finalize several mandated decisions. Others were pushed out to next year, when the talks will take place in Ethiopia. No cover decision was required from this year’s summit, but the COP31 presidency had insisted on reaching a deal. 

“This is a day for the first time in my 31 COPs that I say it is better not to have a decision that sets us back, that goes against what small islands and vulnerable people are saying,” former German climate envoy Jennifer Morgan told reporters.

articles.title: ‘Brexit is done’: Theresa May tells Burnham to move on
articles.summary:
Former U.K. Prime Minister Theresa May has said she is “aghast” that Andy Burnham might be considering rejoining the EU after her Labour successor opened a debate about Britain’s future relationship with the bloc.

“People voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on,” May said in a BBC interview broadcast Sunday.

Her intervention follows Friday’s Brussels summit, where Burnham and EU leaders announced agreements on food trade, emissions trading and youth mobility.

Burnham has said he wants Britain to rejoin the EU in his lifetime but has not committed his government to pursuing membership. On Friday, he proposed an “informal brainstorming process” to explore the future relationship, without explicitly putting rejoining on the agenda.

His European relations minister, Hamish Falconer, told POLITICO on Friday that the government would take its time setting out those options, given the divisive nature of the debate.

May said she was “slightly aghast” at the prospect of further negotiations over EU membership, warning that such talks would consume time across government, from the prime minister to officials.

She also accused Burnham of patronizing voters who backed leaving in the 2016 referendum.

“He wants to pat them on their head and say, you know what, remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn’t you? So have another go and come out with the right answer,” she added.

May campaigned to remain in the EU but became prime minister after the referendum, promising to carry out the result. She resigned in 2019 after repeatedly failing to get her Brexit deal through Parliament.

articles.title: All flights to and from Brussels, Charleroi airports canceled Monday amid strike
articles.summary:
All flights to and from Brussels and Charleroi airports will be canceled Monday as air traffic controllers join a nationwide strike against the Belgian government’s austerity measures.

Belgian air traffic control provider Skeyes said it would be unable to provide normal services between 7 a.m. and 9 p.m. local time, effectively grounding commercial flights at the country’s main airports.

Brussels Airport confirmed Sunday that all arriving and departing flights would be canceled during the 14-hour shutdown, while Brussels South Charleroi Airport said no aircraft would be able to take off or land.

Charleroi’s management criticized Skeyes for the short notice of the action, saying the company had informed it of the disruption less than 36 hours in advance, despite the airport having prepared to operate normally.

In a statement Saturday, Charleroi accused air traffic controllers of showing a “completely cavalier attitude” toward airlines, passengers and airport staff.

It said thousands of travelers and some 3,400 people working at Charleroi would be affected, and called on Belgian authorities to develop a coordinated plan to prevent recurring disruptions.

“Skeyes has been informed that a group of air traffic controllers will participate in the national strike on Monday, November 23,” the agency said in a press release, adding, “Staffing levels will be insufficient to ensure the management of normal air traffic under optimal safety conditions during this period. Consequently, Skeyes is compelled to temporarily suspend the affected services.”

Monday’s protest is organized by Belgium’s main trade unions against spending cuts and economic reforms pursued by Prime Minister Bart De Wever’s government.

Public transport across Brussels is also expected to be disrupted.

Passengers have been advised to check with their airlines before heading to either airport.

Tommaso Lecca contributed to this report. This story has been updated.

articles.title: 14 missing after Russian strike as Zelenskyy presses US over Patriot missiles
articles.summary:
A Russian drone strike partially destroyed a five-story apartment building near Kyiv, leaving 14 people unaccounted for, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday.

Rescuers were searching the rubble in Dymer, north of Kyiv, where part of the building collapsed and a fire broke out. Nine people had been evacuated, Zelenskyy added, warning that others could remain trapped.

The attack prompted the Ukrainian president to renew pressure on Washington to approve deliveries of U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles financed by Ukraine’s allies, amid mounting Russian aerial attacks. “It is particularly difficult to understand the delays in supplying anti-ballistic interceptors to Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said on X.

He urged Washington to authorize the transfer of Patriot missiles already paid for by Ukraine’s partners through NATO’s PURL program, which allows allies to purchase American weapons for Kyiv.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said earlier this month that deliveries under the program, including Patriots, were continuing.

Russia launched 186 drones overnight, including 72 jet-powered models, Ukraine’s air force said. Ukrainian defenses shot down or disabled 161, while strikes were recorded at 18 locations.

Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked 20 Ukrainian regions over the past week, launching around 2,700 drones, nearly 1,460 aerial bombs and 165 missiles.

Many were ballistic missiles, including North Korean-made weapons, he said, accusing Moscow of helping Pyongyang improve their accuracy.

articles.title: Europeans dare to believe Trump could deliver security for Ukraine
articles.summary:
BERLIN — The proposal from U.S. President Donald Trump’s negotiating team to give Ukraine a NATO-style collective defense guarantee has triggered an unusual new mindset among some of Kyiv’s allies in Europe: optimism.

European officials close to the peace negotiations are cautiously hopeful that the offer could signal a shift in America’s position in Ukraine’s favor — even though they remain wary that the price Trump will demand for such a sweeping commitment could be too high. 

After two weeks of shuttle diplomacy, Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner proposed the security guarantee at last week’s press conference in Berlin, claiming the U.S. president is “open” to such a “big deal” and the Russians are now “comfortable” with it too. 

Neither is yet certain, and one Russian official dismissed the idea. 

But Russian President Vladimir Putin himself has not yet publicly rejected Kushner’s plan, and European negotiators are taking it seriously, even if they want more information about how it would work. 

A security guarantee for Ukraine based on NATO’s Article 5 collective defense clause, which states that an attack on one member shall be treated as an attack on all, would change the game when it comes to deterring Russia from invading Ukraine again after this war ends. That is particularly true if, as implied, America, with its mighty military, is bound into such a guarantee.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, French President Emmanuel Macron, US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, back, and U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner leave a Coalition of the Willing media call in Berlin on Nov. 19, 2026. | Pool photo by Hannah McKay/Getty Images

While few details are known about the proposal, it would, if backed up by robust legal, military and political commitments, mean that a new attack on Ukraine would risk a direct conflict with the U.S. 

An aide in French President Emmanuel Macron’s office said the U.S. is heading in “the right direction” but called on the White House to go a step further and give Ukraine full NATO membership. 

An Article 5 guarantee “is obviously the best guarantee of solidarity among allies,” said the aide, who, like others, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “So, if we say we’re giving Ukraine Article 5-type guarantees, we shouldn’t overcomplicate things: It means that Ukraine is joining NATO. The alliance’s credibility rests above all on Article 5. Article 5 is an article of faith.”

Shifting the mood 

One reason why some Europeans believe Kushner’s offer is a genuine one is that he was not speaking off the cuff. In private, U.S. officials have been floating the idea for months. There has even been discussion behind the scenes of the French proposal for full NATO membership. 

Although Ukraine joining NATO is seen as a red line issue Russia would never agree to, Kushner and co. clearly believe their efforts to discuss an Article 5-like option with the Russians have found support in Moscow. 

And the mood in some parts of Europe has shifted as a result. 

Families shelter overnight at a Kyiv metro station following warnings of possible Russian air attacks late on Nov. 19, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. | Roman Pilipey/AFP via Getty Images

Diplomats and officials who have spent much of the past two years of Trump’s second term despairing about his repeated torchings of the Western alliance — and worrying that he will sell out Ukraine — now sound relaxed about the U.S. 

“Clear progress has been made on security guarantees,” said one European official close to the negotiations. “On peace talks there is alignment with the U.S., no maximalist demands and no discussion on European security without the Europeans.” 

The aim now is that more progress will be possible toward targeted ceasefires in the energy sector and the Black Sea the next time the U.S. convenes peace talks between Russia and Ukraine, not least because Europeans will have their places at the negotiating table. That meeting is yet to be scheduled but officials expect it to take place in Abu Dhabi sometime after the American Thanksgiving holiday on Nov. 26. 

Details matter

Not everyone is convinced. Speaking after Kushner’s announcement, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was “not sure” everyone had the same understanding of what an Article 5-like guarantee would mean.

“What does it mean, Article 5? That there are some forces of partners on your land. So, my question is: What about American soldiers?” He said Ukraine “would be happy” if the U.S. put military bases in the country “like in the Middle East.” 

Other Europeans agreed that there was still a lack of detail about exactly what Kushner’s plan would involve. 

People walk across a bridge during a blackout in Kyiv caused by attacks on Ukraine’s energy facilities on Nov. 20, 2026. | Genya Savilov/AFP via Getty Images

The most skeptical Europeans are to be found in countries that share borders and a history with Russia, such as Poland and the Nordic and Baltic states, which are often the most hawkish toward Moscow. Poland will be part of the official European negotiating team, which is expected to join the next round of direct negotiations between Russia, the U.S. and Ukraine.

One risk Europeans are alive to is that the cost of such a security guarantee could prove to be too high. Americans asked Ukraine recently whether it would give Russia the whole of Donbas in exchange for full NATO membership. That would mean handing over land to Putin that he has not managed to win by fighting. 

Keeping Russia happy

Ukraine’s territory is not the only issue on the table in these negotiations. Kushner has been equally insistent that revising the entire security framework that had governed Europe before the war is essential, including NATO’s relations with Russia. His broad argument is that if Europe’s security framework had been working properly, the war would never have happened. 

Among Ukraine’s more than 35 allies who gathered in Berlin for the Coalition of the Willing meeting last week, some see Kushner’s point. That’s why the EU’s institutions are happy to offer Putin the chance to discuss European security in a “parallel” track with a peace deal for Ukraine.

To other more hawkish officials, Kushner’s argument about overhauling the continent’s defense framework still sounds dangerously like Putin speaking. They comfort themselves with the thought that no decisions will be taken without Europe “at the table” — but being present doesn’t necessarily equate to being in control. 

“The danger is that an Article 5-style guarantee could somehow become a Trojan Horse in the case of a wider bargain with Moscow, in which Ukraine would surrender the Donbas and ⁠NATO would accept restrictions on its military presence in Eastern Europe,” said Grégoire Roos, of London’s Chatham House think tank.

Russia’s President Vladimir Putin, China’s President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump meet in Shenzen, China, on Nov. 19, 2026. | Pool picture by Andres Martinez Casares/Getty Images

“Let’s face it: That would basically give Russia a de facto veto over European security. So, yes, we could potentially end up offering Ukraine the vague promise of collective defence while sapping the basic conditions that would actually make it credible.” 

Roos said he did not believe the Europeans would fall for such a trap. In Poland, for example, officials are watchful for traps and remain steadfast in backing Ukraine, he said. 

Trump’s friends 

Timing is also a factor that could be decisive. A European official said Trump wants a deal within weeks — even by the time he hosts G20 leaders in Florida in mid-December, though that won’t happen. Zelenskyy told reporters on Saturday that Americans “really wanted to get all this done before Christmas.” Another key deadline could be Jan. 3, when the new Democratic-controlled Congress starts work.

Some leaders who met with Kushner and Witkoff in Berlin last week had feared Washington would be exerting much more pressure for a deal by the end of the year, according to one person present. But in the end leaders were relieved that the U.S. was not strong-arming Ukraine and its allies to rush to an agreement, the person said. 

Then there is the influence of another key group to keep in mind: Trump’s friends. 

While EU diplomats voiced relief that the summit in Shenzhen between Trump, Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping did not deliver a worse outcome for Ukraine and Europe, it still resulted in a joint “peace” declaration in which the trio pledged to reform the United Nations, slapped down the International Criminal Court, and promised to keep talking among themselves about nuclear arms. 

Trump doubled down on the value of having a close relationship with his “friend” Putin in a press conference on his return to Washington on Friday. “He’d love to end the war,” Trump said of the Russian leader — on the same day that two Russian missiles and a drone hit Poland, and Danish police announced they had thwarted a Russian plot to assassinate a Ukrainian rapper.

The China summit serves as a reminder to European optimists that whatever they discuss with Kushner and Witkoff in Berlin or Abu Dhabi, ultimately only one person will make the key decisions for the U.S. — and Putin’s line into him just got stronger. 

“A precedent was created,” said another European official involved in recent diplomacy. “It wasn’t great.” 

Clea Caulcutt contributed reporting from Paris.

articles.title: Electrically induced glass transition of polyelectrolyte complexes enables kinetic ionic diodes
articles.summary:
Nature Communications, Published online: 22 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79559-6

Here the authors demonstrate an electrically induced glass transition in a polyelectrolyte complex, sandwiched between two oppositely charged ionoelastomers and applying time-temperature-salt superposition principle.

articles.title: What is the Riemann hypothesis and why is its solution so monumental?
articles.summary:
Bernhard Riemann set out a problem mathematicians have been trying solve for more than a century

The Granger Collection/Alamy

The cadence of prime numbers has a pattern; it isn’t simply chaos. Mathematician Bernhard Riemann suspected this was the case, but he never proved it conclusively, and his mathematical successors have spent more than a century trying to demonstrate that he was right. The Riemann hypothesis may now be proven, and it could reveal the most basic structure of our number system, while also opening the door for a new understanding of the vast world of mathematical functions.

Read more

Mathematicians and AI in behind-the-scenes battle over what’s true

In 1859, Riemann made a casual remark about a mathematical function in his memoir, qualifying a statement about it as “very probably” true. The fact that he never proved it more definitively has held the world of mathematics in suspense ever since, and the “Riemann hypothesis” became the field’s most famous and stubbornly unsolved problem – until now. A new AI-assisted proof by Levent Alpöge at Anthropic may have just ended a whole era of mathematics by confirming Riemann’s hunch from nearly 200 years ago.

“This result, if true, will be the culmination of a struggle thousands of mathematicians have attempted in the past,” says Christopher Hughes at the University of York in the UK. The proof of the Reimann hypothesis is also one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s Millennium Prize Problems, each of which comes with a $1 million prize for a solution.

Advertisement

The Riemann hypothesis has loomed so large over mathematicians for decades because it concerns mathematics’ most simple yet hard-to-understand objects: prime numbers. These are numbers that aren’t divisible by any number other than 1 and themselves, and any number can be built by multiplying primes. In this way, primes are the bones of all systems of numbers; everything is built on top of them. But how primes are distributed among all numbers is, on the face of it, unpredictable. This is where Riemann made an intervention.

He hypothesised that the way primes are spaced throughout the number line can be inferred from another set of numbers, now tied to a mathematical function called the Riemann zeta function. These numbers are complex – so each is actually a pair of numbers, one called real and one called imaginary – and when they are plugged into the Riemann zeta function, the function spits out zero. Confusingly, these numbers that result in a zero from the function are called “non-trivial zeros”. Riemann discovered that summing over a sequence of these complex numbers allowed him to predict the distribution of primes up to a certain high number. Effectively, he came upon a formula that could make sense of primes’ seemingly random appearances among numbers.

But the formula only works if all the zeros always sit on the same vertical line when plotted in a coordinate system where the horizontal axis tracks their real number constituents and the vertical axis their imaginary ones. Riemann calculated some of these zeros, which confirmed his idea, but could not prove the hypothesis more generally. It became the biggest unsolved problem in all of mathematics. “It is a legendary problem, the queen of all the Millennium Problems,” says Scott Armstrong at Sorbonne University in Paris. “For the whole field of mathematics, there could not be a bigger theorem.”

In the intervening years, mathematicians used computers to verify that the first 12 trillion nontrivial zeros line up on Riemann’s vertical line and much work has gone into proving that the zeros at least must lie in a strip of the coordinate systems around this line. In fact, a previous release of AI proofs by OpenAI on 6 October contained the proof of a weaker version of the Riemann hypothesis, placing the non-trivial zeros in the neighbourhood but not exactly on the line Riemann predicted.

In a statement released to the public, Alpöge wrote that his proof, developed with Anthropic’s Claude AI, is over 250,000 pages long, and it has not yet been fully read, digested or understood by the mathematics community. Even its translation into the language of the proof-checking software Lean is 17,000,000 lines long. That means it will take time to carefully adjudicate. “I have not had a chance to read the 17 million lines of Lean, so cannot speak to their truth,” says Alex Walker at University College London. And the announcement didn’t illuminate the details of the method, he adds.

The most interesting mathematical discoveries in OpenAI’s 722 new papers

OpenAI has released hundreds of papers claiming to make progress on the biggest open problems in mathematics – here are some with the most potential

Consequently, it is currently unclear exactly what mathematical tricks the AI leveraged, though early commentators suggest that it drew on a vast swathe of mathematics spanning several fields including number theory and arithmetic geometry. Some have suggested the AI made connections across these fields that don’t already clearly exist in the literature.

The Lean code is in the process of being adapted to efficiently run on a computer that can review it, which will provide a crucial check on the new proof. “While Lean itself has some issues, so far none of the AI results with Lean certificates have had to be retracted,” says Scott Aaronson at the University of Texas at Austin. Still, it may take years to unravel all the details of the new proof and reap any of its mathematical insights, he says. But the ramifications will certainly be enormous and extensive.

Notably, it resolves the biggest open question of number theory by finally making primes make sense. Numerous results also build on the assumption that Riemann was right and will now stand on firmer ground. And then there are implications for functions similar to the Riemann zeta function, known as the generalised Riemann hypothesis. “An extremely large number of results have previously been proven subject to the generalised Riemann hypothesis,” says John Nicholson at the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in Germany. He says there are also a number of fast algorithms for computing quantities in algebraic number theory whose correctness depends on the generalised Riemann hypothesis. The Riemann hypothesis even has ties to theories of chaos in quantum systems in physics.

“The failure of the Riemann hypothesis would create havoc in the distribution of prime numbers,” wrote Enrico Bombieri at Princeton University when outlining the Millenium Problem more than a quarter of a century ago. Now, thanks to a combination of human ingenuity and relentlessness, and the computational power of AI, that distribution may have been shown to be not that dangerous after all.

articles.title: Anthropic mathematician claims AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis
articles.summary:
The Riemann hypothesis describes a pattern within the prime numbers

ROBERT BROOK/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Alamy

A mathematician at AI company Anthropic claims to have discovered, and verified with formalisation, a proof of the Riemann hypothesis – one of the most infamous and thorny problems in all of mathematics.

The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution.

Read more

OpenAI has dumped 722 maths papers – now it must clean up the mess

Levent Alpöge at Anthropic published a statement today claiming to have solved the problem with the aid of Anthropic’s Claude AI.

Advertisement

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” writes Alpöge. “It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.” In August, Anthropic announced previous work on the Riemann hypothesis, but that stopped short of a full proof.

Alpöge hasn’t published a human-readable version of the proof, saying it would be “obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop'”, though he says an unpublished version ran to more than 250,000 pages.

Instead, Alpöge has released a version of the proof written in Lean, a computer code mathematicians use to mechanically verify proofs as a series of logical steps in a process called formalisation. This process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, meaning that the code compiles, it is considered to have been proved correct beyond all reasonable doubt.

However, the process isn’t without vulnerabilities, and the code and mathematics will need to be thoroughly checked by humans. “Let’s see if it compiles first,” says Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London, reacting to the news. “Might be a while before we find the relevant experts who are able to tell us the thrust of the argument, assuming it’s all true, of course, which it probably will be because of course Alpöge will have [a] huge amount of egg on [his] face if the Lean code doesn’t compile or is deficient in some way.”

A golden age of maths is dawning and mathematicians are freaking out

Mathematicians are stunned at the progress AI is making in solving advanced problems, leaving some questioning whether there will still be room for humans

Alpöge says the proof may also help solve the generalised Riemann hypothesis (GRH), which widens out the concept to different properties of prime numbers, and could expand our understanding of a broader family of mathematical structures. “There are numerous results that are conditional on the generalised Riemann hypothesis, and now those are theorems!” says James McKee at Royal Holloway University of London. “I suppose most mathematicians believed, or the more cautious ones merely suspected, that GRH was true, so its proof will not be unsettling. What is both unsettling and tremendously exciting, is the rapid progress in recent months towards automated proofs of significant mathematical results. It is both a wonderful time and a terrible time to be a research mathematician.”

Alpöge has been involved in a number of recent discoveries involving AI. In July, he announced that the Jacobian conjecture – which academics have spent decades trying to prove was true – is actually false, giving a tiny, 216-character counterexample as proof.

He and Tristan Buckmaster at New York University also announced that they had cracked three significant problems considered “stepping stones” to the Navier-Stokes problem, hours before OpenAI controversially revealed a full solution.

Anthropic listed on the stock market on 19 November, and Alpöge appears to suggest that he waited to announce the proof until after. “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier,” he writes, saying that he spoke to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and determined that “there was a constraint to respect” before the announcement could be made.
