articles.title: [Ask the Tax Whiz] The new BIR chief’s 3 crosses: Will he dare audit the powerful?
articles.summary:
From the Marcos estate tax to Sara Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth and the fortunes of political dynasties, Commissioner Rolando Ligon Jr. faces a defining test: Can the Philippines enforce tax laws without political exceptions?

What happens when the country’s chief tax collector must confront the financial interests of the President who appointed him, a Vice President who could succeed him, and some of the most powerful political families in government?

For newly appointed Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) Commissioner Rolando Ligon Jr., these are three crosses he must carry—not merely to meet revenue targets, but to restore public trust, strengthen governance, and rebuild investor confidence.

In 2025, the BIR collected ₱3.105 trillion, with ₱3.03 trillion—or 97.55%—coming from voluntary payments. Yet high-profile unpaid taxes, allegations of unexplained wealth, and corruption involving public funds continue to test the credibility of tax enforcement.

The question is no longer simply how much government collects, but whether it can collect what is legally due without fear, favor, or political interference.

First cross—Will Ligon collect the Marcos estate tax from the family of the President who appointed him?

In 1991, the BIR assessed ₱23.3 billion in estate taxes following the death of Ferdinand Marcos Sr. In 1997, the Supreme Court upheld the assessment’s finality and the legality of the BIR’s collection levies in Ferdinand R. Marcos II v. Court of Appeals.

By 2021, the reported liability had reached approximately ₱203.8 billion, including accumulated interest and penalties. Former BIR commissioner Caesar Dulay confirmed a written demand to the Marcos heirs dated December 2, 2021. (READ: [ANALYSIS] Inconvenient truth: The Marcos estate tax liability)

With 1Sambayan warning of a December 2, 2026 deadline, Ligon must immediately establish the certified outstanding liability, previous recoveries, and remaining enforceable collection remedies.

Crucially, another demand letter does not automatically extend prescription. The legal effect of previous collection proceedings, including levies initiated in 1993, must be determined.

The liability concerns the estate and its heirs to the extent provided by law. (READ: [ANALYSIS] The estate tax liability of the Marcos Estate)

After 35 years, will the President’s appointee demonstrate that even the First Family is subject to the same tax laws as ordinary Filipinos?

Must Read

[Ask the Tax Whiz] An open letter to President Marcos: Filipinos feel overtaxed, yet underserved

Second cross—Will the BIR independently investigate Vice President Sara Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth?

Duterte faces an impeachment trial involving allegations of approximately ₱817.87 million in unexplained wealth and undeclared assets associated with her and her husband from 2022 to 2025. Her defense disputes these findings.

The Senate impeachment court has admitted relevant financial records, including Statements of Assets Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs), bank records, tax documents, and corporate disclosures.

But impeachment and tax enforcement are distinct legal processes.

Where credible evidence establishes potential tax violations, the BIR can initiate a lawful investigation independently of the impeachment proceedings.

The investigation must reconcile declared income, assets, business interests, and financial transactions against tax records. Unexplained wealth is not automatically proof of tax evasion, and due process must be observed.

If financial discrepancies involving a possible future President warrant scrutiny, will the BIR investigate regardless of political affiliation?

Tax enforcement must neither protect political allies nor become a weapon against political opponents.

Must Read

[Ask the Tax Whiz] How SALN, lifestyle checks, and citizen action can expose corruption

Third cross—Will Ligon investigate political dynasties, their family businesses, campaign donors, and government contractors?

The concentration of political power in the Philippines is staggering.

In its landmark August 2026 anti-political dynasty ruling, the Supreme Court cited research showing that 216 of 253 district representatives—approximately 85%—in the 19th Congress had relatives previously or currently in public office, or seeking election in 2025. The figure remains approximately 83% in the 20th Congress, with 212 of 254 district representatives linked to political dynasties.

At the local level, 71 of 82 governors belong to political dynasties.

Meanwhile, former House speaker Martin Romualdez, President Marcos’s cousin, faces a ₱7.44-billion plunder case involving alleged kickbacks from government infrastructure projects. He denies wrongdoing. An Anti-Money Laundering Council witness recently testified that ₱560.5 million in examined remittances to his accounts was not linked to flood-control transactions.

Separately, the Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism reported that Romualdez’s Leyte district received approximately ₱57 billion in public works allocations from 2023 to 2025, while presidential son Sandro Marcos’s district received the largest share of discretionary district infrastructure allocations.

These allocations do not establish corruption or tax evasion. But credible evidence of procurement irregularities, unexplained financial discrepancies, or conflicts of interest should trigger independent investigation.

The BIR must look beyond individual politicians and, where justified by objective risk indicators, examine family-controlled businesses, campaign donors, contractors, and beneficial ownership structures—from Congress to provincial, city, and municipal governments.

Follow the money: Who received government contracts? Who ultimately benefited? Were the proceeds properly declared and taxed?

No political surname should confer immunity. Equally, family relationships alone must never create a presumption of guilt.

Must Read

[Ask the Tax Whiz] The Al Capone strategy: Why PH must follow the money in corruption cases

What policy reforms can make tax enforcement genuinely independent, effective, and accountable?

Four reforms can transform Philippine tax administration beyond collection targets and digitalization.

First, establish an Unexplained Wealth Tax Audit Program. Use objective, risk-based criteria to reconcile SALNs, income tax returns, corporate ownership, campaign donations, procurement records, and property transactions. Coordinate with the Ombudsman, Customs, AMLC, Commission on Audit, Securities and Exchange Commission, and Commission on Elections under lawful data-sharing arrangements. Establish independent audit-selection safeguards and publish aggregate enforcement outcomes, including assessments, actual collections, and prosecution referrals.

Second, reform bank secrecy and financial transparency laws. Authorize proportionate, legally supervised access to relevant financial information for serious tax and corruption investigations. Strengthen beneficial ownership disclosure and campaign finance transparency while protecting legitimate privacy rights.

Third, modernize compliance through AI-assisted risk assessment, electronic invoicing, and integrated financial data. Prioritize substantial discrepancies and sophisticated evasion schemes instead of subjecting compliant MSMEs, professionals, and online sellers to unnecessary, repetitive, and potentially abusive audit.

Fourth, establish an independent National Revenue Authority (NRA). Pursue legislation to integrate the BIR and Bureau of Customs under a professionally governed, semi-autonomous revenue institution, with merit-based appointments, operational independence, independent oversight, transparent performance standards, and strong accountability mechanisms.

An NRA must do more than merge agencies or modernize technology. It must reduce political interference, professionalize tax and customs enforcement, strengthen taxpayer rights, and make corruption and selective enforcement harder to conceal.

Must Read

[Ask the Tax Whiz] Corruption is the Philippines’ biggest hidden tax

For foreign investors, predictable and impartial tax administration matters as much as competitive tax rates and investment incentives.

Tax reform must be measured not only by how much government collects, but by how fairly, efficiently, and independently it enforces the law—especially when the taxpayers under scrutiny are rich, powerful, or politically connected.

The ultimate test: Who carries the burden?

The Philippines does not need another tax commissioner who aggressively pursues small taxpayers while politically sensitive financial cases remain unresolved.

It needs an institution capable of investigating credible evidence, recovering legally collectible taxes, and holding public officials accountable regardless of political connections.

The Tax Code itself recognizes the gravity of tax offenses committed by public officials.

Under Section 253(c) of the National Internal Revenue Code, a public officer or employee convicted of an offense punishable under the Code faces the maximum applicable penalty, dismissal from public service, and perpetual disqualification from holding public office, voting, and participating in elections.

The law expressly provides that such an offender shall be “perpetually disqualified from holding any public office, to vote and to participate in any election.”

This severe consequence requires a conviction under the applicable law—not merely accusations, audit findings, or the filing of charges.

The principle is unmistakable: Public office is no shield against tax accountability.

For Commissioner Ligon, the three crosses converge in one defining test:

Will he dare collect the Marcos estate tax, investigate Sara Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth, and follow the money in Congress—or protect the powerful who control the nation’s purse?

The President may appoint the BIR commissioner. But neither the President, the Vice President, nor any politician or political dynasty enjoys an exemption from the Tax Code.

Public office is a public trust—not a family business or a tax exemption. – Rappler.com

Mon Abrea, CPA, MBA, MPA (Harvard) is a global tax policy expert and Chief Tax Advisor of Asian Consulting Group (ACGlobal), an international tax and investment advisory firm. He advises governments, multinational enterprises, and international organizations on tax policy, investment competitiveness, and fiscal reform. He is the author of Reimagining the World Without Corruption and Why Invest in the Philippines? CREATE MORE Edition, and has represented the Philippines in policy dialogues at the OECD, World Bank, and other international forums.

Must Read

[Ask the Tax Whiz] As PH growth slumps, what will Marcos’ economic reshuffle do?

articles.title: COP31 climate talks collapse as EU and others reject deal
articles.summary:
ANTALYA, Turkey – UN climate talks collapsed on Sunday, November 22, as the European Union and others rejected a final draft deal put forward by COP31 presidents Turkey and Australia, saying it was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.

The failed talks reflect world governments’ struggle this year to muster ambitious action to address the worsening consequences of climate change, as wars, economic pressures and other crises compete for their attention.

After more than two weeks of negotiations that spilled two days into overtime — making it the longest COP on record — Turkey’s conference president Murat Kurum said at the closing plenary that he could see there was no agreement and confirmed he would not advance any new text.

“There is nothing to do, we did all that we could,” he said. “There will be no new text from now on.”

He later left the stage in the midst of speeches being delivered by country representatives.

Australia’s COP31 President of Negotiations, Chris Bowen, called the outcome “very disappointing” and said disagreements over fuels and climate finance were the dealbreakers.

The last time UN climate talks failed to get a deal adopted by all was in Copenhagen in 2009.

Ireland’s environment minister Darragh O’Brien said the European Union could not support the proposed deal in part because it made no mention of the fossil fuels that scientists say drive global warming.

“It is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels,” he said.

Saudi Arabia and other big oil producer countries had lobbied hard to keep their mention out of the text, according to observers at the summit.

Panama also said it could not support the text because it failed to address the scale and urgency of the climate crisis.

This year’s COP is the first since the UN’s environmental body in October confirmed the rise in global temperature was set to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), a threshold countries agreed at Paris climate talks over a decade ago to try not to exceed, and beyond which extreme weather impacts intensify.

Belgium’s Climate Minister Jean-Luc Crucke said the failure of the deal was a difficult outcome, but appropriate.

“It’s not the end of multilateralism, but there has to be courage to say no,” he said.

While a blow to efforts to ratchet up international action, the failure to agree a political declaration in Antalya does not erase the obligations agreed by previous UN conferences or remove the technical and legal frameworks governing multilateral action against climate change.

Pressure from Saudi Arabia and other oil producers

The failed deal had acknowledged the planet’s projected temperature overshoot and called for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse it.

That was a big ask from oil-producing countries.

While scientists say removing carbon from the atmosphere — when paired with steep emissions cuts — is vital to avoiding the worst impacts of climate change, critics of the proposed deal said they worried the carbon removal language would be used as a licence to keep pumping oil.

A representative for the Saudi delegation, which supported the deal’s mention of carbon removal, told the summit at the closing plenary that he was surprised at the resistance to technology, which he said offered a concrete solution.

Developing countries had also criticized the deal for not providing sufficient new climate finance to help them adapt to a warming planet. The deal had called for a tripling of such finance, but did not specify from what baseline.

The failed deal had also included a goal put forward by Turkey to expand electricity’s share of total final world energy consumption to 35% by 2035, from around 23% now.

Proponents of that pledge said it could cut greenhouse gas emissions by speeding the transition away from fuel-powered cars, furnaces, and other equipment. But critics said it could force more costs onto poor nations without providing a clear path away from fossil fuels.

The COP process is the main vehicle through which countries coordinate their efforts to curb global warming. Its annual meeting provides an opportunity for nations to signal they are willing to work together to find solutions and help finance the problems rising temperatures cause. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘Proud Bisdak’ KZ Tandingan wants Filipino music to transcend borders
articles.summary:
The Filipino music scene has long largely operated in the metro, with many of today’s most successful local acts starting out as performers in dive bars around different cities close to the capital before their meteoric rise.

Major concerts are usually held in venues across Pasay and Quezon City, and the TV shows that are known to produce successful stars operate from Metro Manila, too. 

And to get a shot at making it big, aspiring artists from provinces often have to travel long hours and spend thousands on plane rides just to audition for these music shows. 

It’s a reality KZ Tandingan is all too familiar with. In 2012, the acclaimed singer-songwriter, who hails from Digos, Davao del Sur, packed her bags to audition for the first season of X Factor Philippines. 

Just 20 years old then, Tandingan had joined the reality singing competition with a brave mission to help her family, and to prove that you didn’t need to conform to traditional beauty standards to become successful. 

“Gusto ko pong sumali ng ‘X Factor’ hindi lang para tulungan ang pamilya ko, kung ‘di patunayan na ang industriya ng musika sa Philippines ay hindi lang para sa mga magaganda, sa mga makikinis ang balat, sa mga matatangkad, at sa mga biritero’t biritera,” she said during her audition. 

(I want to join X Factor not just to help my family, but to prove that the music industry in the Philippines isn’t just for the beautiful, for those with clear skin, those who are tall, and those who can belt easily.) 

Play Video

Tandingan had confidently told the judges that she would sing her own version of “Somewhere Over The Rainbow,” and she had, right off the bat, proven that her soulful, raspy vocal tone would take her places far and wide. It was a goal she would see through at each round of the competition, until she would eventually emerge as X Factor Philippines’ first-ever winner. 

And over a decade, countless chart-topping hits, and plenty of large-scale shows later, Tandingan has not once forgotten where she came from. 

Far from home

Tandingan had developed most of her career in Manila — having been signed to major record labels before going independent earlier this year. Despite being so far away from home all the time, she and her husband, fellow famed musician TJ Monterde, have made it a point to stand as staunch advocates of music sung in different languages across the Philippines.  

Play Video

“For a really, really long time, when music is recognized, artists who sing in their native tongue would always be boxed into that small category of regional music. I think a big factor is that we don’t expose the whole Philippines to all the songs sung in different languages,” Tandingan told Rappler in a mix of English and Filipino. 

With the platform she’s built with her own craft, Tandingan then makes it a point to sing in Bisaya as much as she can. 

Just take her latest Coke Studio track “Bugsay” for example. It’s sung entirely in Bisaya, and it was a creative choice Tandingan knew she had to make.

“‘Di ba, sabi nga nila, kunwari, nag-Bibisaya ako, tapos lumipat ako ng Manila, [nag-Fifilipino] na ako ngayon. If hindi ko ipapractice ‘yung Bisaya ko, if I don’t get to connect with my roots, makakalimutan mo ‘yun. And part ‘yun ng kultura ko as a Mindanaoan,” she told Rappler. 

(They say that, for example, I speak Bisaya, then I moved to Manila and started speaking Filipino. If I don’t practice my Bisaya, if I don’t get to connect with my roots, you’ll forget it. And it’s part of my culture as a Mindanaoan.) 

“Bugsay” is a Bisaya word for “oar.” It carries a strong message: to keep paddling, no matter how strong the current gets. 

While the song strives to inspire those who listen to it, it bears a bigger aspiration for Tandingan: to make it known that there are songs by musicians from across the archipelago that aren’t just sung in Filipino or English. After all, some stories are better told in their original languages. 

“If ‘Bugsay’ is able to [encourage more Filipinos to listen to non-English and Filipino songs], nagawa ko na ‘yung purpose ko as an artist. That’s why it’s important for me to always champion my roots — kasi Bisaya ako. Proud Bisdak talaga ako.” 

(If “Bugsay” is able to encourage more Filipinos to listen to non-English and Filipino songs, I’ve fulfilled my purpose as an artist. That’s why it’s important for me to always champion my roots — because I’m Bisaya. I’m a proud Bisdak.) 

A long way to go, but hope remains

The “Two Less Lonely People in the World” singer is still waiting for the day music auditions become more accessible to people from all over Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao. 

“I know so many talented artists that weren’t given a chance to audition because of the fact that you have to pay for a plane ride to Manila. That’s already a luxury for so many talented musicians back home,” Tandingan said in a mix of Filipino and English. 

There’s still a long way to go, but Tandingan remains hopeful. 

Play Video

“Masaya pa rin ako sa nangyayari sa atin ngayon kasi ang daming mga bagong salta na mga musician and they’re not afraid to sing in their own language. May mga kumakanta ng Ilocano, ng Bisaya, at Chavacano,” she mused. 

(I’m still happy because there are so many newly minted musicians who aren’t afraid to sing in their own language. There are people who sing in Ilocano, in Bisaya, or in Chavacano.) 

It’s always heartwarming for Tandingan to see Filipino musicians shine as they are. More and more Filipino artists are now unafraid to break out of the mold of what supposedly means to be successful, and are more than willing to gamble on the big possibility of virality that singing in more widely recognizable languages can give them. 

Through it all, they do it all in the name of honoring the roots and the land they came from. – Rappler.com

articles.title: The US midterm elections and this Norman Rockwell painting
articles.summary:
The US midterm elections, especially in Mississippi where Democratic challenger Scott Colom became the state’s first Black senator since 1874, reminded me of this painting by Norman Rockwell. 

Play Video

It depicts the final moments of three young men: voting rights activists James Chaney, a 20-year-old Black Mississippi native, and two Jewish New Yorkers, Michael Schwerner, 24, and Andrew Goodman, 20. They were kidnapped, beaten and killed by Klu Klax Klan members in June 1964 for taking part in the campaign to register Black voters in Mississippi.

DEFIANCE. Norman Rockwell’s painting “Murder in Mississippi,” depicts a defiant civil rights advocate Michael Schwerner (in white shirt), with his colleague, a wounded Black Mississippi local James Chaney clutching his arms, facing a US deputy sheriff and Klan conspirators holding guns (only their shadows are seen in the painting), as displayed in the Norman Rockwell Museum in Massachusetts, USA. Screenshot from Norman Rockwell Museum YT

Michael Schwerner, in white shirt, is shown holding his colleague in the voting rights campaign, a wounded Mississippi local James Chaney. Another colleague in the campaign, Anthony Goodman, is lying face down on the ground. 

There’s a look of defiance on Schwerner’s face. What was he thinking shortly before he too was gunned down?

They were killed the day after I was born in Manila. That’s one reason what happened to them resonated with me — even though I didn’t know about them until I moved to California in my ’20s.

Play Video

I first heard their names in Mississippi Burning, which drew heavy criticism for downplaying the stories of Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner and the activists of the Freedom Summer campaign. FBI agents, played by Gene Hackman and Willem Dafoe, were the heroes in the movie. (READ: Actor Gene Hackman and wife found dead alongside dog at home)

I learned more as a student at the UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism where we watched Jon Else’s documentary Eyes on the Prize. The series led me to read Taylor Branch’s books bout the Civil Rights movement, Parting the Waters, Pillar of Fire, and At Canaan’s Edge.

Play Video

Years later, I came across Race Beat: The Press, The Civil Rights Struggle and the Awakening of A Nation, by the legendary journalist Gene Roberts and Emory University professor Hank Klibanoff. The winners of the Pulitzer Prize in 2007, this powerful book is an account of the US Civil Rights movement through the eyes of the journalists who covered it.

I spent a bit of time in the South last summer.

My family and I spent a week in Alabama to celebrate my son’s graduation from Army flight school at Fort Rucker. We visited our other son in New Orleans where he lived while interning at the NASA Space Center in nearby Mississippi. We celebrated the Fourth of July in the New Orleans Riverfront and watched fireworks on the Mississippi River. (READ: Letting go on the road to Idaho: Notes on fatherhood)

I had one regret about my summer in the South, which became more pronounced after the midterms.

Just a two-hour drive from New Orleans, at the intersection of County Road 515 and State Highway 19 near Philadelphia, Mississippi, there’s a plaque marking the area where James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner were killed.

KILLED. Newspaper clipping shows voting rights advocates Michael Schwerner, James Chaney, and Andres Goodman. Courtesy of Normal Rockwell Museum YT

I had thought of driving there to see it. But that didn’t happen.

It would have been nice to visit the marker, to remember James Chaney, Michael Schwerner and Andrew Goodman. To say, “Thank you.” – Rappler.com

(This article was first published in the author’s LinkedIn.)

Benjamin Pimentel is a journalist and technology editor based in the San Francisco Bay Area. His novel, ‘Mga Gerilya Sa Powell Street,’ won the 2007 National Book Award for Fiction and was staged by the Cultural Center of the Philippines’ (CCP) Tanghalang Pilipino in 2008.

articles.title: [Inside the Newsroom] Why road safety is a budget issue
articles.summary:
I’m Patrick Cruz, a multimedia reporter for Rappler covering transportation, among other beats. Every day, millions of Filipinos navigate a chaotic, congested, and often perilous transport system. But the true cost of our daily commute isn’t just measured in lost hours and lost productivity; some lives are also lost on the road.

In Metro Manila alone, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority records an average of 239 road crash incidents every single day. That is roughly 10 accidents every hour. 

The national picture is even more alarming. According to recent data from the Philippine Statistics Authority, 3,133 people already died due to road crashes from January to April 2026 — not even half a year! 

This staggering figure makes road accidents the 13th leading cause of death in the country. 

The government acknowledges that this is a crisis. The Philippine Road Safety Action Plan (PRSAP) 2023–2028, led by the Department of Transportation (DOTr), laid down an ambitious target to reduce road traffic deaths and injuries by at least 35% by 2028. It has a long-term vision of zero road deaths.

But here is the glaring disconnect: ambitious goals require adequate funding, and right now the money simply isn’t there.

The DOTr proposed a modest P111.29 million to fund the PRSAP. However, under the House General Appropriations Bill (HGAB), that allocation was reduced to exactly zero.

Similarly, infrastructure designed to protect our most vulnerable road users has been gutted. The Active Transport Bike Share and Safe Pathways Program — essential for protecting cyclists and pedestrians — received a measly P33.9 million allocation. That is a mere 3% of the proposed P1.13 billion needed to build and maintain safe active transport networks.

Without this funding, millions of Filipinos who rely on active transport are left to fend for themselves on fast-moving, heavily motorized thoroughfares. 

Advocates are rightfully sounding the alarm. The Move As One Coalition has pointed out that no funding has been provided for road safety for the past three years. 

“There’s no funding for road safety for the past three years, which is why we ask the Senate: Please, if you’re really serious in helping prevent road crashes, in making sure that our most vulnerable are protected, fund road safety,” Move As One Coalition representative Lou Gepuela said during the budget deliberations in the Senate.

The road safety budget now sits in the hands of the Senate. Will our lawmakers finally put their money where their mouth is to protect commuters? Or will we see another year of zero funding for a crisis that claims thousands of Filipino lives? 

Let’s keep a close eye on how government officials craft our national budget. Follow our #BudgetWatch page for more stories on where your taxes go (and where they don’t). – Rappler.com

articles.title: Washington governor calls ICE 'out of control' after Seattle airport arrests
articles.summary:
The governor of Washington state called US federal immigration agents “out of control” after they arrested two people at Seattle’s main airport on Saturday.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers have conducted raids across the United States, part of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, which has forged ahead despite a rebuke by voters at this month’s midterms.

Video footage widely shared on social media on Saturday showed two people being apprehended by masked men at an airport jet bridge.

ICE later confirmed it had detained two people it said had overstayed their visas.

Washington Governor Bob Ferguson said the agency was “completely and totally out of control”.

“Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities,” Ferguson wrote on X.

“Today’s actions at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport are just the latest example of ICE’s deeply un-American tactics.”

Ferguson said at a news conference that the ICE agents may have broken a state law limiting facial coverings for law enforcement, and that he was looking into how they accessed the jet bridge.

The federal immigration agency said its officers “conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an illegal alien from Mexico who overstayed his visa” on Saturday morning.

The agency confirmed it had detained a second person whom it said would be charged with assaulting a federal officer, alleging she had thrown hot coffee on an ICE agent.

“The individual… was identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, an illegal alien from Mexico and visa overstay. She was subsequently arrested as well,” ICE posted on X.

Alaska Airlines, which operated the flight that Mendoza and Mejia tried to board, said on Saturday it was “concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action”.

“Alaska Airlines is required to comply with applicable laws and regulations when interacting with law enforcement officials” but does not “direct or coordinate immigration enforcement activity”, the company added.

The Port of Seattle, which operates the airport, said: “We are outraged about this morning’s incident involving ICE and two passengers.”

This month, Trump appointed Stephen Miller, architect of his hardline immigration policy, as his new chief of staff.

Miller faced widespread criticism after the deadly shootings of two protesters by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January — incidents that sparked mass demonstrations.

articles.title: Any talks with India on terrorism must be 'evidence-based', says Musadik Malik
articles.summary:
Federal minister Musadik Malik said on Sunday that any dialogue between Pakistan and India on terrorism must be “based on evidence”.

Malik is in New Delhi on a three-day trip to attend the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, making him the first Pakistani minister to visit the neighbour since former foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari attended an SCO meeting in May 2023.

Pakistan has repeatedly offered to hold talks with India to resolve outstanding disputes, including the water issue.

In video clips shared by India’s ANI news agency on Sunday, Malik responded to queries from Indian media and stressed that he had repeatedly presented Pakistan’s stance before the reporters.

“I am giving you a stable response that whenever discussions take place, they will be based on evidence, and they will certainly happen,” he affirmed, saying if New Delhi wanted a “lasting solution”.

“You must also have some issues, [though] our issues are much greater than yours, and we also need a lot of evidence […] Whenever dialogue takes place, it will be based on evidence,” the climate change minister reiterated.

Malik said Pakistan had repeatedly stated that evidence relating to terrorism could be presented through both bilateral and multilateral forums. “You may bring evidence; we also have evidence that we want to present,” he added.

India’s foreign minister had said in June 2024 that his country wanted to “find a solution to the issue of years-old cross-border terrorism” with Pakistan. However, a military conflict between the neighbours last year has intensified tensions and escalatory rhetoric from India.

In May 2025, a four-day confrontation between Pakistan and India was sparked by an attack on tourists in occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam, which New Delhi, without evidence, linked to Pakistan.

Islamabad had strongly denied responsibility while calling for a neutral investigation.

In another clip, Malik noted that India had invited a representative from Pakistan to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum, a multilateral event.

“I am your guest. You invited me to a specific forum; I am present before you. I answered all those questions you asked about this forum,” the minister said, remarking that he had conveyed the “voice of my heart” to the people across the region through the forum.

Malik stated, “You are today asking me questions for which you did not invite me. When you invite me for that question, I will appear. However, you first ought to invite me and say ‘we want to speak bilaterally with you’.”

‘Will speak on IWT when invited to do so’

The minister was also asked about his remarks on the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), but said he would comment on the matter when invited to do so.

“You have currently invited me to speak on topics about which I have already spoken, that when temperatures rise, climate is destroyed, Glofs happen. Glofs and glaciers are blind, they do not know whether to fall on the right or the left,” he said, highlighting the shared threat climate change poses to both neighbours.

He further said, “You have called me for culture and civilisation [discussions]. I am your guest, you are my host […] You have asked me the same question a 100 times and I have responded to it a 100 times.”

In his remarks at the SCO forum on Saturday, Malik had termed climate change an “enemy” of civilisations and pointed out its impact on South Asian countries that bore the brunt of climate destruction.

Water and the IWT remain a contentious issue between Pakistan and India, following New Delhi’s unilateral abeyance of the accord in April last year after the Pahalgam attack, which was followed by the four-day military conflict between the two sides.

Following India’s move, Pakistan termed any attempt to suspend its water share an “act of war”, noting the IWT had no provision for unilateral suspension. It later argued that New Delhi’s action was a violation of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.

Backing Islamabad’s stance, the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) on Aug 31 ordered New Delhi to uphold the IWT, declaring that the treaty remained fully in force, as India had no justification for ending or suspending the agreement.

The IWT, brokered by the World Bank in 1960, allocates the three western rivers — Indus, Jhelum and Chenab — largely to Pakistan, and the three eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas and Sutlej — to India.

The treaty has survived wars, crises, and political tensions for more than six decades and is considered a rare example of durable water-sharing cooperation between the two neighbours.

articles.title: Varma century in vain as Pakistan Shaheens down India A in Asia Cup Rising Stars clash
articles.summary:
Pakistan Shaheens overcame a late challenge from Tilak Varma to beat India A by 48 runs in their Asia Cup Rising Stars match in Doha on Sunday, defending a total of 313 after bowling out their opponents with five balls to spare.

Skipper Varma struck a century before becoming the last man dismissed for 100 off 149 balls, while Shahbaz Ahmed made 56 in a seventh-wicket stand that briefly revived India’s hopes.

But Pakistan’s bowlers held their nerve in the closing overs, with Hasan Nawaz claiming three wickets and Ali Raza taking three for 56.

India’s chase had begun to unravel after an explosive start from Abhishek Sharma. The left-hander made 70 off just 42 balls, hitting six fours and six sixes, but his dismissal at 93-3 in the 16th over left the visitors with considerable ground to make up.

Pakistan’s spinners then tightened their grip. Sufyan Moqim bowled Kumar Kushagra for two before Hasan removed Rinku Singh and Suryansh Shedge, leaving India struggling at 129-6 in the 26th over.

Varma, who had struggled to find the boundary during the middle overs, found support in Shahbaz.

The pair added 112 runs for the seventh wicket, taking the score to 241 before Raza broke the stand by having Shahbaz caught by Hasan for 56 off 49 balls.

Raza then bowled Vipraj Nigam for a duck, while Imran Randhawa dismissed Harshit Rana to leave India nine down.

Varma reached his second century of the tournament, but the milestone offered little consolation as Ahmed Daniyal had him caught by wicket-keeper Rohail Nazir in the 50th over to seal Pakistan’s victory.

Controversial toss

Earlier, Pakistan had posted 313 after winning a dramatic toss and electing to bat on a slightly dry surface.

The toss decision was initially called incorrectly by the match referee, who announced tails after Varma flipped the coin on Pakistan skipper Abdul Samad’s call of heads.

Samad pointed out the error and the officials corrected the decision in Pakistan’s favour. The captains did not shake hands, continuing the protocol observed in recent encounters between the sides.

Pakistan’s openers Shamyl Hussain and Maaz Sadaqat gave their side a flying start, putting on 66 for the first wicket. Shamyl made 33 off 23 balls before Ayush Badoni had him caught by Harshit Rana at short third. Rana then trapped Rohail leg-before for a duck, with Pakistan on 67-2.

The exchanges between Rana and the Pakistan batters had added an edge to the powerplay, with the Indian fast bowler involved in heated verbal exchanges and giving Shamyl an animated send-off.

Maaz and Hasan rebuilt the innings, with the former scoring 59 off 63 balls for his second successive half-century.

Hasan went on to make 79 off 82 deliveries, while Farhan Yousaf’s 56 off 48 balls and Imran’s quickfire 23 helped Pakistan push past 300, which was proven enough for the side at the end.

articles.title: More than 2,300 Indian Sikh pilgrims arrive in Pakistan to mark Guru Nanak's birthday
articles.summary:
LAHORE: Over 2,300 Indian Sikh pilgrims arrived in Pakistan through the Wagah Border on Sunday to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, the founder of Sikhism.

The visiting pilgrims were received by Evacuee Trust Property Board (ETPB) Chairman Qamar Zaman, Secretary Nasir Mushtaq, Pakistan Sikh Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee (PSGPC) President and Punjab Minorities Minister Sardar Ramesh Singh Arora, the committee’s secretary general Satwant Kaur and other officials at the Wagah border, where the jatha leaders were presented with bouquets.

Indian Sikh pilgrims wave to the camera after arriving in Lahore through the Wagah Border to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, on Nov 22. — White Star

According to ETPB spokesperson Amir Hashmi, 2,339 Sikh pilgrims arrived from India here on Sunday to take part in the festivities in Nankana Sahib.

The Pakistan High Commission in New Delhi had reportedly issued around 3,100 visas to Indian Sikhs.

Special counters were set up at the Wagah Border to facilitate immigration and baggage screening, while Rangers were deployed to ensure security.

Indian Sikh pilgrims arrive in Lahore through the Wagah Border to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, on Nov 22. — White Star

The ETPB had also established currency exchange facilities at the border, while its teams promptly issued identity cards and bus tickets to the pilgrims to ensure a smooth onward journey, he added.

“The pilgrims subsequently left for Nankana Sahib in three separate convoys under tight security to attend the main ceremony on Nov 24 marking Baba Guru Nanak’s birth anniversary at Gurdwara Janam Asthan, his birthplace,” Hashmi said.

He added that over 20,000 Sikhs — from Pakistan and across the globe — are expected to take part in the formal festivities, which begin today and continue until Nov 24.

Indian Sikh pilgrims gather after arriving in Lahore through the Wagah Border to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, on Nov 22. — White Star

Federal Minister for Religious Affairs Sardar Muhammad Yousuf, along with other federal and provincial ministers, will attend the event as special guests.

The event participants will perform religious rituals, including Bhog and Akhand Path Sahib, followed by a traditional palanquin procession, known as Nagar Kirtan.

Speaking on the occasion, ETPB Chairman Zaman said the board was making every effort to ensure that the visiting pilgrims faced no inconvenience during their stay in Pakistan.

He said the Indian Sikh pilgrims would return home with fond memories of love, peace and brotherhood.

Indian Sikh pilgrims including a wheelchair-bound woman arrive in Lahore through the Wagah Border to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, on Nov 22. — White Star

Minister Arora urged the Indian government to immediately reopen the Kartarpur Corridor, which provides Sikh pilgrims with access to Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Kartarpur, one of the holiest sites in Sikhism.

India suspended movement through the Kartarpur Corridor in May 2025 amid the four-day conflict between the countries.

Kaldeep Singh Gurgaj, a leader of the Akal Takht authority from India, said the Sikh community shared a deep bond of reverence with Pakistan, where its members were always treated with respect and honour.

“Our gurdwaras in Pakistan are safe and preserved in their original state,” he said.

Parmjeet Singh, a leader of a Delhi Gurdwara Management Committee delegation, said Pakistan held special significance for Sikhs as the land associated with their guru.

“Pakistan is the land of our guru, and we love it very much,” he said.

Indian Sikh pilgrims arrive in Lahore through the Wagah Border to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, on Nov 22. — White Star

After attending the main ceremony, the Sikh pilgrims will visit Gurdwara Sacha Sauda in Farooqabad on Nov 25 before proceeding to Hassan Abdal, where they will stay overnight at Gurdwara Panja Sahib.

They will travel to Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Kartarpur, Narowal, on Nov 27.

The visiting devotees will then spend Nov 29 and 30 visiting various historic gurdwaras in Lahore before returning to India through the Wagah border by road on Dec 1.

Sikh pilgrims frequently visit Pakistan to observe events of religious significance. In June, around 600 Sikhs arrived from India to observe the death anniversary of Guru Arjan Dev Ji, known as Jore Mela; before that, about 2,800 visas were issued to pilgrims to celebrate the Baisakhi festival in April.

articles.title: IBCC plans fully online attestation from Jan 1, ending office visits and courier submissions
articles.summary:
The Inter Boards Coordination Commission (IBCC) will launch a fully online attestation service on Jan 1, 2027, allowing students to apply for attestation and download their attested documents without visiting an IBCC office or sending documents by courier.

The decision was taken at a meeting of the IBCC Board of Directors chaired by Executive Director Dr Ghulam Ali Mallah. The service will cover qualifications issued by 29 examination boards across Pakistan, as well as eligible qualifications from madressahs.

Under the new online service, applicants will submit their documents through the IBCC portal. Once the commission processes and approves an application, the electronically attested document will be available in the applicant’s account to download and print. The new system will eliminate the need for courier delivery in either direction.

Students needing to submit the same document to several institutions will be able to print multiple copies without paying a separate IBCC attestation fee for each copy. They can use the copies for submissions to universities and, where required for use abroad, to the foreign ministry, subject to its applicable requirements.

Dr Mallah said the commission had developed the system on the directions of Federal Secretary for Education and Professional Training Nadeem Mahbub, after the IBCC Board of Governors took up the automation of the entire attestation process.

He said the commission expected the service to benefit an estimated 400,000 to 500,000 students by cutting travel and courier costs and saving them time spent visiting and waiting at IBCC offices. The shift would also reduce the commission’s workload by eliminating the need to receive, handle and dispatch physical documents.

The IBCC is an umbrella board of 29 educational boards in the country that verifies matric and intermediate certificates and provides equivalence certificates against O/A levels and other foreign qualifications.

In February 2025, the board said it had digitised the process for verification of academic degrees issued by boards of intermediate and secondary education. It said this would ensure the integrity and authenticity of the data as well as streamlining the process, ensuring faster and more efficient attestation.

articles.title: Search for Indonesia factory fire missing to resume on Monday, police remove 24 body bags
articles.summary:
Indonesian police removed 24 body bags from a factory destroyed by fire in Java on Sunday as firefighters battled remaining hotspots a day after the blaze tore through the building and a search for dozens of missing workers was suspended overnight.

Metro TV footage showed distraught family members weeping outside the factory as they waited for news of relatives feared to have been caught in the blaze.

Search operations are scheduled to resume on Monday morning, Hendra Kurniawan, the police chief of Indonesia’s Banten province, told Metro TV.

Steven Erwin Wijaya, the CEO of the factory, said at a press conference that around 300 people were present for Saturday’s shift.

In a later statement, the factory said that 24 of the 65 workers involved had returned home, 4 were receiving medical treatment, 29 remained missing and the whereabouts of another 8 had yet to be confirmed.

At the same press conference, Wahyu Hidayati, a police disaster victim identification official, said the intensity of the fire had rendered the recovered victims unidentifiable via visual inspection, prompting efforts to collect DNA samples from relatives and the personal belongings of the missing workers, a process that could take two to three weeks.

The number of dead was not immediately clear, with police saying that one body bag could contain parts of more than one person.

Authorities said the cause of the fire was being investigated.

The fire broke out on Saturday evening at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia candy factory in Cikande, in the Serang regency.

Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex.

Photos and videos shared by rescuers also showed officers entering the charred building in search of the missing victims, with small fires still burning in some spots.

Relatives of the missing victims flocked near the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones, footage aired by local broadcasters showed.

Earlier, search teams were combing sections of the damaged building where victims were believed to be trapped, while parts of the building remained at risk of collapse, an official said.

The factory is part of Indonesia’s United Family Food company, founded in 1981, according to its website.

It produces consumer goods across Indonesia, employs about 5,000 people and operates from its national headquarters and four international offices, serving a market of more than 250 million consumers.

articles.title: Multiple Karachi routes briefly closed as political parties hold demonstration, rally
articles.summary:
Multiple roads were closed briefly in Karachi on Sunday as the Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) staged a demonstration in the city and the Jeay Sindh Rehbar Committee (JSRC) — a conglomerate of four Sindhi nationalist groups — held a rally.

The JUI-F staged its main demonstration at Guru Mandir, while the JSRC organised a rally from Sachal Goth to the press club via Sharea Faisal, some stretches of which had been shut for vehicles, the traffic police said.

Traffic was allowed again on the stretch of Sharea Faisal leading to Drigh Road and Karsaz at 4:16pm after about an hour-long closure. Commuters coming from the airport had been diverted via Rashid Minhas Bridge towards Millennium Mall.

The route from Askari 4 to Drigh Road on Main Rashid Minhas Road was reopened for traffic at around 4:30pm following its reported closure at 3:30pm.

The route from Guru Mandir towards Jamshed Road was reopened for vehicles at around 5pm after being closed to traffic shortly after 2pm.

The stretch of Sharea Faisal from Avari Towers towards FTC was reopened at 8:45pm. Vehicles had been diverted from Avari Towers towards Fatima Jinnah Road and Sindh Club.

Both sides of Deen Mohammad Wafai Road had also been closed to traffic, with vehicles diverted from MR Kiani Chowrangi towards Thana Gali and from Fawara Chowk towards Zainab Market.

Main Korangi Road from CSD towards Sharea Faisal was closed at around 11am due to “security” reasons and was reopened to traffic at 9:30pm.

The alerts for road closures had cited “security” as the reason, except for the blockade of the route between Guru Mandir and Jamshed Road. The alert for this closure said the road had been blocked due to a planned demonstration by the JUI-F.

The JUI-F had said in a statement that while its main demonstration would be held at Guru Mandir, protests would also be held at its headquarters, press clubs and other locations across Sindh against the “violation of the sanctity of JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman’s residence, the ongoing smear campaign against him, and the conspiracy to divide Sindh”.

Meanwhile, the JSRC had announced a rally to protest the proposal to create new provinces and divide Sindh.

A four-member PPP committee began efforts on Friday to persuade nationalist parties to postpone their planned rallies in Karachi, but failed to do so.

Over the past few months, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has whipped up a political storm since he called for the formation of new administrative units in the country, saying the current “system” of governance had “collapsed” and needed a “reset”.

The PPP, which is in power in Sindh, has been clear in its stance against carving out any new federating units in the province but has been calling for the creation of a South Punjab province.

The Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan, which is an ally of the ruling PML-N along with the PPP in the Centre and in opposition in Sindh, has been insisting on the creation of new provinces and has thrown its weight behind the proposal to hold a referendum on the matter.

articles.title: Portuguese foreign minister arrives in Pakistan for official visit: FO
articles.summary:
Minister of State and Foreign Affairs of Portugal Paulo Rangel arrived in Pakistan on Sunday for an official visit, the Foreign Office (FO) said.

Rangel is visiting Pakistan at the invitation of Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar from Nov 22 to 23. He was received upon arrival by Additional Secretary Europe Ambassador Ayesha Ali.

According to FO, Rangel will hold delegation-level talks with DPM Dar as well as meetings with Pakistani leadership.

“He is accompanied by a business delegation for the inaugural Pakistan-Portugal Business Forum,” FO said, expressing hope that the visit will provide an opportunity to review the full spectrum of the bilateral relationship.

Speaking to the media, Rangel praised the peace efforts of Pakistan in recent months during the US-Iran war.

“The world needs you. We have been seeing in the very recent months that the role of Pakistan is decisive for global peace, so we count on you to help all the peoples of the world, reaching peace and prosperity,” he told Pakistan TV.

The visit comes as Pakistan and Portugal mark the 77th anniversary of their diplomatic relations, established on Nov 7, 1949, FO spokesperson said in a statement on Saturday.

The two leaders will review bilateral relations and discuss ways to expand trade and investment.

“The visit will also feature a Pakistan-Portugal Business Forum. Companies from both countries will hold business-to-business meetings to explore commercial partnerships and investment opportunities in agri-food, renewable energy, pharmaceuticals, information technology and textiles,” the spokesperson had added in his statement.

Foreign Minister Rangel’s visit will provide an opportunity to build on the longstanding ties between Pakistan and Portugal and to broaden bilateral cooperation across diverse sectors.

articles.title: 3 TTP-linked terrorists killed in village on outskirts of Peshawar: CTD
articles.summary:
PESHAWAR: Three terrorists were killed during an exchange of fire with Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) and military personnel in the Passani village, located on Peshawar’s outskirts, late on Saturday night, the CTD said in a statement on Sunday.

The statement said the CTD received intelligence about the presence of a group of terrorists belonging to Fitna-al-Khawarij on Passani Road — an area located 23 miles south of Peshawar, falling within the jurisdiction of Mattani police station.

Fitna-al-Khawarij is a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).

The CTD said the terrorists planned to carry out attacks on government installations.

“Based on the confirmed reports, CTD’s Special Weapons and Tactics Teams (SWAT), along with personnel of the Pakistan Army, equipped with modern weapons, reached the area to arrest the terrorists,” the statement added.

However, upon seeing law enforcement and security personnel, the terrorists opened fire, to which the teams responded effectively in self-defence, the statement further said.

Following an exchange of fire, a search operation was launched in the area during which the bodies of three terrorists were found, it said. The CTD identified the terrorists as Abdul Rashid, Saeedullah, and Saeed Nawab — members of the banned TTP.

The statement added that other terrorists present at the site managed to escape; meanwhile, the teams recovered two Kalashnikovs, a pistol, three hand grenades, five magazines and computerised national identity cards (CNICs) from the slain terrorists.

A search operation was under way to arrest the escaped terrorists, the statement added.

As per the CTD statement, KP Inspector General of Police Zulfiqar Hameed and Additional IG CTD Jawad Qamar vowed that terrorists would never be allowed to succeed.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif lauded security forces for the successful operation, observing that “timely and decisive action” thwarted a “major threat”, state-run APP reported.

The operations of the security forces against terrorism are a reflection of national resolve and morale, the report quoted him as saying.

Constable martyred in attack in Lower South Waziristan

Separately, a police constable was martyred after unidentified motorcyclists opened fire on him near Mughal Khel village in Wana’s Rustam Bazaar in Lower South Waziristan.

The constable, identified as Abdul Salam Dottani, sustained critical bullet injuries in the attack. He was immediately taken to the District Headquarters Hospital in Wana, but succumbed to his injuries despite medical treatment.

Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP) Nadir Khan Wazir confirmed the incident to Dawn over the telephone, saying that unidentified armed men riding a motorcycle had targeted the police constable and fled the scene after the shooting.

He said police had registered an initial report and launched an investigation into the incident. Efforts were underway to determine the motive behind the attack and identify those responsible for the killing.

The funeral prayers of the martyred constable were offered at the Police Lines in Wana with full official honours.

District Police Officer (DPO) Shah Hassan (PSP), Deputy Commissioner Musarrat Zaman, CTD Superintendent of Police (SP) Gul Rauf Khan, Wana Circle DSP Basharat Khan, Birmal DSP Wazir and other senior police officials, personnel and people from different walks of life attended the funeral proceedings.

A well-equipped police contingent presented a guard of honour to the deceased, while senior police and civil administration officials laid floral wreaths on his coffin to pay tribute to his services and sacrifice.

The participants offered prayers for the departed soul and expressed solidarity with the bereaved family.

Police officials paid tribute to Constable Dottani, saying that he had sacrificed his life while performing his official duties. They described his sacrifice as an example of courage, dedication and commitment to public service.

The incident comes amid a continued surge in attacks targeting police personnel in Upper and Lower South Waziristan over the past two years.

The recurring attacks have raised serious concerns about the security situation in both districts, where police personnel and law enforcement agencies continue to face security challenges.

KP continues to actively face terrorist threats. Last week, 43 terrorists were killed during operations conducted in KP, including 35 in Mir Ali, North Waziristan district, and eight in Orakzai district, the military’s media wing said.

On the other hand, the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), an Islamabad-based independent think tank monitoring conflict and security developments, has reported encouraging trends in KP in its monthly assessment for October.

In mainland KP, PICSS recorded 40 attacks during October, compared with 58 in September, representing a reduction of 31pc. Meanwhile, deaths resulting from these attacks declined from 90 to 38, a decrease of approximately 58pc, while injuries fell from 165 to 19, representing a reduction of 88pc.

The merged districts of KP recorded 30 attacks during October, compared with 34 in September, and deaths resulting from these attacks decreased from 33 to 25, while injuries increased from 11 to 13, the report said.

articles.title: Naqvi hits back at minister for repeated criticism: report
articles.summary:
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has hit back at a federal minister for what he said was repeated criticism against him, Geo News reported on Sunday.

The news website reported that Naqvi, without naming the minister, claimed the latter had been commenting on him on television almost every day to “gain attention”.

The report described the remarks as part of an informal conversation with Geo News and further quoted Naqvi as saying that he had been patiently listening to the minister’s statements for the past two-and-a-half years — the tenure of the incumbent government since the 2024 elections.

“The day I comment on this minister, he will not be able to show his face,” Naqvi warned, according to the outlet.

Naqvi also defended the businesspeople present at an economic forum who he said were criticised by the minister. He said the attendees were respectable citizens who had served as presidents and office-bearers of chambers of commerce at the federal and city levels, according to the report.

While the report did not quote him as mentioning any specific details in this connection, Naqvi’s remarks at the Pakistan Economic Summit in Islamabad in July had been making headlines in recent months. Naqvi had whipped up a political storm by calling for creating new administrative units in the country to “reset” the current “system” of governance while speaking at the forum, which was attended by businessmen.

In his remarks to Geo News, Naqvi stated that the businessmen were also among the country’s highest taxpayers.

“If these businessmen are so bad, why do you take billions of rupees from them in the name of party funds at every election?” the interior minister was quoted as saying.

Naqvi’s remarks have been reported a day after Inter-Provincial Coordination Minister Rana Sanaullah questioned the objectives of some of the businesspeople at that July forum.

In an interview on Geo News programme ‘Jirga’ aired on Saturday, Sanaullah said the “matter got worse in such a way that the debate on provinces began from an economic forum” and Naqvi started the discussion.

Sanaullah, also Naqvi’s predecessor, contended that there were “some objectionable businessmen sitting among the audience of that economic forum”.

“It has been their background that in each tenure, they keep on telling the incoming ruler, especially the army chief, that ‘sir, the whole world is looking at you and only you are the saviour,’” Sanaullah said.

The PML-N leader clarified that he was not referring to the entire business community, but rather “a few people who keep committing crime in business, and here as well”.

On differing stances among federal cabinet members on the issue of new provinces, Sanaullah contended that politicians could express their opinions, as “regimental discipline” could not be brought into the cabinet.

Sanaullah stressed that the debate on provinces was “not wrong”, but he contended that the “debate was being entangled with other matters; saying that the system has collapsed; after that some remarks were made about the prime minister, and similarly about politicians contesting elections in so and so manner”.

The PML-N leader also criticised PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari for further complicating the situation by referring to various matters in his Nov 17 speech, rather than merely voicing his objection to carving out new administrative units out of Sindh.

Sanaullah further termed both Bilawal and Naqvi as “sons” of President Asif Ali Zardari, adding that they were “under his discipline”.

Asked about the independent senator being “under President Zardari’s discipline”, Sanaullah reiterated, “Yes, definitely. He has not disowned him yet. He himself calls him (Naqvi) his son; it is not that we are saying so.”

Referring to a recent meeting between President Zardari and PM Shehbaz Sharif, during which Naqvi was also present, Sanaullah said a “ceasefire was decided” there.

He claimed that, according to information he had, a meeting was held at President House recently, which was attended by President Zardari, Bilawal and Naqvi, and it was decided to reduce tensions.

Replying to a query about the independent senator, Sanaullah remarked that Naqvi was a senator of both PPP and PML-N, as leaders from both parties contributed to the votes for his election.

In September as well, Sanaullah had said that the “debate should have been started in Parliament”, adding that issues of such magnitude should not be reduced to speeches, social media, seminars or business forums.

The PML-N leader has also taken jibes at the interior minister on a few other occasions since the ruling coalition came to power.

On the other hand, Sindh Local Government Minister Nasir Hussain Shah also took exception to Sanaullah’s remarks, asserting that Bilawal was the only son of President Zardari.

“Mohsin Naqvi sahib is worthy of respect in his place, but nothing about him compares to the chairman (Bilawal),” he told reporters.

Shah maintained there was “no such thing” as suggested by the PML-N minister, declaring, “There is only one Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, and only his words will prevail here.”

articles.title: COP31 climate talks collapse as EU and others reject deal
articles.summary:
UN climate talks collapsed on Sunday as the European Union and others rejected a final draft deal put forward by COP31 presidents Turkiye and Australia, saying it was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.

The failed talks reflect world governments’ struggle this year to muster ambitious action to address the worsening consequences of climate change, as wars, economic pressures and other crises compete for their attention.

After more than two weeks of negotiations that spilled two days into overtime — making it the longest COP on record — Turkiye’s conference president Murat Kurum said at the closing plenary that he could see there was no agreement and confirmed he would not advance any new text.

“There is nothing to do, we did all that we could,” he said. “There will be no new text from now on.”

He later left the stage in the midst of speeches being delivered by country representatives.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply disappointed” that the climate talks ended without consensus.

“I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands,” Guterres said in a statement.

“Those who profit from the destruction of our planet must never dictate the terms of the fight to save it. Fossil fuels are driving the climate crisis. ”

Australia’s COP31 President of Negotiations, Chris Bowen, called the outcome “very disappointing” and said disagreements over fuels and climate finance were the dealbreakers.

Earlier, multiple countries and negotiating blocs said they could not accept the version of the text put before them.

“It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted,” Kurum said.

The last time UN climate talks failed to end with a deal adopted by all was in Copenhagen in 2009.

The collapse this time is against the backdrop of competing crises, including wars and public outcry over the cost of living, that have overshadowed the problems caused by a warming climate.

Ireland’s environment minister Darragh O’Brien said the European Union could not support the proposed deal, in part because it made no mention of the fossil fuels that scientists say are driving global warming.

“It is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels,” he said.

Panama also said it could not support the current text because it fails to meet the scale of the climate crisis.

This year’s COP is the first since the UN’s environmental body in October that confirmed the rise in global temperature was set to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius, a threshold countries agreed at Paris climate talks over a decade ago to try not to exceed, and beyond which extreme weather impacts intensify.

Belgium’s Climate Minister Jean-Luc Crucke said the failure of the deal was a difficult outcome, but appropriate.

“It’s not the end of multilateralism, but there has to be courage to say no,” he said.

While a blow to efforts to ratchet up international action, the failure to agree a political declaration in Antalya does not erase the obligations agreed by previous UN conferences or remove the technical and legal frameworks governing multilateral action against climate change.

Pressure from Saudi Arabia and other oil producers

The proposed deal had acknowledged the overshoot, but called for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse it.

Observers at the venue said Saudi Arabia and other big oil-producing nations had pushed hard in negotiations for keeping explicit mention of fossil fuels out of the text, and carbon removal technologies in.

While scientists say removing carbon from the atmosphere when paired with steep emissions cuts is vital to avoiding the worst impacts of climate change, critics of the deal said they worried the carbon removal language would be used as a licence to keep pumping oil.

A representative for the Saudi delegation told the summit he was surprised at the resistance to technology.

“If indeed the climate challenge, as some have mentioned today, is so important, it makes no sense that solutions, concrete solutions… will be taken off the table,” he said.

Developing countries had also criticised the deal for not providing sufficient new climate finance to help them adapt to a warming planet. The deal had called for a tripling of such finance, but did not specify from what baseline.

The failed deal had also included a goal put forward by Turkiye to expand electricity’s share of total final world energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035, from around 23pc now.

Proponents of that pledge said it could cut greenhouse gas emissions by speeding the transition away from fuel-powered cars, furnaces, and other equipment. But critics said it could force more costs onto poor nations without providing a clear path away from fossil fuels.

The COP process is the main vehicle through which countries coordinate their efforts to curb global warming. Its annual summit provides an opportunity for nations to signal they are willing to work together to find solutions and help finance the problems rising temperatures cause.

articles.title: Oman to supply petroleum products, $200m credit facility to PSO under new agreement
articles.summary:
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan and Oman on Sunday signed an agreement under which the Gulf country’s state-owned OQ Trading would supply petroleum products, as well as a $200 million credit line, to the Pakistan State Oil (PSO).

This could provide Pakistan with a means to strategically diversify its sourcing of petroleum products as the Strait of Hormuz continues to be choked by the US-Iran conflict into its ninth month.

According to an announcement from the Petroleum Division, the agreement between the two state-owned entities was signed during Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik’s visit to Muscat, where he met with Oman’s Minister of Energy and Minerals Eng. Salim Al Aufi.

The two sides discussed opportunities for strengthening bilateral cooperation in the oil, gas and minerals sectors.

During the meeting, both ministers discussed avenues for mutually beneficial cooperation and welcomed the establishment of the Pakistan-Oman Joint Working Group on Oil and Gas. They agreed to make optimal use of this institutional mechanism to further strengthen bilateral engagement and advance cooperation in the energy and mining sector.

Following the meeting, the two ministers witnessed the signing of a Sale and Purchase Agreement (SPA) for petroleum products between PSO and OQ Trading (OQT), Oman’s global commodity trading company. OQT has also agreed to extend a $200m credit line to PSO to facilitate petroleum purchases.

Welcoming the agreement, both ministers expressed confidence that its implementation would further strengthen Pakistan-Oman energy ties and support Pakistan’s efforts to enhance energy security through diversification of energy imports.

“The agreement marks an important milestone in the commercial relationship between the two companies and provides a structured arrangement for petroleum product supplies from OQT to PSO, supporting supply reliability amid continued volatility in regional energy markets,” the Petroleum Division’s statement said.

It noted that OQT has already established itself as a major supplier of gasoline to PSO, supplying more than 1m tonnes during 2026. The newly signed agreement builds on this established trading relationship and provides a framework for expanding commercial cooperation, the statement added.

Beyond gasoline, OQT has also strengthened its presence in Pakistan’s liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) market, supplying both state-owned and private sector buyers.

According to the Petroleum Division, OQT’s LPG supplies to Pakistan are expected to exceed 120,000 metric tonnes by the end of 2026, reflecting the company’s continued commitment to meeting market demand and maintaining energy flows amid regional supply disruptions.

The meeting and the signing of the agreement underscore the shared commitment of Pakistan and Oman to expanding bilateral energy cooperation, strengthening commercial partnerships and exploring new investment opportunities across the oil, gas and minerals sectors, the statement added.

Last month, Oman’s Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi made a two-day visit to Pakistan, meeting its top leadership.

He attended the eighth session of the Pakistan-Oman Joint Ministerial Commission (JMC), during which both sides emphasised the importance of promoting exchanges of business delegations from both countries to unlock new opportunities for trade, investment and institutional collaboration.

articles.title: Future wars
articles.summary:
THE four-day military confrontation between India and Pakistan last year and the US-Iran war this year have revealed how today’s wars have become far more complex than the conventional conflicts humanity has experienced over millennia. The days of massed soldiery, mechanised armour, and standardised formations are over. Today’s wars are hybrid and employ every instrument of power a state can muster.

These wars involve cyberattacks, economic coercion, psychological manipulation through electronic and social media, and cultural invasions.

Critically, today’s wars employ lethal technologies, which have left traditional battlefield concepts behind. These autonomous weapons are guided by specialised semiconductors, microchips, and sensors.

The changing nature of war has coincided with the sharp descent of the world order into disarray. Wars and armed conflicts between and within states have broken out in various parts of the world. The pledge that all states had made to the UN Charter to respect each other’s sovereignty and territorial integrity is no longer being honoured.

Two distinguishing features of today’s warfare are advanced missiles and armed drones, which have transformed the nature of war by enabling high-precision, long-range, and rapid response capabilities.

In last year’s India-Pakistan war, Pakistan used missiles to down several Indian aircraft flying well beyond visual range. In the US-Iran war this year, both sides relied mostly on missiles guided by infrared sensors and satellite communication rather than conventional confrontation.

Autonomous weapons lack the capability to understand the context.

Advanced robotic systems are being employed for intelligence, surveillance, and even targeted strikes. Drones and robotic dogs can provide real-time data, improve combat efficiency, and operate for high-risk functions such as clearance of mines or locating captured personnel. Unarmed aerial vehicles provide real-time intelligence, and are equipped with AI-driven capabilities to analyse data. Targets can be independently tracked and even struck by loitering munitions or suicide drones. Transporting supplies and ammunition entails no life losses thanks to unarmed ground vehicles. Drone swarms can now be trained to carry out coordinated attacks. It’s only a matter of time before humanoid robots are deployed for military roles.

The spectrum of modern wars employs other technologies as well, such as quantum computing, which solves complex problems faster than classical computers. It ensures unhackable and secure data transmission during conflict situations. Next-generation structural battery composites can store energy for longer periods.

Future wars will move further away from face-to-face engagement or human-controlled systems. Intelligent autonomous systems will be central to making decisions, often without human intervention. However, this raises some serious ethical questions.

Autonomous weapons lack the capability to understand the context or apply compassion. There is greater likelihood of violating the laws of war and committing war crimes without assigning accountability. Further, the speed and agility of these technologies could cause conflicts to spiral out of control.

These technologies will also be used to break an adversary’s morale by targeting its economic assets or supply chains. During the Iran war, for instance, President Trump threatened to destroy Iran’s power grid and bridges, even its civilisation.

The kind of technologies a nation possesses will now determine the extent of damage that a future war would impose on an adversary’s policy options. The ability of a nation to acquire and em­­ploy modern technologies is thus critical to both wag­-ing future wars and surviving them.

What makes future wars more frequent and unaccountable is the evolving global ecosystem, where use of force has emerged as the primary arbiter of international relations. Major powers have no qualms about using force illegally, unilaterally, and disproportionately to overpower adversaries.

In such an uncertain environment, middle and small powers are looking for ways to fend for themselves and make alliances with like-minded countries. This has nudged countries to focus more on R&D for developing not only war-related technologies but also their own digital and satellite-based communication links. That requires a stronger economy, credible information instruments, and creative narrative-building to deter aggression.

Diplomatic tools must be geared up to avert such complex multidomain future wars. The world needs a new global compact of indivisible security, akin to the UN Charter, to bind states into mutual respect for each other’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. This is the only way to avert the devastating wars of the future.

The writer is Chairman Sanober Institute and former foreign secretary of Pakistan.

Published in Dawn, November 22nd, 2026

articles.title: PTI MNAs demand to know whereabouts of party leaders detained in KP, seek their court production
articles.summary:
ISLAMABAD: PTI lawmakers from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Sunday reiterated their demand for the immediate disclosure of the whereabouts of all detained PTI leaders and workers, their production before the courts and the provision of their legal right to defence.

The demand was made during a meeting of PTI’s elected members of the National Assembly (NA) from KP, held in Islamabad under the prevailing political and constitutional situation, according to a statement by the party.

At the meeting, the lawmakers called for the immediate disclosure of the whereabouts of now non-functional chief minister Sohail Afridi, KP Assembly Speaker Babar Saleem Swati, provincial president Junaid Akbar Khan and other detained party leaders and workers.

Afridi — whose role as the chief minister was rendered non-functional due to governor’s rule — Swati and some other lawmakers have been in “preventive detention” since emergency was imposed, according to police. KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi also said last month that Afridi and Swati had been placed under house arrest.
