articles.title: The philosophical reason AI Christmas ads leave audiences feeling cold
articles.summary:
Alliance Images/Shutterstock

It’s that time of year when Christmas adverts start appearing, and brands offer up a slice of consumerist comfort as you curl up in front of a screen.

Yet companies are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) to produce their ads. Last year proved how quickly that strategy can backfire. In the Netherlands, McDonald’s pulled an AI-generated Christmas ad depicting chaotic holiday mishaps after just three days following fierce backlash over the undisclosed usage.

This kind of omission is now restricted under new EU transparency rules that govern how AI-generated content is labelled. Coca-Cola’s 2025 festive campaign drew similar criticism. The advert featured AI-generated scenery and animals that many viewers found uncanny.

Undeterred, this year brands including Very and Plusnet have pressed ahead with AI productions. Because UK law does not require on-screen disclosure, their use of the technology is often tucked away in separate press releases and trade announcements rather than flagged to viewers. Even so, the UK Advertising Standards Authority prohibits misleading omissions if an advert falsely implies human creation to deceive consumers.

Read more:
What does an ‘AI-generated’ label in advertising actually tell us?

Other brands are more subtle with their AI use. While Royal Mail’s 2025 Christmas ad relied on traditional live-action footage, it recently emerged that the campaign used an AI voiceover to narrate the spot.

Replacing human performers – even behind the microphone – has fuelled growing anxiety among both industry insiders and the general public, echoing the fears that sparked the 2023 Hollywood writers’ and actors’ strikes.

AI was used for the voiceover in the 2025 Royal Mail Christmas advert.

Losing trust in animated ads

This growing scepticism means even traditional animation is no longer safe from scrutiny. Dior’s Christmas short film, for example, has generated suspicions among some viewers. Described as hand-drawn and directed by French animator Sylvain Chomet, with an all-star cast featuring Rihanna and Robert Pattinson, it centres on the fashion designer Christian Dior’s friendship with film star Marlene Dietrich.

Commenters praised its authentic visual appearance, while a behind the scenes page was published on Dior’s website highlighting the actors and design sketches, warding off accusations of AI-generation.

Despite this, some viewers believed that Dior’s advert showed several hallmarks of AI. A telltale sign of AI-generated content is garbled hands and fingers. Some viewers pointed to what they perceived as missing fingers and strange hand transitions in the advert.

Dior’s Christmas film.

In an interview with Variety, Chomet and producer Aton Soumache insisted that the advert was hand-drawn and generative AI was never used. But they have confirmed using a process known as “automated interpolation” to generate intermediate frames as “a very small part of the process” for the “repetitive, mechanical part of animation, not the creative work”. Automated interpolation is a standard digital animation tool that precedes AI, but now often involves its use.

The Dior case is illustrative of how vigilant audiences have become about AI use. Just as the presence of deepfakes risks undermining our trust in all images online, a few undisclosed AI-produced adverts can lead to scepticism of all advertising as viewers hunt for evidence of brands cutting corners rather than hiring creatives.

Why care about AI in ads?

Even when specific accusations prove unfounded, the broader shift in advertising toward undisclosed generative AI raises deeper ethical and aesthetic questions for the industry as a whole.

AI models are often trained on artists’ work without compensation and threaten to put them out of work – not to mention AI datacentres’ impact on communities and the environment.

There’s also an irony in major brands baulking at the tedious task of getting the details right, and giving a misleading impression of fully human creation. These moral defects can diminish our aesthetic experience of AI adverts.

But putting aside morality, the revelation of AI use renders ads aesthetically worse in another way. Philosophers of art argue that forgeries are worse as artworks because they misrepresent achievement. We usually appreciate what the artist did in creating a work. So when we learn that a painting is not a genuine Vermeer, but a 20th century forgery by Van Meegeren, we judge it differently. (One philosopher even likens this betrayal to sexual infidelity – perhaps a bit much!)

The praise showered on traditional productions proves that audiences still care deeply about craft.
fast-stock/Shutterstock

Similarly, when we discover a beautiful, animated Christmas ad was produced with AI, we might lose appreciation for its creative process. The appearance of delicately hand-animated characters is a façade, generated not by artistic imagination but raw computational power. It’s not fraud, but it diminishes the experience.

Using AI to assist in creating complex scenery isn’t easy, and there can be skill to its use – some philosophers liken it to gardening. But it’s not the real process of hand-drawing and animation. To present it as such is a misrepresentation of achievement, imitating a style without the requisite labour behind it.

In response to these quandaries, some brands have taken to detailing the human processes behind their animated Christmas ads. Prada’s campaign emphasises traditional hand-drawn animation, with a separate behind-the-scenes video highlighting its artists. Others have followed suit. Barbour and Thatchers Cider each employed Aardman (producers of Wallace & Gromit) to hand-animate their adverts, while Etsy’s festive campaign is not-so-subtly titled “celebrate being human”. There are also video game studios which have detailed their refusal to use generative AI.

The praise showered on these traditional productions proves that audiences still care deeply about craft. A season built on warmth and sincerity cannot be manufactured by an algorithm that has never felt either.

Alex Fisher has received research funding from the Society for Applied Philosophy, the Leverhulme Trust, the Aristotelian Society, and the Royal Institute of Philosophy.

articles.title: Expect to see fewer and smaller potatoes this Christmas – it’s the ‘worst harvest since 1950s’
articles.summary:
Potato prices are rising after a severe drought. BearFotos/Shutterstock

Britain’s potato harvest this winter could be one of the smallest in decades.

This is partly down to the hot summer and a poor growing year. Potatoes have shallow roots and need steady moisture, so dry spells cut yield and size. Where farmers had stored water to regularly irrigate, crops fared better.

With 75% of England in drought in September, and Wales also affected by dry conditions, one model estimated that British potato yields would be 11% below average. It used the 2018 harvest as a guide. Some farmers reported a greater than 50% drop in how many potatoes they were harvesting.

Wholesale prices had already risen by more than 40% by early August. By September, big British buyers were reportedly paying more than £300 a tonne for potatoes.

The Food and Drink Federation has warned of the worst potato harvest since the 1950s.

Growers have warned supermarkets to expect smaller potatoes and tighter supplies this year, so shoppers may need to accept wider variation in size and quality. This is partly because other European countries, which often provide supplies to the UK, suffered the same hot summer, and this affected their crops, too.

But shoppers may not feel the full effect of higher wholesale prices this winter. Potatoes are more likely to become significantly more expensive next year. It is also worth noting that many supermarkets subsidise potato prices.

Lidl has announced that a 2kg bag will cost 9p in the week before Christmas. The supermarket says it is funding the low price itself, so this price tells shoppers nothing about what the crop costs to grow.

Supermarkets agree prices and volumes with farmers well in advance. Retailers may absorb some of the higher costs this year rather than risk losing customers to competitors.

The bigger question is whether British farmers will carry on planting Britain’s favourite vegetable in future, and what happens if more decide it is no longer worth the risk.

How does potato production work?

In 2025, the issue was too many potatoes heading for shops – the UK produced 5.5 million tonnes, 8.5% more than the year before. This caused prices paid to farmers to collapse.

By February 2026, top-quality maris piper potatoes were fetching about £180 a tonne on the open market, less than half the £400 of a year earlier. Contract prices for the following year were also weaker.

Growers did what economics predicts: they planted less. Analysts put this year’s area in Great Britain at around 101,000 hectares, well below the 117,500 recorded in 2020.

Then came the heat and drought.

Why can’t farmers cash in?

Higher prices should encourage farmers to plant more. But a price spike helps only those with potatoes to sell at open-market rates. Most crops are grown under contract, and growers who struggle to deliver the agreed tonnage or quality may miss out.

Some big buyers that normally rely on contracts are buying open-market potatoes as fast as they can, so growers with uncommitted crops may do well.

Meanwhile, costs for farmers keep climbing. Conflict in the Middle East has pushed up energy and fertiliser costs. Labour and machinery are also more expensive.

Meanwhile, the end of the basic payment scheme (an annual payment for farmers that followed environmental guidelines) and controversies about its replacements may have removed a financial cushion that once helped farms through bad years.

The potato contract price is fixed in advance, so growers have little room to pass costs on. Tighter margins are also hitting buyers, packers and processors, but it is growers that carry the bulk of the weather risk.

Economists call this pattern the cobweb cycle. In the textbook version, farmers plant according to last season’s price, so a glut leads to a price crash, then cuts in planting, then shortage and high prices, then over-planting again. Potatoes have followed this familiar cycle almost to the letter this year.

Yet several forces pull the other way. Speaking before the summer’s hot weather and drought, in May, Scott Walker, chief executive of the industry body representing the potato sector, GB Potatoes, said that many growers were weighing up how much exposure they would carry into 2027. The body has warned that growers could leave the business or reduce their crop.

Contract prices were weaker this year, costs are higher, and drought has shown how exposed the crop is. Depressed cereal markets offer little alternative income, so a wholesale exit is not certain either.

Farmers will be looking closely at what supermarkets offer them in 2027. High open market prices alone will not bring growers back.

Two things matter most: the contracts offered this winter, and whether farmers can secure water supplies for next summer. Signs are that water access may remain tight. For instance, the Environment Agency put England’s reservoirs at only 54% of capacity in early October. Higher prices could prompt a rebound in planting, but a normal-weather harvest could tip the market back into glut, forcing prices down again.

Will British farmers stop planting potatoes?

In September 2026, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs saw no indication that winter supplies were at risk but added that it was too early to assess the drought’s full impact on potato production and that there was, at that point, no indication that winter potato supplies were at risk. Registered potato farmer numbers fell from about 2,466 in 2000 to 1,611 in 2020, when the statutory body collating data on potato farmers was discontinued. But each bad year pushes more to ask whether the crop is worth it.

Tim Rooke, National Farmers’ Union potato policy group chair, said in 2025 that the UK imports approximately 1 million tonnes of frozen chips a year, because the risk against return on investment of growing potatoes is astronomically high.

A food system that leaves a shrinking number of growers to absorb the weather and price risk should not be surprised when they plant less. One option could be fairer contracts that share risk, and investment in water storage. But less certain supply chains and more volatile prices could cost shoppers more.

Climate change means water shortages and high temperatures will happen more often across Europe. Potato farmers are, therefore, likely to face these challenges more regularly in the future.

Robin Gowers does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Your brain may be hiding Alzheimer’s from you – and that’s not always a good thing
articles.summary:
Better verbal memory may explain women's brain resilience. superbeststock/ Shutterstock

When scientists examine the brains of older people after death, what they find can often be puzzling. One such puzzle is that around a third of people who showed no signs of dementia when they were alive, had brains which contained key indicators of Alzheimer’s disease.

Neuroscientists describe these people as being “resilient” to Alzheimer’s. They see this trait as a good thing, and have spent decades trying to understand what makes a brain resilient.

The hope is that if we can find out, we may then be able to protect more people from the disease.

But coping with a disease isn’t the same as being protected from it. A brain that copes well may also be hiding the disease – sometimes until it’s too late to act.

Hiding disease

Alzheimer’s disease unfolds in stages. First, proteins called amyloid and tau build up in the brain as plaques and clumps known as “tangles”. Then the brain cells (neurons) are damaged and die. Finally, memory and thinking begin to fail.

Some people never accumulate much amyloid or tau despite having a high genetic risk of Alzheimer’s disease. Researchers call this “resistance”.

Others experience a build up of amyloid and tau, but cope with it. This is resilience.

There are two key forms of resilience. In the first, someone may have plenty of amyloid and tau in the brain but they don’t lose many brain cells.

In the second form, this amyloid and tau build-up does result in the loss of brain cells – but the person may still continue thinking clearly. Or, if there is cognitive decline, it’s very slow – so symptoms are less noticeable.

This second form of resilience should worry us most, because a person can seem perfectly well while their brain is quietly shrinking.

This situation is often seen in women. On average, women have better verbal memory than men throughout life, meaning they have better recall of language-based information such as words, names and stories.

But this can be a problem when identifying Alzheimer’s, as the memory tests used to diagnose the disease rely heavily on verbal memory. Research has even found that women with signs of Alzheimer’s scored better on memory tests than men who had similar signs of the disease.

Read more:
Dementia: how brain resilience, immune health and the menopause play a role in women’s risk

A similar pattern is also seen in people with high “cognitive reserve”. Cognitive reserve is the brain’s ability to adapt and improvise when it faces a setback – such as those caused by ageing or disease. Cognitive reserve is built throughout life by things such as education and mentally demanding work.

People with high cognitive reserve tend to develop Alzheimer’s symptoms later. But once symptoms do appear, brain function tends to decline more quickly. This is usually because by the time symptoms develop the disease is already quite far along.

So although resilience can protect a person’s cognitive health for years, the disease eventually outpaces the brain’s ability to cope. The resilience that was once beneficial to us is suddenly no longer helpful.

This can be a problem for several reasons.

Resilience may hide Alzheimer’s, even when the disease is present in the brain.
ART-ur/ Shutterstock

The first problem is that it can delay diagnosis. This means a person won’t get the support they need at a crucial stage.

Another problem with resilience is that if it hides the disease until it’s in its advanced stages, people may miss the window for when treatment could help most. The only drugs currently approved to slow the progression of Alzheimer’s must be taken in the early stages of the disease to potentially have any effect.

Resilience can also make it difficult when researching and testing new Alzheimer’s drugs. People who cope well decline slowly overall – whether they receive a drug or a placebo. This could make a drug look weaker or stronger than it might actually be. It may also be one of the reasons why a drug may not work equally well for all people who have Alzheimer’s disease.

For example, one Alzheimer’s drug was found to be more effective in people who were less resilient. For people who were highly resilient (even though they had high levels of tau in their brain and similar cognition as the less resilient people), there wasn’t a clear benefit.

Understanding resilience

There’s still much scientists don’t know about resilience.

Although genetics can provide some information about a person’s Alzheimer’s risk and the disease’s likely progression, it unfortunately can’t tell us very much about resilience.

We still need to figure out what’s happening in the brains of people who stay well, and what exactly changes in the brain when that protection starts to fail.

But ongoing research may help us answer these questions someday. Biomarkers, which are measurable signs of a disease, can detect Alzheimer’s from a blood sample. If paired with a cognitive test, this could let researchers see how much disease a person carries, how much damage it’s doing and how well a person’s cognitive function has held up.

Biomarkers could also improve research for treatments by showing which interventions really have an effect in slowing the disease or making people resilient or even resistant.

When it comes to Alzheimer’s, resilience shows us that carrying the disease doesn’t have to mean losing your memory or your independence. But it can also hide signs of the disease until it’s too late.

Uncovering the biology behind resilience could allow us to offer protection to those who need it – and intervene earlier for those who are highly resilient.

articles.title: 300 years after the woman who ‘gave birth to rabbits’: why the legendary hoax still matters
articles.summary:
The portrait of Mary Toft is innocuous enough. But the sitter’s firm grip on the rabbit in her lap is the clue to the extraordinary story it depicts. Toft’s distinction was to be the only woman, as far as I know, to have claimed to give birth to rabbits.

Three hundred years on, and as I discuss in my book, The Imposteress Rabbit Breeder, the questions raised by this case continue to resonate.

You may be familiar with these rabbit births. Hilary Mantel referred to them in her 1998 historical novel The Giant, O'Brien. They were also obliquely referenced in the 2018 film The Favourite, about Britain’s Queen Anne. If you had lived within reach of English news or gossip in 1726, you would almost certainly have heard the story.

Toft was 23 and living in Guildford, Surrey, when she supposedly started giving birth to rabbits that September. Soon, major British newspapers were devoting front-page column inches to the affair. The fullest account was delivered to readers in the Daily Journal on Monday November 14, when it reported that “a poor Woman” had been “delivered by Mr. John Howard, an eminent Surgeon and Man-Midwife living at Guildford, of a Creature resembling a Rabbit”.

In 1726, Toft was asked for her own account of the rabbit births. She explained that she and her fellow workers had chased a rabbit in a field. Unable to catch it, she had been plagued by thoughts of rabbits night and day.

Her explanation drew on a medical theory known as the maternal imagination: the belief that a pregnant woman’s thoughts and experiences could physically shape her unborn child. Toft, or someone close to her, evidently knew enough about this theory to make her story seem plausible.

But, and no surprises here, the rabbit births were a hoax. In the end, a porter at the London establishment where Toft was being kept reported that rabbits had been smuggled into the building. The game was up.

A poor woman who could not read or write had apparently hoodwinked members of the medical establishment, including doctors connected to King George I’s court. In this deeply unequal and patriarchal society, Toft was a profoundly unsettling figure. As my research suggests, the response to the hoax was shaped by wider anxieties about social disorder and the behaviour of the poor.

After interrogation, Toft confessed and blamed the affair on her mother-in-law, as recorded in her final surviving statement of December 1726.

But people had largely stopped listening. She was presented as somewhat incidental to the events at the time, as you can see from the following contemporary satirical engraving by William Hogarth: doctors crowd around Toft’s bed, examining the supposed births while the woman herself lies almost forgotten at the edge of the scene. Historians have often taken a similar approach, focusing on the gullibility of the doctors or the scandal that engulfed them.

Mary Toft (Tofts) appearing to give birth to rabbits in the presence of several surgeons and man-midwives sent from London to examine her. Etching by W. Hogarth, 1726.
Wellcome Collection.

Centring women’s experience

My study of Toft’s accounts) instead places her experiences at the centre of the story. Her three surviving statements, although recorded under interrogation, offer a window into her social and emotional world.

Toft described two sets of events. The first was a difficult miscarriage. Her moving and visceral descriptions of pain and prolonged bleeding provide a rare historical account of early pregnancy loss.

The second was the hoax itself. Again, the details of Toft’s experiences are graphic. Animal parts were placed inside her body and subsequently removed during supposed deliveries. For all the written and visual satire the case produced, the hoax involved a real and potentially dangerous physical ordeal.

Toft repeatedly described being surrounded by women. At first, they were supportive, but in her telling they became increasingly menacing. She accused them of abusing their power and forcing her to perform the role of rabbit-breeder, risking her health and liberty.

Perhaps they were punishing her for the miscarriage. Perhaps they hoped to make money from this curious spectacle. Or perhaps Toft’s account was shaped by her desperation to escape punishment.

We may never know.

Toft’s descriptions of pain and bleeding give us a rare account of what miscarriage felt like to a woman in the 18th century. In maternity care today, how staff respond when a woman describes her pain can affect when she’s examined or offered pain relief. In England’s 2025 maternity survey, almost one in five respondents who raised a concern during labour or birth felt it hadn’t been taken seriously. Some described asking for pain relief and feeling that staff didn’t believe how much pain they were in. As one respondent put it, “I feel my contractions were not taken seriously during my induction.”

The doctors who examined Toft left a record of what they thought they saw. Her own statements give us an account of what she felt and what she said others did to her. Taking those statements seriously brings us closer to understanding what happened to her.

articles.title: The UK shouldn’t worry about taxing big companies that threaten to leave
articles.summary:
Actium/Shutterstock

There are huge companies making vast amounts of money in the UK. And some of those firms pay very little tax on the money they make.

This makes some people angry. It seems unfair, after all, that a company the size of Starbucks – worth over US$100 billion (£75 billion) – paid no corporation tax in the UK last year. Or the year before that.

Research suggests that some companies manage to do this by using a variety of clever strategies (not readily available to smaller firms) that help them to legally shift profits out of countries with higher tax rates to countries with lower tax rates.

In theory, each of these complex arrangements could be forensically examined by the UK’s tax authorities.

But doing so in practice would be a considerable burden in terms of scrutiny and enforcement. There could also be time-consuming appeals processes and legal challenges.

An international approach is also problematic. One country imposing a tax on global profits raises difficulties for tax authorities in confirming the veracity of international declared accounts.

But if the UK really wanted to do something about international firms paying zero (or nearly zero) corporation tax, there are options.

What if, for example, the tax authority charged Starbucks a flat, minimum level of corporation tax per outlet based on what comparable domestic businesses in the area pay?

If Starbucks chose to close stores rather than pay up, this would be fine.

The coffee shop market is a popular one, or in economic terms, “highly contestable”. So if Starbucks decided to abandon its branch on your local high street, another coffee shop – let’s call it “Moonpounds” – is likely to step in.

And while there may be dedicated fans of Starbucks coffee, there are others who are not, and who would happily spend their money at other coffee chains, or indeed independent coffee shops.

Moonpounds would retain jobs and contribute more effectively to the local economy and tax base – and not channel profits abroad.

The idea here is that whether or not a particular multinational corporation continues operating in the country should be of no interest to the tax authority, which should respond to threats with a shrug. It’s an approach to taxation one might term “existential indifference”.

Under a principle of existential indifference, threats of ceasing trading should be ignored. Similarly, impassioned defences based on job losses and VAT receipts to the exchequer should be ignored as jobs and VAT receipts would also be provided by new market entrants.

This means that there are many potential new entrant businesses that could easily replace a given Starbucks cafe if it closed. They would routinely be contributing more to the vibrancy of the local economy and the UK exchequer.

Supported by Smith?

The same theory applies to many other big businesses.

Delivering items to people’s homes is another highly contestable market. And there are plenty of tech companies that would be happy to help with your internet searches. The same goes for cloud data storage or app sales.

For many of these services provided by large companies, there are plenty of potential new entrants and competitors who would be happy to take over.

The idea of pushing taxes on big firms who employ lots of people can sometimes be seen as anti-business or anti-growth. But the idea of fairness in the corporate world was something that past economic thinkers encouraged.

In the 18th century, for example, Adam Smith, the “father of economics”, was not an advocate of taxing profits. Yet he was also not in favour of tax outcomes causing persistent income or revenue inequality.

Cafes are poplular.
Indran5/Shutterstock

In the 20th century, John Maynard Keynes primarily viewed corporation tax as just one lever of fiscal policy to be increased or decreased depending on the stage of the economic cycle. He also viewed taxation as an appropriate response to excess profits.

Economic thought on taxing the profits of big international companies has now evolved to the position where even the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) actively promotes a minimum corporation tax rate (15%) to stop multinational companies from shifting profits to low-tax havens and to try to obstruct the competitive lowering (or race to the bottom) of tax rates among countries.

The OECD appears to support the idea that effective and fairer corporation taxes can be designed with sufficient political will. And that political will should not be weakened by the worry that some international firms will leave along the way.

Alan Collins has previously received funding from various grant providing bodies including the Economic and Social Research Council, Engineering and Physical Science Research Council and the European Commission. He is a very passive member of the Labour Party.

articles.title: Acupuncture-like treatment linked to sustained weight loss in new study
articles.summary:
Andrey_Popov/Shutterstock.com

A form of acupuncture that leaves dissolvable threads under the skin may help people lose weight, a small trial in China suggests.

Women who received the treatment lost about 2kg more, on average, than those given a sham treatment after 12 weeks. By 24 weeks, the difference had grown to about 3kg.

The technique is called acupoint thread embedding. Acupuncturists use fine needles to insert absorbable threads into chosen points on the body.

They check that the points are being stimulated by looking for a particular needle sensation, known as de qi. The 1–2cm threads then dissolve over several weeks. Until they do, they keep stimulating the points.

In standard acupuncture, needles go into the same points and produce the same sensation. But they come out at the end of each session.

That means thread embedding may have longer-lasting effects. It could also mean fewer, less frequent treatments for patients, although the study didn’t test for these things.

The study was published in the Annals of Internal Medicine. It randomly assigned 132 women to either the real treatment or a sham one.

Experienced acupuncturists, specially trained for the study, gave six sessions over 12 weeks. The threads were made of a biodegradable material called polydioxanone. They were inserted 2–4cm deep.

The sham treatment took place in the same setting. The same acupuncturists used the same type of needles at the same points. But the needles went in only 1cm, so the de qi sensation – an aching or tingling – was not triggered and no threads were used.

This allowed the researchers to rule out other explanations. These include light stimulation of the points, the practitioner–patient relationship and patients’ expectations, known as the placebo effect.

It seems to have been convincing. The women did not know which treatment they had received. So the difference in results can be put down to the threads.

The staff measuring the results and the statisticians didn’t know either, which helps to reduce bias.

Women were measured at the start, at 12 weeks (the end of treatment) and at 24 weeks. Researchers tracked weight, body mass index (BMI), waist and hip size, body fat, heart and metabolic health, and self-reported measures such as appetite.

As well as losing 2–3kg more, women who had the real treatment saw bigger drops in BMI, waist and hip size, body fat and self-reported appetite. Together, these give a fuller picture, because several measures are needed to judge weight-related health.

Weight loss was sustained for 12 weeks after the treatment ended.
Ahmet Misirligul/Shutterstock.com

Some measures changed similarly in both groups. Compared with the sham treatment, the threads made no difference to cholesterol or fasting blood sugar. Nor did they affect anxiety, wellbeing or weight-related quality of life.

Side-effects such as bruising or pain at acupuncture points and the number of women leaving the study were also similar in both groups. But larger studies are needed to spot rare side-effects.

The researchers reached their planned number of participants. But 132 women was too few to test whether the treatment works differently in different groups. For example, does it work better for women who start at a higher weight?

The women were Chinese, aged 18 to 45, generally healthy, and were overweight with a BMI of at least 24 at the start. While in the UK a BMI of at least 25 is considered overweight, in China a BMI of 24 counts as overweight because the effect of BMI on health varies by ethnicity.

The study cannot say what the threads do for men, women over 45 or under-18s.

It also cannot say how the threads led to weight loss. Women who had them reported a bigger drop in appetite. That suggests changes in eating habits might partly explain the result.

But the researchers didn’t measure food intake or energy burned. So we don’t know whether a smaller appetite meant eating less, or whether something else was going on.

Will the weight stay off?

The weight loss lasted for 12 weeks after the 12-week course ended. But, as many people know from experience, losing weight is hard and keeping it off is harder.

Most people regain weight in the months and years after behaviour-change programmes, weight-loss drugs and other treatments. People who lose more weight tend to regain more, and faster. Regular support from health professionals can soften this. Thread embedding may offer a new approach to this problem.

Larger studies should test other groups of people and look at longer periods. They should also check whether top-up treatments are needed.

They should also compare the costs and benefits with treatments recommended in official guidelines.

The answers could help health services decide whether to offer acupoint thread embedding.

Flis Bishop has received speaker's fees from the British Acupuncture Council and has received grant funding for projects related to acupuncture from the NIHR and Arthritis Research.

articles.title: Jensen Huang scandal illustrates why human nature is cybersecurity’s weakest link
articles.summary:
Huang is hardly the first powerful person to lower their defenses. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

The end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony. The chief executive of a company whose growth has been propelled by the seemingly unstoppable rise of artificial intelligence was brought down by a vulnerability that no algorithm can eliminate: human nature.

Huang’s resignation from the chipmaker he co-founded followed reports of multiple affairs, most notably one with Alice Huang, a business executive whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The company says no secrets were leaked.

In a world increasingly focused on protecting private information against high-tech hacking schemes, Huang’s downfall is a reminder that, as the infamous hacker Kevin Mitnick observed, the “human factor is truly security’s weakest link.”

Huang is hardly the first person in a powerful position to lower their defenses. In 2023, Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni spoke candidly about foreign affairs in a call with Russian pranksters who recorded and released the conversation. In 2011, former CIA Director David Petraeus gave his biographer, with whom he was having an affair, access to notebooks containing classified information.

These cases raise an important question: Why would someone with an entire security apparatus at their disposal let their guard down in an ordinary conversation or an intimate moment?

Part of the answer comes down to the ways in which we are wired to react to other human beings. As a social psychologist who studies how people respond to requests, I’ve seen how a human voice, a simple touch or the mere physical presence of another person can be persuasive. Social cues that increase a sense of familiarity and intimacy can make people feel safer, more trusting – and more willing to hand over money, comply with requests, divulge information or take risks.

The comfort of a human voice

Mitnick has been called “the most notorious hacker of all time.” Until his arrest in 1995, he spent years gaining access to privileged information at companies such as Nokia and Motorola. He pulled off his espionage not by writing sophisticated code-breaking software but by having conversations with his targets.

He would call people up and talk them into handing over their passwords by claiming to be the new IT guy or someone’s boss’s colleague. The people he spoke to overwhelmingly believed him.

In other words, Mitnick recognized the power of the human voice.

Studies show that hearing a person’s voice, as compared to reading their written thoughts, makes that person seem more capable and relatable. Interactions via phone, video chat and voice chat also create stronger social bonds than the same kinds of interactions via text or email.

Perhaps for these reasons, people are more effective at persuading others to do things for them over the phone compared to when they make the same requests by text. In a study I conducted with social psychologist Mahdi Roghanizad, participants asked other people for favors through randomly assigned communication channels. They received about twice as many “yes” responses over the phone as they did by email.

When it comes to obtaining company secrets or circumventing export laws, a human voice may be all you need. And that isn’t the only edge people have.

The Midas touch

Studies have found that human touch can also have surprising effects on tipping behavior, acquiescence and risk-taking.

In a famous 1984 study, a server who lightly touched diners as she handed them their change received bigger tips. In another classic psychology study, female experimenters approached 178 strangers and asked them for change to use a nearby pay phone. When the experimenters lightly touched the arm of a person they approached, that person was 76% more likely to agree to give the change.

The researchers theorized that these light touches created a sense of familiarity. That familiarity, in turn, made people more willing to open their wallets.

Other research suggests that light touch can also make people feel safer and more willing to take risks. In a 2010 study, participants were more willing to take financial risks when a female experimenter gave them a light, comforting pat on their shoulder.

A reassuring touch can make people more generous and more willing to take risks.
abezikus/iStock via Getty Images

The power of face-to-face

Perhaps the most well-known study of influence, Stanley Milgram’s infamous shock experiment, illustrates how much it can matter to be in the room when you ask someone to do something they may be feeling uneasy about.

In the original study, an experimenter stood behind participants and instructed them to administer purportedly dangerous shocks to someone they thought was just another participant. The experimenter asked participants to incrementally increase the intensity of the shocks. Nearly two-thirds of participants went all the way to the highest shock setting. In a variation of the study, however, the experimenter left the room and gave instructions over the phone. In this version, only 22.5% went that far.

Although researchers continue to debate how to interpret Milgram’s findings, my colleagues and I have similarly found that people are far more likely to say yes when we ask them to do something face-to-face.

In one study, participants who made requests in person were 34 times more likely to get a yes than those who made requests by email. In another study, in-person requests were significantly more effective than requests made over the phone or video call.

Cyberattacks and phishing emails pose real threats to security. But sometimes the biggest threats come from the people in the room with you. While we don’t know exactly what transpired between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, her proximity to the Nvidia CEO illustrates a vulnerability that even the best cybersecurity measures can struggle to guard against.

articles.title: Fighting in Yemen has made crossing the Bab el-Mandeb even more dangerous – jeopardizing aid and refuge for millions
articles.summary:
In recent days, Iran-backed Houthi forces have gained greater control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital hub of trade, travel and migration between the Middle East and Africa.

The partial closing of the Strait of Hormuz as part of the war in Iran – and escalating conflicts in Yemen, Ethiopia and Eritrea – had already brought this narrow waterway into new global prominence. Control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains critical to military operations and commodity markets throughout the region.

However, the Bab el-Mandeb’s strategic geopolitical and commercial shipping importance has largely overshadowed its role as a critical humanitarian corridor.

Bab el-Mandeb means “gate of lamentation” or, more poetically, “gate of tears” in Arabic. It remains one of the most dangerous migration passages in the world. Last year, more than 900 people died or went missing trying to cross. In October 2026, a boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti carrying nearly 300 people, many of whom were escaping violence and persecution.

Meanwhile, millions of people in Yemen and throughout the Horn of Africa face destitution or death without access to lifesaving deliveries of humanitarian relief supplies shipped through the strait.

Our years of research and forthcoming book “Refugees Without Refuge” demonstrate how the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is key to the lives of millions of people throughout the region seeking safety, opportunity and humanitarian assistance. Protecting the safe movement of people and goods through the strait is key to averting future tragedies.

A corridor for travel, trade and escape

Located at the southern mouth of the Red Sea, between the arid coastlines of Eritrea, Djibouti and Yemen, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait connects the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and Suez Canal. On a clear day along the wide beaches and mangrove forests on the coast of Djibouti, you can see the sandy hills on the shores of Yemen, only about 20 to 30 miles away. On starry nights, the scattered lights of coastal towns twinkle across the waters.

For centuries, passage through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has been vital to global trade in salt, spices, coffee, livestock and other goods. Religious pilgrims, travelers, migrants and traders have long used the strait for relatively easy transport between continents.

Today, people crossing the strait are also escaping poverty, war, political persecution, disasters and gender-based violence.

Hot, tired, financially depleted and frequently sick or injured, refugees and migrants traverse the Bab el-Mandeb at all hours.

Most negotiate passage across the strait on derelict boats with “delalas” – facilitators, brokers or smugglers – in the shadows of coast guard and police patrols and outside United Nations and governmental migration controls.

The numbers of people crossing the strait are difficult to estimate. Between January and August 2026, the U.N.’s International Organization for Migration recorded 122,258 arrivals to Yemen from the Horn of Africa – even more than had crossed by that time in 2025. Most of these migrants were from Ethiopia, and most traveled without passports or visas.

Since August, displacement and insecurity throughout the region has worsened, making accurate figures for the numbers of people migrating and the numbers of people dying trying to cross impossible to estimate.

A lifeline for those escaping conflict

Despite the dangers of this crossing, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains an economic lifeline for millions of people living in Ethiopia, Kenya, Somaliland, Somalia and elsewhere who rely on commercial goods imported from the Middle East and Asia. However, the Houthi forces in charge of increasing swaths of southwestern Yemen now control most critical ports and islands in the strait, increasing the risks and costs of transit and trade.

The strait has either been closed or has become a bottleneck, allowing only limited shipping traffic since September 2026. Many cargo ships have been delayed or rerouted, causing businesses in fragile regional economies to pass higher transport and fuel costs on to their customers.

The economic effects of costly and delayed shipping and trade through the strait has compounded the broader effects of increased violence and displacement throughout the region. In front of the U.N. General Assembly on Sept. 26, 2026, Djibouti foreign minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar expressed “grave concern” about the sudden influx of Yemeni refugees putting a strain on underresourced coastal towns and refugee camps. The United Nations relief agency, UNHCR, is reporting an outbreak of cholera in the Markazi refugee camp, the primary home to thousands of Yemenis who have fled across the strait into northern Djibouti.

Members of the Djiboutian coast guard inspect boats seized from ‘delalas’ attempting to transport migrants to Yemen on April 12, 2026.
Luis Tato/AFP via Getty Images

On top of that, the potential for a return to civil war in Ethiopia, and the potential involvement of Eritrea in regional conflicts, may increase population displacement and further disrupt economic markets on both sides of the strait.

As each of these conflicts unfolds, additional pressure will likely be put on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. It provides the only feasible passage for many people seeking safety and opportunity abroad.

A humanitarian corridor

Keeping the Bab el-Mandeb open and safe is also vital for the delivery of humanitarian aid. Like challenges of commercial shipping, the maritime transit of relief supplies, including food and medicine, has been undermined by security risks, shipping delays and the rising costs of food and fuel.

UNICEF’s latest situation report for Somalia, published in August 2026, estimates that nearly 5 million people there are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance. At least another 5.5 million people in Ethiopia are also in need, due to the effects of conflict combined with below-average rainfall linked to El Niño.

In Yemen, an estimated 321,000 people have been displaced since Aug. 1, 2026, and ongoing water scarcity combined with conflict has left 17 million people without access to clean water, sanitation and hygiene services. As casualties mount and cholera spreads, hospitals have struggled to obtain essential supplies.

The Bab el-Mandeb Strait sits at the center of all of these crises. It remains a vital human and humanitarian corridor for millions of people needing refuge and relief. It is a lifeline as much as a geopolitical and economic linchpin.

Ensuring the safe passage of people and supplies of humanitarian relief through these waters is necessary to save lives and protect precarious livelihoods throughout the region.

Lauren Carruth has received funding from the National Science Foundation, the National Institutes of Health, the Russell Sage Foundation, the International Organization for Migration, and American University.

Lahra Smith has received funding from the Henry Luce Foundation, the National Science Foundation, Fulbright, National Endowment for the Humanities and Georgetown University.

articles.title: An atlas of vanished places: how climate change is rewriting the books on our shelves
articles.summary:
Pavel L Photo and Video/Shutterstock

On August 26, 2026, a huge mass of rock and ice broke away at an altitude of around 5,200 metres in the Himalayas. Within minutes, it became an avalanche of debris and water that hurtled down towards the Nepal-Tibet border, with such force that the seismic signals were initially mistaken for an earthquake.

The region’s glaciers are visibly retreating, and thawing permafrost may well have contributed to destabilising these Himalayan slopes. Above all, the Nepal landslide illustrates something that will only become increasingly familiar: places that appear stable can change almost without warning.

While events like the Nepal landslide have an immediate, devastating impact on the people who live in these environments, they also leave their mark in a less obvious sphere: literature.

Biologist Rachel Carson’s 1951 book The Sea Around Us reminded readers that the boundary between land and sea has never been stable. Throughout our planet’s very long history, the oceans have advanced and receded. What makes the current situation exceptional is the speed of this transformation, as well as human activity’s decisive contribution to it.

Rising sea levels are one of its most visible manifestations. Since 1993, the global average sea level has risen by around ten centimetres.

And when a landscape changes, it also changes the world depicted in books. One scene from Lore Segal’s 2013 Half the Kingdom, for instance, takes place on a Brooklyn beach that a reader in the not-too-distant future might find submerged.

Philip Hoare’s The Sea Inside, also from 2013, explores coastal areas from England to Sri Lanka that may soon be underwater. The sandbanks of the Java Sea, where Joseph Conrad set his 1912 novel Freya of the Seven Isles, may have already been swallowed by rising sea levels.

When the landscape changes, these works all stay the same. Instead it is we, as readers, who change.

Leer más:
Three things historical literature can teach us about the climate crisis

Reading from the future

The field of comparative literature has long been exploring how works take on new meanings as they circulate across eras and cultures. Climate change adds an unexpected dimension to this problem: the future can also influence the history of a work.

In 1888, Theodor Storm published The Rider on the White Horse. The novella’s protagonist, Hauke Haien, studies geometry and applies his knowledge to the construction of new dykes on Germany’s North Sea coast, convinced that they will stand for centuries. A major flood tests both Haien’s engineering feat, and humanity’s confidence in our ability to master the sea.

The Thwaites glacier, in the eastern Antarctic, is shrinking fast, and is losing significant amounts of ice.
NASA/James Yungel, CC BY-SA

Storm, of course, was writing before global warming, but today we – unlike the author and his original readers – know that the conditions that determine the behaviour of coastlines are changing. This allows us to read his story differently today. Not because we have discovered what Storm “really meant”, but because we are reading it from a different future.

An unexpected atlas

Something even stranger can happen with the settings of literary works. Texts that we used to see as realistic might start to seem fantastical to us because they describe landscapes that no longer exist. And some works of fantasy might go the other way.

In Edgar Allen Poe’s only novel, 1838’s The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket, the author imagined a temperate region in Antarctica. When the book was published, it was a fantastical vision, but how will someone a hundred years from now interpret it?

Leer más:
The Antarctic ice sheet is melting. And this is bad news for humanity

Part of our library could thus become, without changing a single word, an unwitting atlas of vanished places. This is what lies at the heart of my research on literature, oceans and climate change.

Books do not predict the future, nor can they replace climatology, glaciology or oceanography. They do something else: they preserve experiences of places, and connect timelines that no single human life can encompass. When the world changes, landscapes do not disappear from the page – they remain there, exactly as they were. What changes is the way we read them.

articles.title: Bond has always reflected the masculinity of his time – Robert Pattinson’s 007 will need to embody a new era
articles.summary:
James Bond has always reflected the cultural anxieties and zeitgeist of his era.

Sean Connery’s Bond embodied the confident western post-second-world-war masculinity of the early cold war. George Lazenby brought the character’s emotional vulnerability to light, reflecting the upheavals of the late 1960s. Roger Moore’s performance, meanwhile, added camp humour, theatricality and escapism in the 1970s.

In keeping with Ian Fleming’s more psychologically complex literary creation, Timothy Dalton brought a darker, more ruthless Bond to the screen. Stripping away much of the Moore era’s comedy and camp, his portrayal foregrounded emotional intensity and moral ambiguity. This reflected late-cold-war anxieties as geopolitical certainties unravelled and new threats emerged.

Next up, Pierce Brosnan incarnated a glamorous post-cold-war masculinity, with his lingering sexism teased out by Samantha Bond’s witty Moneypenny and the disruptive casting of Judi Dench as M, the head of MI6. And in the 2000s, Daniel Craig’s Bond was a physically tough but emotionally vulnerable character. His wounded body and scarred mind linked emotional detachment to childhood trauma.

Pattinson’s career

Pattinson’s acting credentials make him one of the most established actors to take on the role. Since the Twilight saga (2008-2012), he has grown to be among the more versatile actors of his generation, with a penchant for challenging, often downright strange roles.

From the psychological intensity of Good Time (2017) to Robert Eggers’s claustrophobic gothic The Lighthouse (2018), the characters he has played are anything but straightforward leading men. Even when turning to action, his Batman (2022) was unexpectedly brooding and introspective.

There is certainly scope with his casting to extend the darker vision of Bond first introduced by Dalton and subsequently developed by Craig.

Visually, too, Pattinson seems almost a composite of previous Bonds. Declared the world’s most handsome man in 2020, Pattinson has the chiselled good looks of Brosnan. Although he might not have Connery’s physique, the intense training he underwent for Batman suggests that he could manage the demanding physical aspects of the role. This, however, may be more challenging, given that Pattinson, at 40, is already ten years older than former producer Barbara Broccoli had anticipated the next Bond would be in 2024.

Pattinson’s Bond

As a white Englishman whose image is associated with an upper-middle-class, heterosexual masculinity, Pattinson might seem a safe, even predictable, choice for Bond. And yet, he is not unfamiliar with the challenge of portraying unconventional masculinity.

In Little Ashes (2008), he explored the young Salvador Dalí’s intimate relationship with the poet Federico García Lorca. Much like Craig, he has shown himself willing to explore queer desire and the instability of masculine identity.

I think what Craig’s era could have done more with is humour, and Pattinson might well bring a fresh comic sensibility to the next incarnation of Bond.

Beneath his often brooding intensity lies a nuanced comic performer. Humour has allowed Pattinson to question conventional masculinity in some of his roles. In Damsel (2018), he challenged the traditional western hero by playing an inept cowboy whose masculine confidence far exceeded his capabilities. Elsewhere, his darkly camp rendition of Louis the Dauphin in The King (2019), the tragi-comic The Drama (2026) and the self-aware short Fear & Shame (2017) all seemingly serve to undermine male vanity.

Perhaps Pattinson’s history of darkly strange and funny characters will create space for this new Bond to, playfully or otherwise, explore our current preoccupations with toxic masculinity, sexual consent and male vulnerability.

Fleming thought of his secret agent as an “unobtrusive … neutral figure – an anonymous blunt instrument”. Screenwriter Steven Knight now faces the challenge of using Bond as a blank canvas to highlight the clash between the character’s traditional roots and modern culture.

Read more:
I write James Bond novels – here’s why Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight will bring a crackling new intensity to 007

In particular, the new Bond would benefit from a more diverse supporting cast whose backgrounds are woven naturally into the story, reflecting his global audience without feeling forced.

I’m thinking female characters not defined by their relationships with Bond, villains who call out Bond’s elitism, queer characters that could complicate his seemingly straight world. Bond girls and villains will play a crucial role in delivering these (or failing to do so). But it will be Pattinson and his choices for this iconic character at the centre of it all, deciding whether the franchise will sink or swim.

Monica Germanà does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Dunkelflaute: why cloudy, windless weather is a challenge for power networks that rely on renewables
articles.summary:
T.W. van Urk / shutterstock

In early November 2024, a large mass of still, cloudy, cold air settled over much of north-west Europe. For much of a week, wind turbines barely moved and the output from solar farms was negligible. In some areas, cold temperatures meant people needed extra electricity to heat their homes.

Something similar happened on a smaller scale in early November 2026, when low wind-power generation across Europe left the UK scrambling for extra electricity. These are examples of a so-called dunkelflaute, German for “dark doldrums”, a weather-related challenge for electricity systems as they become increasingly reliant on renewables. Wind and solar generation now accounts for more than a third of the electricity produced in Great Britain, for example, from a baseline of almost nothing just 20 years ago. This shift is central to efforts to reach net zero, and will play a key role in decarbonising other sectors such as heating and transport.

The introduction of large amounts of weather-sensitive generation has created new challenges for power-system operators. A central concept within this is “balancing” – the need to ensure the supply of and demand for electricity match in near real-time.

This used to be relatively simple. When demand increased, power plants would burn more coal or gas. These days, maintaining balance can be extremely challenging in periods of unfavourable weather conditions and, if left unchecked, mismatches in supply and demand could quickly spiral into disconnections and blackouts.

Putting power systems under pressure

A dunkelflaute is usually associated with high-pressure weather systems over north-western Europe. As these move slowly and cover large areas, their effects can persist across several countries for days at a time, reducing the availability of wind and solar power simultaneously.

In winter, these high-pressure systems are typically associated with colder temperatures in northern Europe, thereby driving up the demand for electricity. This combination of reduced renewable generation and higher demand puts individual power systems under strain.

The overall impact is exacerbated when neighbouring countries experience the same conditions at the same time, limiting opportunities to import electricity to compensate. As these events can last several days, electricity storage can become depleted – particularly given that current storage capacity is typically designed to provide power for several hours at most.

Thick clouds can mean a solar farm generates just 10% of the electricity it would produce in sunshine.
sorao -yamao / shutterstock

How electricity systems can cope

Power systems can cope with dunkelflaute conditions in several ways. At present, as many countries are still transitioning away from fossil fuels, a common approach has been to use existing power stations as a backup.

Gas power stations, for example, can adjust their output relatively quickly to match changes in demand and renewable generation. This makes them a convenient way to maintain supply during a dunkelflaute, though it can be expensive, especially when the supply-demand balancing act is very tight. The UK National Energy System Operator’s Clean Power 2030 advice proposes keeping around 35GW of gas power to provide backup when renewable generation is low.

In the longer term, power-system operators and planners may seek to make electricity systems more flexible, reducing the need to match generation and demand instantaneously. Several measures can help to do this, and some are already in use.

Electricity use can be shifted to times when the weather is favourable, for instance, perhaps by offering lower prices during windy or sunny days. Strengthening transmission connections within and between countries also helps to make better use of regional differences in renewable generation and electricity demand.

Building more electricity storage could also help absorb surplus generated electricity and release it when supplies are low, from large batteries to alternatives such as pumped storage hydropower which works by moving water between two reservoirs. Linking electricity systems with other forms of energy use could help here. For example, excess electricity could be used to produce hydrogen, which can then be stored and used as a fuel.

Understanding the severity, geographical extent and duration of dunkelflaute conditions, and the extent to which they may affect electricity supplies, is therefore an important challenge, both in the present and under a changing climate.

However, it is worth remembering that dunkelflaute periods were only identified as a significant risk to power systems because of the growing reliance on wind and solar energy. Before these technologies became widespread, few would have considered these otherwise benign conditions to be a weather hazard compared to more familiar threats such as flooding or storms.

This underlines the importance of being alert to emerging weather risks as energy systems evolve, and for more collaboration between energy and climate researchers. This collaboration will be essential to managing weather risks as renewable energy becomes the norm and the climate keeps changing.

David Brayshaw has worked on research projects with a variety of funders, including UKRI NERC, the UK government, and the energy industry.  He is currently seconded part-time as an advisor to Ofgem.  Any views he expresses are as an independent researcher at the University of Reading.

articles.title: Burundi’s refugees are under pressure to return: why some choose silence when they do
articles.summary:
Burundi has experienced repeated cycles of political violence and displacement, notably following the assassination of President Melchior Ndadayé in 1993. Further unrest followed during an election-related political crisis in 2015.

These cycles of unrest have resulted in thousands of deaths and forced hundreds of thousands of Burundians to flee their country. Over the past two decades, more than 1.1 million have sought refuge in other countries, primarily in neighbouring Tanzania. Others have fled to Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and further.

There’s growing pressure from the Burundian state, as well as from neighbouring host countries, including Tanzania, Uganda and Kenya, to encourage repatriation. This reflects a broader regional shift in which the continued presence of Burundian refugees outside their country is becoming increasingly conditional.

Indeed, under international initiatives led by the UN refugee agency, Burundi has established a formal policy framework for repatriation. But return to contexts of forced displacement, violence and other forms of persecution has prompted questions about whether it can work and how it is experienced by those who return.

My doctoral research examines the governance of return migration, specifically its long-term implications for returnees. In a recent article, I explore the experience of Burundian returnees, drawing on 23 interviews with returnees, focus group discussions, and participant observation conducted in Burundi in 2024 and 2025.

My research shows that return to “post-crisis” Burundi is much more than a physical or administrative process. It is a politicised action within the country’s history of conflicts and repeated displacement. I found that returnees were typically evasive about life in exile and chose their words carefully, so as not to give away too much about themselves.

Their silence proposes, in its own way, an alternative account of return. It is an account that unsettles official narratives of “successful” return, reintegration and stability, and insists on the unresolved tensions that continue to structure life in Burundi.

Return by all means

Voluntary repatriation has been on Burundi’s policy agenda for decades. Burundi and Tanzania first agreed to a tripartite mechanism for refugee repatriation in 1998, with the support of the UN. The agreement has since been reactivated, most recently in December 2025. Between January and August 2026 alone, 96,602 refugees returned from Tanzania, and Nduta and Nyarugusu refugee camps were progressively closed.

Officials on both sides have portrayed this “acceleration” of return as a success story. Burundian authorities have repeatedly framed returns as evidence of restored stability, constructing the country as a “safe zone” to reinforce its political legitimacy.

In practice, however, return has been shaped less by voluntariness than by a combination of incentives and constraints. In Tanzania, authorities have taken measures to deter new arrivals and encourage refugee returns. They have reduced humanitarian aid, limited access to healthcare and education, and carried out forced repatriation. This questions the character of these “voluntary” returns, and highlights their coercive nature.

Several factors complicate the prospect of return as a lasting solution, including:

a severe economic crisis

limited access to employment, housing and essential services

concerns about deteriorating human rights

the possibility of renewed displacement.

Return under a political cloud

My paper draws on field research in two sites: the borderland province of Muyinga, one of Burundi’s largest return destinations; and Bujumbura Mairie, the capital.

Interviews reveal that return has become more politically charged, particularly since the 2015 political crisis, which triggered renewed displacement and intensified political repression. Returnees affiliated with opposition movements or particular ethnic factions may attract suspicion or surveillance and face fears for their safety, depending on where and when they were exiled.

My research shows how silence provides space to navigate life upon return.

Some returnees were evasive, carefully managing who to tell about their displacement, and who not to tell. One returnee confided his 2015 flight to a Tutsi friend while in exile, but swore him to secrecy, while avoiding the subject entirely with fellow Hutus. He felt they might ask why he left “when we stayed to defend our country”.

For some, perceptions were informed less by who they were than by where they had been. They recalled that those who stayed behind could never be sure whether returnees had come back as “the Burundians they had once known”, or had returned changed, implicated in rebellion or sent back to destabilise the country.

Others described forms of concealment centred on identity. One second-generation returnee adjusted her own accent so that she wouldn’t sound like an outsider.

These forms of silence are about navigating political uncertainty and negotiating a place within an evolving social and political order.

Silence, in this sense, can itself be a form of political agency. In selecting what aspects of their experience to disclose, to whom, and in what context, returnees are not simply protecting themselves. They are shaping the terms on which their experience enters public life at all.

Understanding post-return

The experiences of Burundian returnees show that silence is not simply an absence of speech, but an active practice through which experiences of displacement are continuously negotiated.

As more refugees are encouraged, pressured or compelled to return, understanding these post-return experiences becomes ever more important to help inform more realistic and responsive approaches to return.

It matters for understanding the social and political conditions returnees encounter, but also the decisions they continue to face – whether to stay or to move again.

Nina Soudan receives funding from the Research Foundation Flanders (FWO).

articles.title: Five things that shape body weight – by an obesity expert
articles.summary:
Dikushin Dmitry/Shutterstock

What you eat when you’re tired and hungry might come down to what’s open on the way home and what you can afford. Both appetite and access to food shape decisions that can look, from the outside, like simple matters of choice.

The World Health Organization describes obesity as a chronic disease shaped by the interaction between biology and the conditions people live in. In my new book, Obesity: Life Beyond the GLP-1 Injection, I look at what shapes body weight and what that means for treatment and prevention. Here are five findings that informed the book.

1. Losing weight can make you hungrier

In one study, adults who lost weight on a very low-calorie diet still reported feeling hungrier a year after the diet ended than they had before it began. Their levels of leptin, a hormone that helps tell the brain how much energy the body has stored, were still lower than before the diet.

A lighter body takes less energy to maintain and move. A review of studies found that energy use can sometimes fall even further than you’d expect for a person’s new weight. This extra drop tended to be smaller in better-designed studies and could fade once weight stabilised.

That leaves some people trying to manage stronger feelings of hunger at a time when their bodies need fewer calories. It helps explain why keeping weight off can be difficult even when someone is still making a deliberate effort.

2. Genes influence appetite

Some of the differences in body weight between people come from the genes they inherit. In rare cases, a change in a single gene can cause severe obesity in early childhood. More often, many genetic differences each contribute a little. Studies of both patterns point to the parts of the brain involved in appetite, which helps explain why some people may feel full sooner than others.

In a Norwegian study, researchers used DNA to group people by their inherited tendency to have a higher body mass index, or BMI, a measure of weight relative to height. Over several decades, average BMI rose across the groups, with a bigger rise among those with the strongest genetic tendency.

The rise across groups points to changes in the conditions people lived in. The bigger rise in some groups suggests that the same changes can affect people differently.

3. Sleeping less can make you eat more

A review of experiments found that people tended to eat more when their sleep was cut short. There was much less evidence that cutting sleep changed how many calories they burned.

Researchers then tested what happened when people who usually slept less than six and a half hours a night got more sleep. In a two-week trial of 80 adults with overweight, one group received advice tailored to their sleep habits and the other kept its usual routine.

Those given advice slept about an hour longer and took in about 270 fewer calories a day, on average, compared with the other group. Both groups were free to choose what they ate. Whether the difference in calorie intake lasts is still unclear, and keeping regular sleep hours can be difficult for people who work nights or care for someone.

4. Semaglutide can lower the risk of serious heart problems and stroke

Semaglutide mimics GLP-1, a hormone that helps regulate appetite. The medicine can help people feel fuller and less hungry.

In a large trial of adults with existing heart or circulation problems and overweight or obesity, none of whom had diabetes, researchers compared semaglutide with a placebo, an injection with no active drug. Over an average of just over three years, 65 in every 1,000 people on semaglutide died from cardiovascular causes or had a non-fatal heart attack or stroke, compared with 80 in every 1,000 on the placebo. About 17 in every 100 people taking semaglutide stopped because of side effects, compared with eight in every 100 taking the placebo.

A separate study followed people for a year after their semaglutide and lifestyle support ended. On average, they regained about two-thirds of the weight they had lost. People who stop taking the medicine may still need support to manage their weight.

5. Food policy can change what’s on offer

In a hospital study, the same 20 adults spent two weeks on a diet high in ultra-processed foods and two weeks on a diet based on unprocessed foods. They could eat as much or as little as they wanted. They ate about 500 more calories a day on the ultra-processed diet and ate those meals faster. Eating speed is one possible explanation for the difference, and the study shows how much the food on offer can affect what people eat even when they decide their own portions.

The UK’s soft drinks levy gave manufacturers a reason to change their recipes: using less sugar could reduce or avoid the charge. An analysis of English school measurements found that after the levy came into effect, there were about 16 fewer cases of obesity per 1,000 girls aged 10 and 11 than researchers would have expected if earlier trends had continued. Researchers found no overall reduction among boys of the same age or among children aged four and five. But other changes around the same time could have contributed to the result.

People living with obesity need access to effective treatment and long-term support. Governments can also help prevent obesity by changing how foods are made and marketed and by making nutritious food more affordable in the places people already shop.
